items.title: ROLE OF INSECTS IN AGRICULTURE AND ENVIRONMENT
items.abstract: Abstract: Insects are among the most ancient and successful organisms on Earth, having existed for over 400 million years. They form the most diverse group of living organisms, constituting more than 75% of all known animal species. Found in almost every habitat, insects play essential roles in agriculture, natural ecosystems, climate regulation, biodiversity maintenance, and food webs. Their interactions with plants, animals, and microorganisms create intricate ecological networks that support life on Earth. In the context of agriculture, insects occupy a unique dual position: they are both indispensable allies and challenging adversaries. Beneficial insects contribute to pollination, soil formation, nutrient cycling, and natural pest regulation, thereby facilitating sustainable agricultural productivity. Conversely, insect pests cause extensive crop losses, transmit plant diseases, and damage stored food, resulting in significant economic impacts globally. In an era of rapid climate change, land-use transformation, and pesticide overuse, the conservation and management of insect populations have become crucial. Understanding their ecological functions and integrating this knowledge into agricultural practices is a key step toward achieving sustainability, food security, and environmental resilience. Keywords: Environment, ecology, balance, ecosystem
authors: Neha Negi, Jag Mohan, Bharti Gautam, Babita Bharti and Ridhima Arya

items.title: Explaining Human Psychology Evolutionarily
items.abstract: Abstract Evolutionary psychology aims to fulfil Darwin’s vision—articulated towards the end of The Origin of Species— of providing a new foundation for the scientific study of human psychology. The field holds that human behavior should be explained using the same biological principles and empirical approaches applied to non-human animals, emphasizing how different evolutionary forces have influenced the functioning of their psychological mechanisms. Scholarly debate has long centered on issues such as adaptationism, testability, cognitive modularity, and the role of culture. More recently, however, evolutionary psychology has faced a new wave of critiques. These include that it presupposes, but cannot support, that human psychological mechanisms are “vertically homologous” with those of their ancestors; that it neglects several important evolutionary processes; that it relies on an outdated computationalist view of the mind; and that it does not yet satisfy the criteria for a mature, normal science. This article aims to present a balanced account of these emerging critiques, along with a set of original responses that, to date, have not been fully articulated in the literature. In general, we argue that the critiques involve unsound argumentation with false premises, attack a straw man position, are vulnerable to reductios , or rely on an implausible philosophical model of how scientific works ought to be evaluated.

items.title: Probable post-traumatic stress disorder after miscarriage: psychological, social, and healthcare-related factors in a mixed-methods study
items.abstract: Abstract Background: Miscarriage is commonly managed as a short-term obstetric condition, yet its psychological consequences may extend beyond physical recovery. This study aimed to estimate the prevalence of probable post-traumatic stress disorder (PTSD) after miscarriage and to examine psychological, social, and healthcare-related factors shaping PTSD symptom severity and recovery experiences. Methods: A theory-informed sequential mixed-methods study was conducted at the Post Abortion Care clinic of a tertiary Grade-A women’s and children’s hospital in Sichuan Province, China. In the quantitative phase, 293 women who had experienced miscarriage before 20 completed weeks of gestation completed a digital survey assessing PTSD symptoms, psychological resilience, perceived social support, rumination, coping style, distress disclosure, self-efficacy, anxiety, depression, and post-traumatic growth. Probable PTSD was defined as a Post-traumatic Stress Disorder Checklist–Civilian Version score of 38 or higher. Between-group comparisons, Spearman correlations, and hierarchical multivariable linear regression models were used. In the qualitative phase, nine women participated in semi-structured interviews, which were analyzed thematically and integrated with quantitative findings. Results: The mean PCL-C score was 33.5 ± 12.1, and 95 women (32.4%) screened positive for probable PTSD. Women with probable PTSD had lower psychological resilience than those without probable PTSD (55.4 ± 12.7 vs. 66.4 ± 16.4) and lower perceived social support (59.3 ± 14.0 vs. 66.3 ± 13.8). Higher resilience and perceived social support were associated with lower PTSD symptom severity, while intrusive rumination showed the strongest positive association. Hierarchical regression showed that sociodemographic and reproductive variables alone explained little variance in PTSD symptom severity (adjusted R² = 0.007), whereas adding healthcare-related, psychosocial, and psychological process variables increased explanatory power (adjusted R² = 0.161 and 0.538). Qualitative interviews identified four themes: self-regulation after miscarriage, partner and family support, social safety and stigma, and healthcare communication and care-process burden. These findings contextualized the quantitative associations and highlighted modifiable family, social, and health-service factors. Conclusions: Probable PTSD was common after miscarriage and was shaped by more than individual psychological vulnerability. Post-miscarriage care should move beyond procedure-centered management toward trauma-informed, partner- and family-sensitive, and patient-centered support that includes psychological screening, clear communication, stigma reduction, and attention to care-process burden.

items.title: Efektivitas Pengelolaan Sumber Daya Alam dalam Memenuhi Kebutuhan Ekonomi Masyarakat
items.abstract: Natural resource management is often assumed to improve community welfare, yet empirical evidence shows mixed outcomes. This article synthesizes research on natural resource management in forestry, fisheries, mangroves, and related sectors, internationally and in Indonesia, to assess how far such management meets the economic needs of communities. Using a library research approach, it synthesizes 29 scholarly journal articles through thematic grouping and interprets the findings with economic concepts such as property rights, scarcity, opportunity cost, externalities, and benefit distribution. The findings show that natural resources contribute roughly 22–38% of rural and coastal household income, and that various management schemes are reported to raise income or food security by 18–45%. However, Indonesian studies indicate that abundant resources do not automatically generate stable income, owing to land tenure problems, weak coordination and regulatory enforcement, pollution, and technological constraints. Management effectiveness should be assessed across four dimensions: economic, ecological, equity, and institutional. Policies should recognize community management rights, strengthen regulatory implementation, and provide alternative livelihoods when resource use is restricted

items.title: From intracellular force maps to organelle and organism physiology.
items.abstract: The mechanical properties of the cell interior are heterogeneous, varying across components and compartments according to function, location and time. However, many current mechanical models of the cell do not fully reflect this, either treating the cell as a simplified isotropic mechanical continuum or focusing on complex mechanics of isolated cellular structures, leaving the integration of mechanical features at cellular-to-tissue levels unresolved. To link mechanics with biological function, complete, spatially and temporally resolved maps of subcellular to mesoscopic mechanical properties in living systems and organisms are needed. Despite major technical advances in mechanobiology over the past decade, only snapshots of these heterogenous material properties have been obtained. Crucially, the integration of quantitative force measurements with microscopy approaches remains a challenge in connecting cell mechanics with biological structure and function. This limitation underlines the urgent need for novel imaging methods to visualize how different organelles, cells and organisms respond to forces and how their mechanical properties are coupled to function and physiology. In this Review, we outline recent developments in this rapidly advancing field and discuss what lays ahead in order to bring spatially and temporally resolved imaging of subcellular mechanics into a quantitative and broadly accessible framework for cell biology.

items.title: The Cylinder Test: Development and clinical validation of a tool for assessing hand opening.
items.abstract: Background Impaired hand opening following neurological injury can limit functional grasp and object handling. Existing upper limb assessments do not specifically evaluate functional hand opening or distinguish between active and passive components. Purpose To describe the development of the Cylinder Test (CyT) and evaluate its preliminary face validity, manual clarity, feasibility, and perceived clinical relevance among clinicians and individuals with neurological upper limb impairment. Study design Clinical measurement, cross-sectional study. Methods The CyT was developed through iterative clinical refinement and literature review. The final CyT version comprises 14 plastic cylinders (20-150 mm diameter) and four subtests assessing active and passive functional hand opening. Face validity was evaluated in 33 individuals with neurological upper limb impairments due to cervical spinal cord injuries (cSCI) or spasticity and 31 clinicians experienced in neurological upper limb rehabilitation. Clinicians reviewed the CyT manual and completed a study-specific questionnaire assessing clarity, perceived clinical usefulness, relevance of the subtests, and scoring criteria. Participants performed the CyT and subsequently rated its relevance and perceived effort. Data were summarized descriptively. Results All clinicians (31/31, 100%) reported that the manual provided sufficient guidance for independent administration, and all considered the CyT potentially useful in clinical practice. The purpose of the CyT was rated as clear or very clear by 26/31 clinicians (84%), and no clinician rated any subtest or scoring criterion as inappropriate. All participants (33/33, 100%) rated the overall CyT as relevant or very relevant, and ratings of the individual subtests were predominantly relevant or very relevant. Six of 15 participants with spasticity rated the test as demanding compared with 2/18 participants with cSCI. Conclusions Preliminary evaluation supports the face validity, manual clarity, feasibility, and perceived clinical relevance of the CyT for assessing functional hand opening in neurological upper limb rehabilitation. The CyT may provide hand therapists with a clinically feasible approach to assessing active and passive hand opening. Further evaluation of reliability, construct validity, and responsiveness is required.

items.title: Molecular detection of Borrelia puertoricensis and a Coxiella endosymbiont in Ornithodoros puertoricensis from northern Veracruz, Mexico.
items.abstract: Tick-borne relapsing fever (TBRF) is a neglected zoonosis caused by Borrelia spp. and transmitted by soft ticks of the genus Ornithodoros. Although Mexico has a long history of human TBRF, the current distribution of relapsing fever borreliae and their associated vectors remains poorly understood, particularly in the Mexican Gulf Coast region. This study investigated the presence of tick-borne bacteria in ticks collected at a​ veterinary clinic in northern Veracruz, Mexico. A total of 164 Ornithodoros puertoricensis ticks were identified using morphological characteristics and 16 S mitochondrial ribosomal RNA sequencing. DNA extracts were screened by conventional PCR for Borrelia, Rickettsia, Bartonella, Coxiella, and Ehrlichia/Anaplasma, followed by DNA sequencing and phylogenetic analyses of positive samples. Borrelia puertoricensis DNA was detected in six ticks (3.66%), in four nymphs and two females. Phylogenetic analyses of the flaB gene confirmed that all sequences clustered within the B. puertoricensis clade with strong bootstrap support. In addition, a Coxiella endosymbiont was detected and assigned to clade B based on 16 S rRNA phylogenetic reconstruction, representing the first molecular evidence of this lineage in O. puertoricensis. None of the DNA samples were positive for Rickettsia, Bartonella, Ehrlichia, or Anaplasma. These findings provide the first molecular evidence of B. puertoricensis and a Coxiella clade B endosymbiont in O. puertoricensis from Veracruz, extending the known distribution of both microorganisms in Mexico. The detection of these bacteria in ticks collected at a veterinary clinic capable of treating wild animals highlights the importance of integrated acarological and molecular surveillance at wildlife-domestic animal-human interfaces to improve understanding of the ecology and public health significance of neglected tick-borne zoonoses.

items.title: The wild avian resistome: metagenomic insights into antimicrobial resistance ecology.
items.abstract: Antimicrobial resistance (AMR) in wild birds is increasingly studied as an ecological component of the wider One Health resistome, yet the evidentiary meaning of a resistance gene detected in avian material varies markedly with study design. This review synthesizes culture-based, whole-genome and metagenomic evidence with emphasis on what modern sequencing can and cannot establish about acquisition, persistence, mobility and transmission. Wild birds encounter antimicrobial-resistant bacteria and antibiotic resistance genes (ARGs) through wastewater, landfills, livestock-associated environments, surface waters, sediments and food webs; resident synanthropic species can be as informative as long-distance migrants. Shotgun and genome-resolved metagenomics have expanded the known avian resistome, enabled host assignment and revealed links with mobile genetic elements and viromes, but DNA detection alone does not demonstrate viable carriage or directional dissemination. We therefore organize the evidence through an evidence-to-inference framework of five complementary domains: ARG detection, microbial-host assignment, genomic mobility, viable carriage and persistence, and transmission, the last separated into sharing between compartments and direction of movement. Applying the framework to published sequencing studies shows that most reach only detection or host assignment, rely on relative abundance, rarely report negative controls and come predominantly from China. The framework clarifies why wild birds are often best regarded as ecological sentinels unless persistence, viable hosts and directionality are shown. Combining metagenomics with long-read sequencing, targeted culture, isolate genomics, environmental sampling and movement ecology offers the strongest route toward biologically meaningful One Health surveillance.

items.title: From subjects to experts: Methodological reflections on interviewing preschool-aged children about sensitive topics.
items.abstract: Preschool-aged children remain underrepresented in research on illness, death, and bereavement, reflecting ethical concern and the fit between conventional interview methods and children's developmental and communicative capacities. This article draws on three Danish studies. These were a home-based sand tray interview with parentally bereaved children, a laboratory timeline task on understanding death, and a practice-based evaluation of a family bereavement network. Across the three studies, participants were aged three to eight at data collection. We use preschool-aged children throughout to refer to this broad group, recognizing that the term is defined more narrowly in some national systems, and we note where age-related differences within the group mattered for participation. Together the three studies show how children can be included in sensitive research. Participation depended less on simpler questions than on designing encounters that gave children ways to engage, supported distance from difficult material, and visible opportunities to continue, pause, or stop. Setting, interviewer judgment, and infrastructure shaped the ethics of participation and the knowledge produced. Recognizing children's expertise means broadening what counts as data, including play, gesture, objects, silence, and advice. The task is not to make children speak like adults, but to build methods that recognize what they communicate.

items.title: Measurement properties of instruments assessing self-stigma and help-seeking stigma in youth: a systematic review protocol.
items.abstract: Objective This systematic review will evaluate the measurement properties and methodological rigor of self-report instruments assessing internalized self-stigma and self-stigma of seeking help among youth and emerging adults (aged 12-25 years). The review will map global evidence to identify geographical gaps in psychometric equity, focusing on instruments validated for Arabic-speaking youth as a critical test of cross-cultural validity and measurement invariance. Introduction The transition between ages 12 and 25 years represents a critical period for mental health. Internalized self-stigma is a significant proximal barrier to professional help-seeking; however, existing tools often lack sufficient evidence of cross-cultural validity. Without psychometric equity, particularly in collectivist, Arabic-speaking contexts, current instruments may contain measurement bias. Eligibility criteria We will include original peer-reviewed primary research and academic dissertations reporting the development, translation, cross-cultural adaptation, or validation of self-report instruments measuring internalized self-stigma or the self-stigma of help-seeking in youth (aged 12 to 25 years) across any cultural context, with a secondary focus on Arabic-speaking populations (including regional dialects). Studies published in English, Arabic, or French published from January 1, 1996, to the date of the final search, will be eligible. Methods This review will follow the COSMIN framework. We will search PubMed, Scopus, Web of Science Core Collection, ProQuest Dissertations & Theses Citation Index, and the Index Medicus for the Eastern Mediterranean Region. Two independent reviewers will screen studies for eligibility, assess methodological quality using the COSMIN Risk of Bias checklist v.3.0, and extract data using a standardized tool. Findings will be synthesized following COSMIN guidance, and certainty of evidence will be evaluated using the modified GRADE approach tailored for measurement properties. Review registration PROSPERO CRD420261290064.

items.title: Beyond the Hangover: Associations Between Binge Drinking, Health, and Performance in Young Adult Resistance-Trained Females.
items.abstract: Purpose The present study aimed to evaluate associations between resistance training and binge drinking in relation to musculoskeletal composition, physical fitness, cognitive function, and psychological wellness in young adult females. Methods Participants were categorized into four groups: sedentary low alcohol consumers (SL; n=12), sedentary binge drinkers (SB; n=12), resistance-trained low alcohol consumers (RTL; n=12), and resistance-trained binge drinkers (RTB; n=12). Measurements included body composition via DEXA scan, muscle quality via ultrasonography, and insulin sensitivity via oral glucose tolerance test. Physical performance was assessed using maximum chair stand power, vertical jump, broad jump, knee extensor torque, grip strength, and push-ups to failure. Tests and questionnaires were used to assess cognitive function and psychological wellness. Results Resistance-trained females had lower body fat than sedentary females (RTL = 29.28±4.27%; RTB = 29.03±3.67%; SL = 37.18±5.32%; SB = 34.83±3.54%; p Conclusions The results suggest that ≥1 year of binge drinking is associated with poorer metabolic health without differences in performance in young females. Further, frequent RT may mitigate the effects of binge drinking on body composition.

items.title: Supporting Males with Suicidal Ideation: Evaluation of an E-Learning for Healthcare Providers.
items.abstract: Suicide remains an important public health issue. Males are at increased risk for suicide, yet display reduced help-seeking, increased drop-out and less lasting engagement. Despite calls for more gender-responsive care, practical training for healthcare providers (HCPs) remains scarce. To address this gap, a training module (e-learning) was developed to support HCPs in offering gender-responsive suicide prevention care to males. This study aimed to evaluate changes in HCPs' self-efficacy and gender-responsive competencies, and their satisfaction with the training. This pre-post trial has been registered at ClinicalTrials.gov (NCT06810713). A single-group pre-post design was used. HCPs completed questionnaires before and after completing the 30-60 minute e-learning module. The surveys assessed self-efficacy and gender-responsive competencies in supporting males experiencing suicidal ideation. In addition, participants evaluated the e-learning using Likert-scale items. A total of 109 HCPs participated, of whom 75 completed the posttest. Results showed statistically significant improvements in both self-efficacy and gender-responsive competencies with moderate to large effect sizes of d = 0.55 and d = 1.98. Participants evaluated the module positively (M = 8.0/10), with good evaluations of its content and format. The psychoeducational model on gender socialization and suicidality, as well as the downloadable summary sheets, were well received. The e-learning module significantly improved HCPs' confidence and gender-responsive competencies in working with males experiencing suicidal ideation. Given its self-paced, freely accessible online format, the training appears feasible and acceptable. Further research is needed to examine its long-term impact, behavioral outcomes in clinical practice, and applicability to more diverse male populations.

items.title: Contribution of risk factors to racial/ethnic disparities in tuberculosis among US-born persons.
items.abstract: In the United States, tuberculosis (TB) incidence rates are substantially higher among racial/ethnic minorities compared with non-Hispanic White persons. However, few analyses have investigated the mechanisms driving these disparities. To assess the contribution of geographic factors and individual TB risk factors to racial/ethnic disparities in TB incidence among U.S.-born individuals. We analyzed TB case data for 2012-2019 from the National Tuberculosis Surveillance System, stratified by race/ethnicity, age, sex, and Public Use Microdata Area (PUMA). Age-sex standardized incidence rate ratios (IRRs) were calculated to quantify disparities across racial/ethnic groups. We decomposed these IRRs to quantify the contribution of differences within and between PUMAs to overall disparities. We also estimated the contributions of racial/ethnic differences in the prevalence of established TB risk factors-diagnosed diabetes, current smoking, HIV infection, and excess alcohol use-to TB disparities. Non-Hispanic American Indian or Alaska Native and non-Hispanic Native Hawaiian or Pacific Islander persons had the highest TB incidence rates compared to non-Hispanic White persons (IRR: 15.3 (95% CI: 12.5, 18.6) and 18.1 (12.3, 26.2) respectively). Within-PUMA TB incidence differences accounted for most of the differences in incidence by race/ethnicity, representing 52-96% of total IRRs for each racial/ethnic population. Racial/ethnic differences in the prevalence of individual risk factors had minimal impact on total TB incidence disparities. Eliminating racial/ethnic disparities in TB will require more than addressing individual risk factors. Combatting structural or community-level determinants of TB, including treating infection to prevent disease, will be important for accelerating TB elimination.

items.title: Multiparametric ultrasound characterizes pediatric cystic fibrosis hepatobiliary involvement.
items.abstract: The contemporary European Society for Pediatric Gastroenterology, Hepatology and Nutrition (ESPGHAN)/North American Society for Pediatric Gastroenterology, Hepatology and Nutrition (NASPGHAN) framework broadens the definition of cystic fibrosis hepatobiliary involvement (CFHBI), but the biological interpretation of individual multiparametric ultrasound parameters within this framework remains unclear. We evaluated the biological associations of shear wave elastography (SWE), shear wave dispersion (SWD), and attenuation imaging (ATI) with histopathological phenotypes in children with cystic fibrosis (CF). In this ambispective cohort study, 119 children with CF underwent hepatobiliary assessment, including SWE, SWD, ATI, Doppler ultrasonography, clinical and laboratory evaluation. Histopathological assessment was performed when clinically indicated. CFHBI was classified according to the ESPGHAN/NASPGHAN framework, with the Debray criteria used as a secondary exploratory comparison. Exploratory phenotype-oriented analyses evaluated ultrasound parameters according to corresponding histopathological phenotypes. Exploratory phenotype-oriented analyses demonstrated significantly higher ATI values in histopathologically defined steatosis (p < 0.001), with good discriminatory performance (AUC 0.813) and an optimal threshold of 0.655 dB/cm/MHz. In contrast, SWE was not associated with histopathologically defined fibrosis (p = 0.151), whereas SWD showed no significant phenotype-specific associations. Secondary exploratory analyses demonstrated significant overall CFHBI discrimination by all three ultrasound parameters, with the highest AUC observed for SWD. The ESPGHAN/NASPGHAN and Debray classifications demonstrated significant disagreement (McNemar p < 0.001), with 22.7% of patients classified as Debray-negative but ESPGHAN/NASPGHAN-positive. Multiparametric ultrasound should be interpreted within the contemporary ESPGHAN/NASPGHAN CFHBI framework rather than as a single diagnostic tool for hepatobiliary involvement. The distinct biological associations of SWE, ATI, and SWD support a phenotype-oriented interpretation of individual ultrasound parameters, whereas overall CFHBI discrimination should be interpreted as a secondary exploratory finding requiring prospective multicenter validation.

items.title: Creatine and CoQ10 with physical activity on muscle function in children with myositis: a proof-of-concept trial.
items.abstract: We aimed to evaluate whether Creatine (Cr) and Coenzyme Q10 (CoQ10) supplementation, combined with a self-paced physical activity program, enhances muscle function in juvenile idiopathic inflammatory myopathies (JIIM). Fifteen participants, (8 male/ 7 female) aged 9-17, from SickKids' JIIM clinic were recruited for a double-blinded, placebo-controlled, randomized, multiple-baseline trial. All participants participated in both the placebo and intervention periods. The primary outcome, muscle function, was measured by the Wingate Test. Secondary outcomes included improvements in jumping height, disease activity, and quality of life. There was a significant increase in peak power (mean difference (MD)=95 Watts; p = 0.02), mean power (MD = 74 Watts; p = 0.02), and minimum power (MD = 47 Watts; p = 0.01) in the intervention periods compared to placebo periods. Vertical jump peak power also increased significantly in the intervention period (MD = 493 Watts; p = 0.02). However, these significant findings were not replicated in the prespecified sensitivity analyses, which incorporated linear mixed models to adjust for individual baseline values. Cr+CoQ10 supplementation combined with physical activity showed positive effects; however, these findings may be attributable to chance imbalances in baseline values. Alternatively, the lack of statistical significance in the sensitivity analyses may reflect a Type II error, as the study size was set for the more powerful primary analysis. Further research is necessary to fully understand the impact of Cr and CoQ10 supplementation in children with JIIM. ClinicalTrials.gov: NCT04286178.

items.title: Maternal mean arterial pressure and serum inhibin A as early predictors of hypertensive disorders in low-risk pregnant women attending a University Teaching Hospital in Lagos, Nigeria: A prospective cohort study.
items.abstract: This study evaluates the role of maternal mean arterial pressure (MAP) and serum inhibin-A level as early predictors of hypertensive disorders of pregnancy (HDP) among low-risk pregnant women attending a University Teaching Hospital in Lagos, Nigeria. This was a prospective cohort study of 254 consecutively consenting, low-risk, normotensive, and non-proteinuric pregnant women at 13-19 weeks of gestation. Receiver operating characteristics (ROC) curves and validity tests were used to determine the performance of serum levels of inhibin A, MAP, and a combination of both in predicting HDP (gestational hypertension and preeclampsia). The mean age and parity of the participants was 30.3 ± 4.9 years and 1 (0-2), respectively. The area under the ROC curves of serum inhibin A (0.9981, 95% confidence interval [CI]: 0.9946-1.000) was higher than for MAP (0.7531, 95% CI 0.6641-0.8421), in predicting the composite endpoint of HDP. The optimum cut-offs for predicting HDP as calculated from Youden's index were 476.8 pg/mL (sensitivity = 100% and specificity = 98.7%) for serum inhibin A and 81.3 mm Hg (sensitivity = 100% and specificity = 50.1%) for MAP. There was no statistically significant difference between the combined predictive ability of inhibin A and MAP compared to that of serum inhibin A alone for predicting HDP (AUC of 0.9984 vs. 09981, P-value = 0.7259. This study demonstrated that serum inhibin A alone and MAP have good and moderate performance, respectively, in predicting HDP in the low-risk cohort of Nigerian pregnant women. The combination of serum inhibin A and MAP has a similar predictive performance as serum inhibin A alone.

items.title: Inside the battery box: a cross-technology assessment of PFAS uses, functions, and substitution potential.
items.abstract: Understanding where and why per- and polyfluoroalkyl substances (PFASs) are used in batteries is essential for evaluating their substitution potential, yet detailed information across battery technologies is scarce. We analyzed more than 5600 submissions to the Annex XV public consultation on the proposed universal PFAS restriction in the European Union and extracted information reporting use, associated substance(s), and stated function(s) of PFASs in batteries. 341 records were compiled into a database using our structured Battery Use & Function Framework that incorporates the Functional Substitution Framework. Among these records, 78 contained sufficient information to qualify as a potential PFAS use and were organized into 36 potential PFAS uses, accounting for overlaps. Each potential PFAS use was evaluated using supporting evidence from previous use-mapping studies, input from battery stakeholders, teardown-analysis studies, and other targeted academic literature. Across all lines of evidence, two PFAS uses in batteries were contradicted, indicating already large-scale availability of PFAS-free alternatives, while 16 PFAS uses were confirmed, primarily in cathode components across several battery technologies and chemistries. PFAS-free alternatives were identified for 13 PFAS uses across battery applications, with an additional five uses showing PFAS-free options for certain applications within the broader use category. The findings indicate that few technical barriers remain for substituting PFASs in most battery components. Our mapping provides a detailed foundation for future alternatives assessments, supports essential-use evaluations, and highlights opportunities and challenges relevant to monitoring and recycling.

items.title: AI Assessment of Heterogeneous Histopathologic Brain Tumor Sub-regions: the RANO MICCAI BraTS-Path 2024 Challenge.
items.abstract: Automated classification of glioblastoma (IDH-wt, WHO CNS Gr.4) histopathologic sub-regions in whole slide images (WSI) is essential for quantitative tumor characterization, but faces substantial challenges from intra-tumoral heterogeneity and inter-observer annotation variability. The AI-RANO & RANO-Pathology working groups organized BraTS-Path 2024, representing the first international benchmarking environment and publicly available spatially annotated dataset, towards promoting the development and fair evaluation of Artificial Intelligence (AI) models to classify specific sub-regions: cellular tumor, pseudopalisading necrosis (PN), microvascular proliferation, geographic necrosis, infiltration into the cortex, and white matter penetration (WM). Multi-institutional H&E-stained WSIs had reference standard samples generated by eight expert neuropathologists, following a rigorous peer review protocol, resulting in 309,118 data samples (training/validation/hold-out testing: 96,485/62,387/150,246). Quantitative performance evaluation of six AI approaches was conducted based on multiple metrics, including Accuracy and Matthew's correlation coefficient (MCC). A robust statistically-aware ranking strategy offered statistical significance of the final rankings. Top-performing approaches employed common strategies, including large pre-trained models, ensembling, and extensive data augmentation, reporting Accuracy=0.69 and MCC=0.58. Key challenges included severe class imbalance, hampering minority class performance, and inter-annotator variability, especially for ambiguous sub-regions such as PN or WM. BraTS-Path represents a valuable public resource for glioblastoma histopathologic sub-region assessment. Our findings indicate the specific task remaining an open research problem, highlighting the influence of rare sub-regions, the absence of a consistent "gold standard" annotation protocol, and the potential of foundation models to improve generalization, guiding future research toward developing more reliable AI tools for quantitative neuropathology.

items.title: CryoET-DDM: restoring high-fidelity signals in cryo-electron tomography via a data-driven diffusion model.
items.abstract: Cryo-electron tomography (cryo-ET) is an essential technique for resolving high-resolution structures of macromolecular complexes in situ. However, the extremely low signal-to-noise ratio (SNR) in tilt series, caused by strict electron dose limitations, remains a major bottleneck for subtomogram averaging (STA). Although existing denoising methods can enhance tomogram contrast, they may compromise the high-frequency structural information required for downstream STA refinement. We introduce CryoET-DDM, a diffusion framework for high-fidelity restoration of cryo-ET tilt series that integrates data-driven noise modeling and fidelity-guided structural preservation. CryoET-DDM incorporates background noise patches extracted from the same experimental tilt series into the diffusion process to model the noise characteristics of low-dose imaging. A fidelity-guided learning objective promotes structural consistency during denoising, helping preserve high-frequency information needed for STA. Experiments on three public datasets (EMPIAR-10499, EMPIAR-10164, and EMPIAR-10651) show that CryoET-DDM improves particle quality, preserves structural fidelity, and yields downstream gains in STA resolution. These results support tilt series denoising as a promising strategy for cryo-ET data processing and improve the reliability of in situ structural biology analysis. Code and models for our experiments are available at https://github.com/xinsheng44/CryoET-DDM. The real datasets used in this study are publicly available from EMPIAR.

items.title: Cost-utility analysis of surgical revascularization versus conservative management for adult moyamoya disease patients with posterior hemorrhage in Japan.
items.abstract: This study evaluates the cost-effectiveness of surgical revascularization versus conservative management for adult moyamoya disease (MMD) patients with posterior hemorrhage from the perspective of the Japanese public healthcare payer. We developed a combined decision tree and Markov model for adult posterior hemorrhagic MMD patients (mean age: 41 years; baseline modified Rankin Scale [mRS] 0-2) over a 60-year lifetime horizon with 1-year cycles. We estimated the treatment effect using the composite endpoint hazard ratio (0.07) from the JAM Trial posterior hemorrhage subgroup as a proxy for the effect on recurrent hemorrhage. We informed health utilities with recent EQ-5D-5L data from the Fukuoka Stroke Registry, weighted by the Japan Stroke Data Bank. We estimated direct medical costs based on the national fee schedule. We discounted costs and outcomes at 2% annually. We set the willingness-to-pay threshold at JPY 7,500,000 per quality-adjusted life year (QALY). In the base case, surgical revascularization yielded 21.49 QALYs for JPY 6,323,426 (USD 40,302), compared with 15.59 QALYs and JPY 5,308,637 (USD 33,835) for conservative management. The incremental cost-effectiveness ratio was JPY 172,220 (USD 1,098) per QALY, which falls below the reference value of JPY 7,500,000 per QALY. In scenario analyses with 5- and 10-year horizons, the ICERs were JPY 8,926,784 and JPY 2,031,693 per QALY, respectively. Probabilistic sensitivity analysis also favored surgical revascularization across the modeled parameter distributions. The base-case estimate of surgical efficacy was based on a composite outcome from a small subgroup, and long-term recurrence risks beyond the 5-year trial period remain uncertain. Surgical revascularization is likely to be cost-effective for adult MMD patients with posterior hemorrhage within the Japanese healthcare system, although limited evidence leaves uncertainty about long-term rebleeding risks and the durability of surgical benefit.

items.title: Reconfiguration of clinical training delivery in a family planning and post-abortion care quality assurance programme in Sierra Leone, 2018-2022: a retrospective programme evaluation.
items.abstract: Health programmes often use both centralised courses and embedded clinical training, but longitudinal descriptions of how training arrangements change - and how competency safeguards are maintained - remain limited. To characterise training-delivery configurations and their implementation context across centre, outreach and public-sector strengthening (PSS) channels in Sierra Leone from January 2018 to June 2022. We undertook a retrospective descriptive programme evaluation of the complete 472-event training register (380 clinical training, seven competency-assessed training-of-trainers and 85 non-competency activities), with event-level stratification by period and service-delivery channel. We interpreted register patterns alongside programme supervision reports, PSS strategy and quality-assurance documents. We did not conduct a controlled effectiveness evaluation. The register contained 286 events in 2018, 52 in 2019, 39 in 2020, 76 in 2021 and 19 in January-June 2022; 209 occurred in outreach, 172 in centres and 91 in PSS. Across 3,817 participant-episodes, 2,571 were recorded in 387 competency-assessed activities; 2,559 had L1-L3 outcomes and 2,013/2,559 (78.7%) attained Level 1. The 2019 workforce-expansion period featured longer residential courses (median 10 days), whereas other periods featured short, service-linked instruction and refreshers. An external 2020 PSS assessment documented quality safeguards and remaining gaps; no pre-implementation QTA baseline was available. Training configurations evolved with programme expansion, changing staffing needs and pandemic adaptation rather than a simple linear classroom-to-workplace shift. Competency-based restrictions, supervised practice and a developing government-linked trainer network formed the clinical governance context. Descriptive programme records and external assessment do not isolate the causal effects of training modality.

items.title: Intrahepatic cholestasis of pregnancy and perinatal outcomes in twin pregnancies: a propensity score matching analysis.
items.abstract: Intrahepatic cholestasis of pregnancy (ICP) tends to be more severe in twin pregnancies and is associated with adverse maternal and neonatal outcomes. However, data on the specific effects of ICP in twin gestations remain limited. This study aimed to investigate comprehensively the maternal and neonatal consequences of twin pregnancies complicated by ICP. This retrospective cohort study enrolled 3,109 twin pregnancies delivered at Northwest Women's and Children's Hospital in China from January 2018 through December 2022. Pregnancy and delivery data were extracted from the medical records of women with twin pregnancies who delivered at the hospital. Women were allocated into two groups: ICP (n = 244) and non-ICP (n = 2,865). ICP was diagnosed based on the presence of pruritus together with serum total bile acid (TBA) concentrations ≥10μmol/L. Propensity score matching (PSM) was used to balance baseline characteristics between the two groups. Multivariable logistic regression and generalized estimating equations (GEE) were applied to evaluate the associations between ICP and adverse maternal and neonatal outcomes. After matching, ICP increased the risk of maternal outcomes, including preterm labor (early preterm birth: OR = 2.87, 95% CI 1.95-4.23; preterm birth: OR = 4.30, 95% CI 2.11-8.77; very preterm birth: OR = 2.97, 95% CI 1.50-5.87) and hypoproteinemia (OR = 2.83, 95% CI 1.12-7.14), as well as adverse neonatal outcomes, including low birth weight (OR = 2.66, 95% CI 1.99-3.55), small vulnerable newborns (OR = 5.30, 95% CI 2.34-12.00), respiratory distress syndrome (OR = 2.43, 95% CI 1.61-3.67), and necrotizing enterocolitis (OR = 5.71, 95% CI 2.34-13.92). Twin pregnancies complicated by ICP were associated with increased risks of adverse perinatal outcomes, including preterm birth, low birth weight, and neonatal morbidity. These findings highlight the importance of heightened clinical awareness and individualized risk assessment in this high-risk population.

items.title: The Nurse Who Never Clocks Out: Kin-Directed Care Coordination, Filial Obligation and Invisible Work in the Care Economy.
items.abstract: To examine the unpaid advisory, navigational and hands-on health work that nurses perform for relatives, friends and neighbours and conceptualise it as kin-directed care coordination. Position paper. A critical discussion drawing on feminist scholarship on care work, filial piety and gendered family care, double-duty caregiving, work-family boundaries and recovery, professional regulation and nurse retention. Feminist scholarship has shown that unpaid care work sustains economies and falls mainly on women. Double-duty caregiving research has described nurses advising relatives, but not the standing role in which a nurse becomes health adviser and navigator for a whole kin network. Filial piety and gender may shape who is asked and how hard refusal is. We describe five practices: interpreting, triaging and advising, brokering access, hands-on care and bearing accountability. It crosses the work-home boundary, may erode recovery, carries professional obligations and is absent from workload measures, workforce surveys and care-economy accounts. Health systems with weak primary care may rely on this work without counting it. Kin-directed care coordination can be understood as a distinct, culturally shaped, probably gendered, and unmeasured form of nurses' unpaid care work that warrants recognition in research, regulation, and policy. Nurse managers, educators, regulators, and researchers can name and measure this work and address it in retention strategies, professional guidance, and ethics education. This paper addresses the absence of a defined concept, and of any measure, for nurses' health work for their wider kin and social networks. It proposes a concept, five practices and a measurement agenda. It will inform nurse leaders, educators, regulators and workforce planners. Not applicable to this position paper. This study did not include patient or public involvement in its design, conduct, or reporting.

items.title: Comparative Risk of Cancer with non-TNF Advanced Therapies Versus Anti-TNF Therapy in Inflammatory Bowel Disease.
items.abstract: Safety is important when selecting advanced therapies for inflammatory bowel disease (IBD). Safety data for anti-interleukin therapy (anti-IL) or vedolizumab come from trials with limited follow-up, and direct comparisons with anti-tumor necrosis factors (anti-TNFs) for incident cancer are lacking. We evaluated cancer incidence in patients with IBD treated with anti-IL therapy or vedolizumab versus anti-TNFs. We conducted a retrospective cohort study of adults with IBD and no prior cancer who initiated anti-IL therapy, vedolizumab or anti-TNFs. Our primary outcome was incident cancer from 90 days after therapy initiation through discontinuation. We calculated incidence rates and performed Cox proportional hazards models. We identified 4,019 advanced therapy starts: 995 anti-IL, 692 vedolizumab, and 2,332 anti-TNF starts, with mean therapy duration of 1096 days. In multivariable analysis, there was a trend towards a lower hazard of all cancers among anti-IL users compared to anti-TNF users (HR 0.47; 95% CI 0.21-1.04), which was significant on sensitivity analyses. There was no difference in hazard of skin cancers (HR 1.56; 95% CI 0.39-6.15); however, the hazard of non-skin cancer was significantly lower among anti-IL users compared to anti-TNF users (HR 0.28; 95% CI 0.09-0.81). When comparing vedolizumab to anti-TNFs, there was no significant difference in the hazard of all cancer (HR 0.52, 95% CI 0.24-1.12) and non-skin cancer (HR 0.63, 95% CI 0.29-1.39). We found no evidence of an increased cancer risk with anti-IL therapy compared with anti-TNF therapy in patients with IBD. There was no difference in the cancer risk between vedolizumab and anti-TNF therapy.

items.title: A Mixed Methods Approach to Implementing the Canadian Spinal Bulbar Muscular Atrophy Guideline.
items.abstract: Spinal bulbar muscular atrophy (SBMA) is an X-linked neuromuscular disease that disproportionately affects Indigenous people in Canada. The first Canadian guidelines for the management of SBMA were recently published. There is limited guidance from the literature to inform optimal implementation strategies. A mixed methods approach was used to determine SBMA guideline implementation strategies. A combination of activities (surveys, roundtable discussion, modified Delphi consensus exercise with experts, Indigenous engagement) was employed to gather opinions from multiple stakeholders and experts (physicians, allied healthcare providers, people with living experience [PWLE] including Indigenous people and patient organizations). Barriers to guideline implementation included lack of awareness of the disease and the need for comprehensive multidisciplinary teams to address the multisystem symptoms and complications of SBMA. A survey of current practice patterns demonstrated several areas for improvement, including attention to cardiac symptoms, laryngospasm and care for female carriers. Roundtable discussion with health experts and patient advocacy groups centered on the following themes: (1) awareness, (2) resources, (3) knowledge translation and (4) policy support. The Indigenous engagement process with the community guiding circle emphasized the need for ongoing involvement of PWLE, Indigenous communities, leaders and health networks in the implementation process. The modified Delphi process with physician experts led to the development of specific implementation strategies, with emphasis on education for healthcare providers and PWLE, including the development of written materials. Intentional partnerships with PWLE, Indigenous communities, patient organizations and healthcare professionals are essential to meaningful guideline implementation.

items.title: Maternal exposure to sleep aids and risk of specific birth defects in the Birth Defects Study To Evaluate Pregnancy exposureS.
items.abstract: Insomnia symptoms are often reported during pregnancy, prompting use of pharmacologic treatments. We explored associations between treatments used during the month before through the third month of pregnancy ("early pregnancy") and risk of birth defects using Birth Defects Study to Evaluate Pregnancy exposureS (BD-STEPS) data from 2014-2021. Pregnancies affected by birth defects ("cases") were identified from surveillance systems in seven states; liveborn infants without birth defects ("controls") were randomly selected from the same catchment areas. Mothers of cases and controls reported early pregnancy exposures via interview, including use of prescription, over-the-counter, or herbal sleep aids. For defects with ≥5 exposed cases, we used Firth's logistic regression to estimate propensity score-adjusted odds ratios (aORs) and 95% confidence intervals (CIs), adjusting for maternal age, race/ethnicity, education, body mass index, previous live birth, history of depression/anxiety, early pregnancy use of antipsychotics, anxiolytics, antidepressants, opioids, cigarettes, alcohol, and prenatal vitamins, occurrence of stressful events, occupation outside the home, health insurance, and site. Overall, 237 (7%) cases and 140 (8%) controls reported early pregnancy sleep aid use. We calculated aORs for 12/22 defects, which ranged from 0.52 for d-transposition of the great arteries to 1.61 for coarctation of the aorta. All CIs included the null. Results suggest sleep aids do not increase risk of most defects studied, but increased risk for coarctation of the aorta cannot be ruled out. Small numbers limited analyses. Studies examining the severity of underlying sleep disorders and impacts of specific sleep aids would be beneficial.

items.title: PANTHER: the protein tree and function resource in 2027.
items.abstract: PANTHER (Protein ANalysis THrough Evolutionary Relationships) is a comprehensive resource of phylogenetic trees of protein-coding gene families. Trees are manually annotated with Gene Ontology (GO) terms describing how protein functional characteristics were gained and lost over time along tree branches, and these evolutionary models are used to create GO annotations for protein-coding genes. Orthologs, paralogs, and xenologs are assigned based on the trees. Here, we describe updates to the PANTHER resource since our previous published report in 2022. Since that time, the content of the database has been systematically improved: GO annotations of the trees have been expanded to increase coverage of genes by 20%-100% depending on the organism; thousands of families have been revised and ~100 added; and the PANTHER release pipeline has been modified to improve stability of the trees across versions. The expanded annotations for all 131 genomes in the PANTHER trees can be downloaded or used for analyzing gene lists directly on the PANTHER website, and users can now generate tree-based GO annotations for any sequence file using InterProScan.

items.title: The Chemical Probes Portal-2026: expanding and enhancing this expert review-based public resource to sustain chemical probe selection and application in bioscience.
items.abstract: The Chemical Probes Portal (https://www.chemicalprobes.org) is an open, international, resource empowering scientific robustness by supporting responsible research using chemical probes. The Portal informs best-practice in the selection and application of small-molecule chemical probes through expert review, manual curation, and community engagement. Used correctly, high-quality chemical probes are powerful, versatile research tools enabling the fundamental study of protein function, target validation, and development of new therapeutics. Conversely, the inappropriate selection and use of these chemical tools can compromise experimental interpretation, reliability, and translational impact, highlighting the need for trusted advisory resources. The Portal addresses this challenge, providing a unique collection of curated data, expert reviews, and related guidance. We describe significant developments to the Portal's content and infrastructure. We have substantially expanded the content, with curated probes increasing by 26% since our last update. We have significantly enhanced website functionality through implementation of new, more informative probe pages, improved search tools and enhancements in data accessibility, machine readability, and interoperability. Together, these developments strengthen the Portal as a trustworthy, user-friendly provider of expert-reviewed chemical probe information and an increasingly valuable source of gold-standard FAIR, accessible data in the era of AI-assisted information discovery, underpinning reliable bioscience research.

items.title: Natural History and Predictors of Progression in Gastric Intestinal Metaplasia: An Australian Longitudinal Cohort Study.
items.abstract: To characterize the burden and progression of gastric intestinal metaplasia (GIM) in the Australian context. Gastric cancer (GC) is uncommon in developed countries such as Australia, but is often diagnosed at a late stage, conferring poor prognosis. GIM is a premalignant lesion that can identify patients for endoscopic surveillance, but only a small number progress to dysplasia or GC. Longitudinal data regarding burden and progression of GIM in the Australian setting are lacking. Patients undergoing oesophagogastroduodenoscopy (OGD) between January 2010 and April 2023 were retrospectively reviewed to determine the rates of GIM and GC. Among patients with GIM, a detailed file review assessed risk factors associated with progression to dysplasia or cancer, with analysis using delayed-entry survival analysis. The cohort was linked to the state-wide cancer registry. Of 13,987 individuals undergoing OGD, 1320 (9.4%) had histologically confirmed GIM. GIM patients were older (mean: 64.6 vs. 54.0), and more often born outside Australia (64.5% vs. 41.0%), most frequently from Southern Europe, Eastern Europe, or Eastern Asia. GIM was associated with higher progression rates (7.2% vs. 0.5%). To examine the natural history of GIM, 1217 individuals were included in delayed-entry Cox regression (19 progressors and 1198 nonprogressors). In multivariable analysis, family history of GC (HR=4.9) and extensive GIM (HR=8.0) were independently associated with progression. GIM is frequently diagnosed on endoscopic biopsy in Australia, particularly among migrant groups. It is associated with higher rates of GC. Extensive disease or a family history is the strongest predictor of progression, regardless of country of origin.

items.title: Serologic Guidance for Extracorporeal Membrane Oxygenation Selection and Survival Using the Cosmos Dataset.
items.abstract: Extracorporeal membrane oxygenation (ECMO) is a life-support therapy for patients with severe cardiac or respiratory failure. Despite its growing use, evidence-based guidelines for ECMO candidacy remain limited due to small, single-center studies and heterogeneous designs. This study leveraged Epic Cosmos, an electronic health record dataset encompassing over 300 million patient records, to analyze outcomes among 42,210 adults treated with ECMO between January 1, 2019, and February 15, 2026, involving 23,116 (54.8%) venoarterial (VA), 14,632 (34.7%) venovenous (VV), and 4,462 (10.6%) hybrid (VA and VV) cases. Hospital mortality varied from 37% (VV) to 50% (VA). Poisson models by ECMO type for in-hospital mortality adjusted for key demographic and clinical variables showed the admitting diagnosis group had the strongest association with subsequent mortality. Several blood chemistry markers measured within the 24 hours before ECMO initiation were also associated with increased mortality, including elevated lactate, elevated creatinine, and lower pH, though strength of association varied by ECMO type. Our findings support the use of large electronic health record (EHR) datasets for ECMO outcomes research and identify exploratory associations between preinitiation biomarkers and in-hospital mortality that require further validation.

items.title: A genome-wide association study and genetic risk score for age at diabetes diagnosis support beta-cell dysfunction in young-onset diabetes in Chinese.
items.abstract: We investigated genetic variations driving young age-at-diabetes-diagnosis (ADD) and developed a genetic risk score (GRS) to identify Chinese individuals at risk of young-onset diabetes (YOD with ADD<40). We performed genome-wide association studies (GWAS) for ADD with internal and external replication in 22,611 individuals with type 2 diabetes (T2D, 20% with YOD) and identified Chinese-prioritized loci by conditioning on the polygenic risk score (PRS) of ADD constructed from publicly available datasets. We constructed ADD-GRS using genome-wide independent variants (p<5E-08) and examined its associations with glycemic traits in diabetes and non-diabetes cohorts. We identified three independent signals at genome-wide significance (P < 5×10-8) mapping to CDKAL1 (rs2206734, β=-0.75 (SE:0.13) per copy of T allele, effect allele frequency (EAF)=0.38, p=2.12E-09), PAX4 (rs61160304, β=-1.01 (SE:0.17) per copy of T allele, EAF=0.19, p=2.51E-09), and KCNQ1 (rs2299620, β=-0.77 (SE:0.14) per copy of G allele, EAF=0.70, p=2.80E-08). The variants at PAX4 and KCNQ1 were independent of the genetic liability estimated by ADD-PRS from Europeans and South Indians. In the diabetes cohort, the ADD-GRS was associated with younger ADD, lower C-peptide, higher HbA1c and pathway-specific T2D-PRS for beta-cell+proinsulin and residual glycemia. Using YOD versus later-onset diabetes as a secondary outcome, LINC02783/PADI1 (rs72895704, OR:1.52 per copy of A allele, EAF=0.02, p=1.93E-06) and TARS2P1 (rs145218437, OR: 1.73 per copy of C allele, EAF=0.02, p=7.57E-08) showed suggestive significance. Both known and novel T2D loci contribute to ADD in Chinese people and may be used to detect high risk individuals for early intervention to prevent or delay onset of YOD.

items.title: Linking dietary-derived arsenic exposure to blood serum arsenic burden, potential food sources, and breast cancer risk in the EPIC-Heidelberg cohort.
items.abstract: Breast cancer is the most common cancer among women worldwide, yet the role of environmental toxicants remains unclear. Arsenic is an International Agency for Research on Cancer classified carcinogen linked to skin, lung, and bladder cancers. The relationship between dietary arsenic intake levels and blood arsenic concentrations, particularly across sexes, and the association between dietary arsenic intake and breast cancer remain understudied. This study aimed to address these gaps. Measurements of arsenic in foods collected from 1995 to 2022 in the German monitoring programme were used to estimate long-term dietary intake. Serum arsenic levels were measured using inductively coupled plasma mass spectrometry. Participants were aged 35-65 years; 2,674 non-cases were included in the arsenic intake-serum arsenic analysis, and 631 incident cases and 1,708 non-cases in the breast cancer analysis. Partial spearman's rank correlation and logistic regression models assessed the association between dietary arsenic intake and serum arsenic levels. Prentice-weighted Cox proportional hazards models with age as underlying time scale were used to assess associations between dietary arsenic intake and breast cancer risk. No association was observed between total or estimated inorganic arsenic intake and breast cancer risk (HR 1.1, 95% CI: 0.93-1.31; HR 0.9, 95% CI: 0.76-1.07), including in subgroup analyses by menopausal status (pre- and post-menopausal), estrogen receptor (ER), progesterone receptor (PR), and human epidermal growth factor receptor 2 (HER2) status. Weak positive correlations were observed between total and estimated inorganic arsenic intake and serum arsenic concentrations (ρ = 0.20 and ρ = 0.07). However, regression analyses showed that total arsenic intake was associated with serum arsenic in both sexes (men: OR 3.48, 95% CI 2.33-5.22; women: OR 2.60, 95% CI 1.84-3.68), whereas estimated inorganic arsenic intake were associated only among women in the second and fourth quintiles (OR 1.53 [95% CI 1.10-2.14] and 1.90 [1.33-2.73], respectively). Dietary arsenic intake was not significantly associated with serum arsenic levels or incident breast cancer.

items.title: An Analysis of Large Language Model Performance on Hematology Key Feature Questions.
items.abstract: Large language models (LLMs) demonstrate strong performance on multiple-choice questions but their ability to independently generate clinical decisions without pre-defined answer choices remains less established. We therefore evaluated LLM performance on post-graduate key feature questions (KFQs), which are designed to assess clinical decision-making at critical points. Thirteen LLMs were assessed in June 2026 using 30 novel hematology KFQs developed and reviewed by two hematologists with training in medical education. Each LLM was then asked to assess each case independently, with context reset between cases. Responses were subsequently evaluated for exact correctness and partial credit. Responses between models were assessed using mixed-effects regression, Cochran's Q test, and Friedman's test. Incorrect responses were classified as knowledge, decision, or comprehension errors and subsequently inter-model analysis was performed. Across 390 responses, exact accuracy ranged from 73.3% to 96.7%. Gemini 3 Flash achieved the highest observed accuracy (29/30; 96.7%; 95% confidence interval, 82.8-99.9%), followed by Gemini 3 Flash Force Thinking and OpenEvidence (both 27/30; 90.0%). DeepSeek V3 had the lowest exact accuracy (22/30; 73.3%). Differences between models were not statistically significant for exact correctness (Cochran's Q = 20.00; p = 0.067) or partial-credit scores (Friedman's χ² = 17.95; p = 0.117). Among 71 incorrect responses, 35 (49.3%) were classified as knowledge errors, 32 (45.1%) as decision errors, and four (5.6%) as comprehension errors. LLMs demonstrated high accuracy on postgraduate-level hematology KFQs, although the limited question bank precludes conclusions about equivalent model performance. Knowledge and decision errors remained common among incorrect responses, supporting evaluation of factual accuracy and clinical judgment alongside aggregate scores. Further research should assess whether learners can recognize model errors and whether LLM assistance improves hematology decision-making.

items.title: Preparedness of U.S. Gastroenterology Fellows to Implement Contemporary Gastric Cancer Prevention: A Cross- Sectional Survey.
items.abstract: Successful implementation of contemporary gastric cancer prevention depends on gastroenterologists' ability to recognize higher-risk populations, manage Helicobacter pylori infection, identify premalignant gastric lesions, and apply risk-based surveillance. However, the preparedness of U.S. gastroenterology fellows for these responsibilities has not been evaluated nationally. We conducted a national cross-sectional survey (2025-2026) of fellows enrolled in Accreditation Council for Graduate Medical Education-accredited adult gastroenterology fellowship programs. An anonymous REDCap survey assessed gastric cancer prevention knowledge, educational exposure, confidence, preparedness, and responses to case-based clinical scenarios. Of 191 fellows who initiated the survey, 169 (88%) completed all required items. Only 20% identified all higher-risk populations for gastric cancer, and only 32% selected the correct approximate 5-year U.S. gastric cancer survival rate. Although 97% correctly answered that Helicobacter pylori eradication reduces gastric cancer risk, only 60% recognized the absence of a U.S. Preventive Services Task Force recommendation for gastric cancer screening. Fewer than half reported formal instruction in key prevention domains (30%-46%), only 23% felt prepared to independently manage premalignant gastric lesions, and 81% identified lack of guideline awareness as the principal barrier to early detection. These findings identify important gaps in the preparedness of the future gastroenterology workforce and highlight opportunities to strengthen implementation of evidence-based gastric cancer prevention.

items.title: Needs and challenges of family members of acutely ill patients admitted from Indonesian emergency departments: A multicentre explanatory sequential mixed methods study.
items.abstract: Family members of acutely ill patients in emergency departments (EDs) face uncertainty and service-related challenges. Surveys identify priority needs but provide limited contextual explanation. A multicentre explanatory sequential mixed methods study was conducted in three Indonesian hospitals. In the quantitative phase, 160 family members of patients triaged as Emergency Severity Index categories 1-3 completed the 40-item Indonesian CCFNI-ED. Quantitative profiles informed purposive selection of eight interview participants. Findings were integrated using a joint display. Overall perceived importance was high (mean 3.432, SD 0.291; scale 1-4). Domain means were similar for support (3.513) and comfort (3.506), and for communication (3.384) and participation (3.380). Interviews contextualised these needs and identified emotional, spiritual, administrative, environmental, and service-related experiences. Communication cut across several themes, linking information with support, comfort, and participation. Family needs were multidimensional. Structured information, active support, privacy, and clinically appropriate family involvement are potential priorities for family-centred emergency care and require prospective evaluation.

items.title: [Working conditions and work-related health events among foreign agricultural workers in Japan].
items.abstract: Preventing occupational injuries among foreign workers is a major challenge in Japan, although very little information is available on them. This study surveyed foreign workers employed in the agricultural sector, an industry prone to fatal injuries, to investigate their working conditions and incidence of occupational injuries. From January to March 2025, we distributed anonymous, self-administered questionnaires in eight languages to foreign agricultural workers through grocery stores, restaurants, Indonesian churches, Vietnamese temples, mosques, foreign support organizations, farms, and Japanese-language schools in Ibaraki and Saitama Prefectures. The questionnaire asked about their demographics, agricultural work, safety practices when using brush cutters, rest conditions at the workplace, near-miss incidents and injuries requiring medical attention, heatstroke symptoms, and lower back pain. We describe this separately for men and women. Of the 220 respondents (168 men and 52 women), with a median age of 28 years, 49% were Indonesian. Men were more likely to engage in work involving brush cutters, tractors, and pesticides than women. Among men using brush cutters, unsafe behaviors were reported, including failure to wear protective eyewear (37%) and removal of grass tangled in the cutting blade without first turning off the engine (27%). Approximately 18% and 16% of men and women, respectively, experienced near-miss incidents. Moreover, 10% and 13% of men and women, respectively, sustained injuries requiring medical attention. Similarly, 48% of men and 43% of women experienced heatstroke symptoms while 49% of men and 58% of women suffered lower back pain. Participants had unsafe behaviors during agricultural work, and injuries requiring medical attention occurred in approximately one in ten participants of each sex. In addition, agricultural-work-related lower back pain and heatstroke were common in both men and women.

items.title: Use and perceptions of AI tools among Australian general practice registrars: a national survey.
items.abstract: Artificial intelligence (AI) tools are increasingly used in health care, yet little is known about how often Australian general practitioner trainees (GP registrars) use them or how they perceive the impact of AI on training and clinical care. This study aimed to examine how frequently registrars use AI tools for clinical care and education, types of AI used, the perceived benefits and risks, and training needs. A national cross-sectional online survey conducted from 7 May to 4 June 2024 invited 3743 Australian General Practice Training or Fellowship Support Program registrars to participate. The survey assessed frequency and context of AI use, practice-level adoption, perceived impacts, training exposure, and ethical-legal concerns. Analyses were descriptive. Among the 727 respondents (19.5%), frequent use (weekly or more) was uncommon; 7.3% for clinical tasks, 5.0% for education. Practice-level adoption was low, with 10.8% reporting subscription to AI tools. Most registrars anticipated benefits, particularly learning efficiency and administrative workload reduction. However, 25.0% perceived increased medicolegal risk. Formal training was rare, with most relying on self-directed learning, though many rated AI education as important. Among clinical users, common tools included large language models (32.5%), remote patient monitoring devices (28.6%), and voice-to-text tools (26.2%). Large language models predominated in education (63.5%). In May-June 2024, AI tool use among registrars was limited, although most perceived potential benefit. Enthusiasm was tempered by concerns about safety, ethics, and legal risks. Structured training and guidelines are needed to support safe, effective integration into GP registrars' practice and education.

items.title: Lessons Learned from Large Scale Dissemination of the Family Talk Approach.
items.abstract: This perspective review provides an in-depth examination of key lessons from three major dissemination efforts of Family Talk (FT), a preventive intervention approach designed to support families facing adversity. We highlight practical insights, common challenges, and implications that may inform future implementation and policy efforts. After initial development and testing for parental depression, FT has been adapted and implemented in a variety of large-scale dissemination efforts, including a country-wide program in Finland and a district-wide adaptation in Rwanda. This approach has also been used with refugee groups, the Navy, and other service branch personnel in the United States. We briefly review each project, then describe and discuss the key lessons learned across these efforts. Our takeaways emphasize the need for understanding risk and resilience in each dissemination effort, the local context and culture at intervention delivery, and the need for stage-sequential planning and multiyear efforts. Successful implementation efforts require careful assessment with standardized instruments at multiple levels. Cultural and linguistic competence is also essential, and multiple adaptations for different conditions are necessary. Integrating the intervention approach into regular service care systems is also imperative. Additionally, this paper highlights the value of long-term partnerships, the importance of tracking development over time, the challenges of changing and evolving clinical presentations and shifting societal and funding priorities, and the need to maintain shared vision and values.

items.title: Multimodal Statistical Analysis in Neuroscience
items.abstract: Multimodal analysis in neuroscience has become increasingly important as brain research comes to rely more heavily on integrated analysis of multiple neuroimaging modalities and complementary data sources. In this review, we adopt a statistics-centered perspective, organizing the literature around three core scientific questions: cross-modal association, which focuses on characterizing shared structure and dependence across modalities; outcome association and prediction, which examine how multimodal signals contribute to clinical and behavioral outcomes; and brain causal analysis, which seeks to identify directed effects and mechanistic pathways. We then discuss some emerging trends, especially the integration of unstructured, nontabular data such as clinical and radiology reports, and the growing heterogeneity of data collected across multiple cohorts, sites, and acquisition protocols. Our central message is that multimodal neuroimaging analysis goes beyond simple data fusion and requires a principled statistical foundation, one that enables clear problem formulation, provides valid and efficient inference, and ensures robustness, as modern neuroimaging and complementary data become more complex and heterogeneous.

items.title: AgentSSL: Can MLE Agents Leverage Unlabeled Data?
items.abstract: Applying machine learning systems to new domains introduces bottlenecks in both labeled data acquisition and manual pipeline engineering. While recent MLE agents show promise in automating pipeline design, they have been studied almost exclusively in fully supervised settings, leaving them untested in realistic regimes where labeled data is scarce but unlabeled data is abundant. In this work, we introduce Agentic Semi-Supervised Learning (AgentSSL), framing SSL as a program search problem and studying how agents navigate this space under limited supervision. We find that even under weak feedback and matched compute, agents can synthesize code that combines and adapts established SSL techniques, exceeding the strongest human-engineered baselines in 8 of 12 settings by up to +21.8%. However, our results identify program selection as a critical bottleneck in AgentSSL, where performance drops by as much as 47% when selecting based on the agent's feedback metric. To systematically study this bottleneck, we introduce ProgramSelectBench, a large-scale benchmark with a combined total of 16,977 agent-generated and human-engineered SSL programs, and evaluate both unsupervised and active program selection methods. We further evaluate AgentSSL on real-world ecology detection tasks, highlighting the opportunities and challenges of transferring agent-discovered strategies beyond controlled benchmarks.

items.title: CoReMem: Cost-Internalizing Memory for Successive Coding Tasks with Prospective Valuation
items.abstract: Coding agents tackle successive tasks on an evolving repository, carrying forward edits and writing memory before the next task is known. Selecting memory for unknown next tasks requires balancing future usefulness against the costs of writing and reading it. The actor must also decide when acting on available memory saves effort as the task unfolds. We introduce Coding-Repository Memory (CoReMem), a cost-internalizing framework that guides memory design and actor adaptation through measured memory value on the next task. Prospective segment valuation compares runs of the next task with and without individual trajectory segments from the same inherited repository state, guiding a compact memory built around anchors: repository locations and executable checks. Actor adaptation estimates on-policy memory value within rollout groups with and without memory, using a reward that prioritizes resolution and penalizes step count in successful runs. Provenance-gated value credit assigns the additional value term to steps identified as using memory-supplied anchors, while every step retains outcome credit. On ChainSWE, CoReMem raises the 27B actor's resolve rate from 21.0% to 25.7%, with 17% fewer steps and 11% fewer total cache-aware tokens, including memory-module calls, relative to the untrained actor model without memory.

items.title: Sketching Language Models for Context Attribution
items.abstract: Context attribution asks how removing parts of a prompt changes a language model's output. We study leave-one-out (LOO) attribution for a prompt of $n$ tokens and a fixed measurement function. Computing all LOO values directly requires $n$ model evaluations. Under a stability assumption, our algorithm estimates all LOO values to error proportional to $\varepsilon$ with constant probability using $O(\sqrt{\log(1/\varepsilon)}/\varepsilon)$ evaluation calls. To complement our upper bound, we prove a matching $Ω(\sqrt{\log(1/\varepsilon)}/\varepsilon)$ lower bound on the number of evaluation calls in an oracle model. Empirically, we verify coefficient decay consistent with stability and evaluate the performance of our sketching algorithm on a small language-model retrieval task. Technically, our result is based on a sketching algorithm for arithmetic circuits whose Taylor coefficients satisfy the stability condition recently introduced by Gunn [Gun26]. A direct adaptation of their forward differentiation sketches would require $\widetilde{O}(\log(n)/\varepsilon^2)$ evaluation calls. Our key observation is that we can apply forward differentiation to the backpropagation circuit, with only constant overhead over a forward sketch of the same Taylor degree. This reduces the variance of the sketches and is key to our improved evaluation bound. Our lower bound builds on the techniques of Amsel, Chen, Duman Keles, Halikias, Musco, and Musco [ACDH+26, SIAM Journal on Matrix Analysis and Applications] for lower bounding the number of matrix-vector queries to estimate the diagonal elements of random matrices.

items.title: Classical Energies Learn to Reason 1,000x Faster than Looped Models
items.abstract: Looped models have emerged as a prominent paradigm for reasoning, with successes on simple reasoning puzzles such as Sudoku-Extreme and Maze-Unique. However, these models can be unstable, slow to train, and use many parameters and FLOPs to solve simple puzzles. Descent on an energy not only mitigates these issues but also offers advantages: built-in early stopping, compute that adapts to problem difficulty, fast training without differentiating through a solver, and interpretable weights that learn the constraints of the puzzle. Here we demonstrate this with a learned version of Hopfield & Tank's energy from the 80s, which we term CRAM, solves 99.996% of Sudoku-Extreme and 100% of Maze-Unique test puzzles after 42 ms and 132 ms of training on one GPU, at least 1,000x faster than looped models on these tasks. CRAM also matches baseline looped models at their highest accuracy on Sudoku-Extreme using at least 282x fewer inference FLOPs. Our work suggests two things. First, that energies are an extremely promising direction for training reasoning from data. Second, a caution against using trivially solvable benchmarks like Sudoku and Maze to test the scalability of looped reasoning techniques.
