items.title: A Parsec-scale Transient High-frequency-peaked Radio Source in the Very Large Array Sky Survey Brightening and Fading over a Decadal Timescale
items.abstract: Abstract A subset of active galactic nuclei (AGN) manifest as compact radio sources with peaked radio spectra, commonly referred to as peaked-spectrum (PS) sources. Generally, PS sources are interpreted as young radio jets, but the early evolution of the jet is rarely observed and not fully understood. Here, we present VT J182357-234511 (VT J1823-2345), a radio transient in the Very Large Array Sky Survey (VLASS) that resembles a PS source. Notable properties of VT J1823-2345 include (i) brightening by a factor of 3 between 1996 and 2021 at 1.4 GHz, (ii) peaked spectra with high-frequency peaks at ν p,obs ≳ 6 GHz, (iii) a peaked 3 GHz light curve that has been fading since 2023, (iv) a resolved Gaussian (major-axis) size of 0.4 mas in 2024, and (v) a linear polarization fraction p L ≃ 0.73% at 8.8 GHz with an extreme Faraday rotation measure RM obs ∼ +12,000 rad m −2 . On the sky, VT J1823-2345 coincides with a supernova remnant and an F-type star, but no background galaxy is seen. Based on the multiwavelength properties, we disfavor Galactic transients, explosive extragalactic transients, and blazar variability as plausible explanations. We argue that VT J1823-2345 is consistent with a “short-lived” parsec-scale PS source with a decades-old jet that does not grow into a large-scale radio galaxy. From comparing the full VLASS light curves, we speculate that VT J1823-2345 is similar to many VLASS nuclear transients reported in the literature, which may represent an emerging class of transient radio jets, perhaps related to episodic AGN activity or jetted tidal disruption events.

items.title: Star Formation History of Draco Revealed by DESI Data Release 1: Suppressed Early Star Formation Efficiency for Milky Way Dwarf Galaxies
items.abstract: Abstract Dwarf galaxies serve as fossils for understanding the early star formation history (SFH) of the local Universe. In this work, we use stellar abundances for individual stars derived from the first data release (DR1) of the Dark Energy Spectroscopic Instrument (DESI) to investigate the SFH of the dwarf spheroidal galaxy Draco. We simultaneously fit the stellar metallicity distribution function (MDF) and the [Mg/Fe]–[Fe/H] trend using the galactic chemical evolution (GCE) model flexCE . Our best-fit models imply a low star formation efficiency (SFE) of 0.003–0.007 Gyr −1 , which is about 10 times lower than values reported in literature, but consistent with recent SFE estimates for ultrafaint dwarf galaxies. By combining recent literature measurements, we find that the SFEs of Milky Way dwarf galaxies scale with stellar mass as SFE ∝ M ⋆ 0.24 . A low SFE is associated with a strong outflow efficiency; we estimate a large wind mass-loading factor η wind of ≃172–260. This is well in line with the observed outflow–stellar mass relation and with the Feedback in Realistic Environment (FIRE) cosmological simulations. Our results demonstrate the power of large-scale, low- to medium-resolution stellar spectroscopic surveys to deliver robust constraints on the early formation history of galaxies in the local Universe.

items.title: Cepheid Metallicity in the Leavitt Law (C--MetaLL) survey. X. First spectroscopic characterization of Galactic Type II Cepheids and calibration of the period--Wesenheit--metallicity relations
items.abstract: Type II Cepheids (T2Cs) are Population II pulsating stars that can be used as primary distance indicators thanks to their period--luminosity relation. Together with RR Lyrae stars and the tip of the red giant branch, they can provide an alternative route to the Hubble constant, independently evaluating possible systematic effects in its determination. We aim to build the largest homogeneous spectroscopic sample of Galactic T2Cs with iron and oxygen abundance measurements to investigate the impact of chemical composition on their period--luminosity relations. We observed 80 Galactic T2Cs with the high-resolution spectrograph UVES at the ESO Very Large Telescope. Starting from the spectra for a sample of 74 T2Cs we derived the stellar parameters as well as the iron and oxygen abundances through a self-consistent spectroscopic analysis based on the equivalent widths of the absorption lines. This sample has nearly doubled the number of T2Cs with spectroscopic metallicity determinations available in the literature. The resulting abundance measurements were used to test theoretical predictions for the instability strip and, together with Gaia parallaxes, to derive the period--Wesenheit--metallicity (PWZ) relations. We find, in agreement with model predictions, that the metallicity term (γ) is small and statistically consistent with zero in all investigated PWZ relations, ranging between γ ≃ - 0.02 and $+0.17$ mag dex -1 . We also estimated the distances to 22 Galactic Globular Clusters hosting T2Cs. The derived distances agree, within the uncertainties, with independent literature estimates. Our results indicate that metallicity has at most a minor impact on the pulsation properties and distance scale of T2Cs, confirming recent theoretical predictions and supporting the use of these variables as robust Population II distance indicators.

items.title: Electrical conductivity structure determined for the lunar lower mantle from Lunar Prospector and Kaguya-Selene magnetic data
items.abstract: The determination of induced magnetic fields in the Moon, produced by the electrical currents that flow within the Moon as a result of the time-variable external magnetic field, have formed the basis of successful electrical-conductivity structure studies of the lunar crust and mantle (e.g., Dyal and Parkin, 1971;Kuckes, 1971Kuckes, , 1973;;Sonett et al., 1971aSonett et al., , 1971b;;Leavy and Madden, 1974;Sonett and Duha, 1975;Hood et al., 1982;Khan et al., 2006;Mittelholz et al., 2021). Also, the lunar core size has been studied considering that it is a highly conducting metallic sphere overlain by an insulating mantle (e.g., Shimizu et al., 2013). In all these studies, the measures of the lunar magnetic fields (at the surface, in orbit, or in passing the Moon) have been provided by several missions (e.g., Apollo, Lunar Prospector and Kaguya Selene). However, none of the aforementioned studies have achieved a precise determination of the electrical conductivity structure for the lunar lower mantle.Consequently, the goal of this study is this precise determination applying the methodology described in the sections 2 (filtering) and 3 (modelling), to the magnetometer data provided by the Lunar Prospector (1998-1999) and Kaguya Selene (2007-2009) satellite missions. This methodology is needed to reduce noise and other undesirable perturbations (Hwang and Mitchell, 1986), increasing the signal/noise ratio to improve the computation of the transfer functions, and the modelling performed in this study has been successfully applied to other previous studies (Corchete 2026a and2026b). Thus, the above-mentioned studies of the lunar crust, upper and midmantle will be completed with the present characterization (in terms of electrical conductivity) of the lunar lower mantle structure.Both, Lunar Prospector (LP; Hood et al., 2001) and Kaguya Selene (KS; Takahashi et al., 2009) missions have provided the magnetic data used in this study. For each dataset (LP and KS magnetic data), the records of each magnetic field component (B x (t), B y (t), B z (t)), with the time t give in seconds and (XYZ) in the Cartesian coordinate system (with origin in the lunar center), are converted to magnetic field components (B r (t), B  (t), B  (t)) measured in a spherical coordinate system (with the same origin). This observed magnetic field B(r, t)  (B r (t), B  (t), B  (t)) is assumed as a potential field, i.e., B(r, t)  grad (V(r, t)), where r  (r, , ) is the position vector of a given location, grad () is the gradient operator, and V(r, t)  V e (r, t) + V i (r, t) is a scalar potential given by (Mittelholz et al., Gauss coefficients of degree n and order m, respectively. The potential field assumption given by (1)implies that the satellites (LP and KS) are in vacuum, but really, they are moving in a low-density plasma (Baumjohann and Treumann, 1996). However, Hood and Schubert (1978) concluded that the magnetohydrodynamic effects for induction sounding are negligible at low frequencies (< 10 3 Hz).Then, the field representation given by ( 1) is justified. On the other hand, for Earth and at periods longer than one day, the structure of the time-varying external field is mostly governed by the magnetospheric ring current, and it can be described by a zonal spherical harmonic of degree one (Price, 1967;Banks, 1969;Olsen, 1999;Kuvshinov et al., 2021). items.title: The Daopological Cosmic Evolution and the Great Physics Forks: From Discrete Topological Phase Transitions to Macroscopic Smooth Approximations
items.abstract: Modern physics is confronted with three massive dilemmas: the mathematical breakdown of General Relativity at singularities, the elusive nature of dark matter after half a century of search, and the fundamental logical contradiction between Quantum Field Theory and General Relativity. Based on the Daopological Physics framework, this paper reconstructs the essence of the universe as a pure mathematical discrete graph network. We provide a unified logical framework to deduce cosmic evolution from discrete topological phase transitions. As the network evolves and undergoes topological phase transitions, physical properties emerge progressively across five distinct stages. This paper not only presents theoretical deductions but also delves into the event-driven asynchronous network mechanism, the statistical limit essence of the speed of light, and the physical truth of gravity as topological equivalent refraction. Crucially, a rigorous "falsification path" is attached to each evolutionary stage, detailing how future high-energy physics, gravitational wave astronomy, and quantum optics experiments can either confirm or falsify this grand hypothesis.

items.title: We Never Experience the Present: A Layered Lookback-Time Framework of Physical and Neural Delays
items.abstract: Human experience feels instantaneous, yet every perception involves a chain of physical and biological delays. Light travels from an object to the eye at a finite speed, followed by visual signal processing in the retina and brain. This paper presents a layered framework for understanding perceptual lookback time by combining physical light-travel delay and neural processing delay. It examines examples ranging from everyday objects, such as mobile phones and nearby people, to astronomical objects such as the Moon, the Sun, and distant stars. The analysis demonstrates that for everyday visual experiences, neural processing delays dominate over the extremely small physical light-travel delays. At astronomical distances, however, light-travel time becomes significant, allowing us to observe celestial objects as they existed in the past. The paper also discusses predictive processing in the brain, the concept of simultaneity in special relativity, and the relationship between perception and the present moment. This work is a review and theoretical synthesis based on established findings in physics, astronomy, and neuroscience. It proposes a simple quantitative framework for understanding why human perception does not provide direct access to an instantaneous present.

items.title: Artificial Intelligence for Scientific Discovery: A Review Of Methods, Landmark Applications and The Emergence Of Autonomous Research
items.abstract: Artificial Intelligence is transforming how science is done by helping researchers analyse complex data, uncover hidden patterns, generate hypotheses and accelerate discovery across disciplines. This review examines the role of AI in scientific discovery, covering methods, applications, benefits, challenges and future possibilities. Machine learning, deep learning, physics-informed neural networks, equation discovery, natural language processing of scientific literature, reinforcement learning and generative AI are explained in terms of how they support data-driven investigation. Landmark applications are reviewed across structural biology, drug and antibiotic discovery, chemistry, materials science, physics, fusion-energy control, mathematics, astronomy and weather and climate forecasting. The emergence of autonomous laboratories and language-model agents that plan and execute experiments is discussed. A five-layer framework for AI-assisted discovery comprising data, representation, modelling, hypothesis generation and experimental validation is proposed, with research gaps, objectives, a comparison of AI roles and challenges including data quality, interpretability, reproducibility, physical consistency and the risk of over-reliance. The review concludes that AI is most powerful as a partner to scientists, accelerating the cycle of hypothesis, experiment and understanding while human judgement guides what is meaningful.

items.title: A Multidimensional Feature Optimization and Machine Learning-Based Predictive Framework for Automated Wine Quality Assessment
items.abstract: Abstract Assessment of wine quality is an essential step in the wine industry, where traditional evaluation methods mainly depend on expert sensory analysis and physicochemical testing. However, these conventional approaches are often time-consuming, expensive, and influenced by subjective human judgment. In this context, wine quality evaluation by alternative computer based-methods is gaining substantial interest to overcome traditional assessment related challenges. In this context, the present study aimed at investigating the wine quality by machine learning based approaches using available wine datasets of different origin and to promote the speed of automation in wine industry. The proposed framework integrates both feature selection methods (e.g., multiple dimensionality reduction techniques, including filter-, wrapper-, and embedded-based) and feature transformation techniques (e.g., principal component analysis (PCA) and Linear Discriminant Analysis (LDA)). Furthermore, we employed other machine learning and ensemble models such as Logistic Regression, K-Nearest Neighbour, Random Forest, Support Vector Classifier, Extra Trees Classifier, Gradient Boosting, Voting Ensemble, Stacking Ensemble, and a Hybrid Ensemble models, for the assessment of wine quality classification. Experimental results demonstrate that the correlation-based filter feature selection method achieved the best overall performance when combined with the proposed Hybrid Ensemble model, obtaining an accuracy of 89.08% and an F1-score of 88.93%. The findings indicate that dimensionality reduction combined with ensemble learning significantly improves prediction performance while reducing feature redundancy and computational complexity. The proposed approach provides an efficient and reliable framework for automated wine quality assessment and decision support in the wine industry.

items.title: Bibliometric Analysis of Global Research Trends on Simulation Studies of AlGaN/GaN High-Electron-Mobility Transistors Using the Scopus Database
items.abstract: Abstract As the design space of AlGaN/GaN high-electron-mobility transistors (HEMTs) grows increasingly complex, simulation has become an indispensable tool for understanding device physics and optimizing performance before fabrication. However, few studies have measured and analyzed the scientific publications on AlGaN/GaN HEMT simulation from a global perspective. In this bibliometric study, our aim was to evaluate the global research trends in AlGaN/GaN HEMT simulation areas based on publication outputs, co-authorships among countries, and co-occurrences of author keywords. Using the Scopus database, a total of 4,492 journal articles and conference papers published between 1997 and 2026 were retrieved and analyzed using VOSviewer. Results have shown that since 2001, the number of publications has increased steadily, with the highest annual output recorded in 2025 (490 articles), resulting in a steady increase in the cumulative total publications. China (1,284 articles) and India (961 articles) are the leading contributors, followed by the USA (695 articles); however, Belgium, the UAE, and Singapore exhibit the highest rates of international collaboration. A keyword co-occurrence analysis of 61 keywords revealed six distinct thematic clusters, dominated by power/thermal management, device/HEMT core, modeling/RF, TCAD/gate, electric field, and machine learning. The most recently active keywords include TCAD simulation, gate leakage current, power amplifier, and S-parameter, suggesting a growing emphasis on simulation-driven design and RF performance in recent years. In conclusion, recent progress in AlGaN/GaN HEMT simulation research includes the following (but not limited to): (i) integration of advanced TCAD and physics-based models for trap dynamics and self-heating; (ii) AI-driven and machine learning approaches for device modeling; and (iii) continued exploration of p-GaN gate and enhancement-mode structures for high-power and high-frequency applications.

items.title: Dream interpretation in the Amazon Rainforest: “Wayusa Space” as an organizing element in a metamethodology for psychoanalytic dream theory 1
items.abstract: Two North American psychoanalysts made a number of journeys into the Amazon Rainforest to interact with dream interpreters practicing in an indigenous culture that places dream interpretation at the center of daily life for individuals and communities. The psychoanalysts found that the work of sophisticated dream interpreters in the Achuar communities of southeastern Ecuador and northwestern Peru showed important similarities, as well as important differences, with psychoanalytic dream interpretation. This article provides a brief description of the Achuar cultural context and describes practices of the Wayusa ritual, named for the Wayusa plant, used to make a tea which is consumed as part of the ritual. Notably, although the Achuar people use hallucinogens for many purposes, the Wayusa plant used in dream-interpreting rituals is not hallucinogenic. Special forms of rationality are used to interpret dreams, distinct from the processes engaged in dreams and hallucinations. This paper sketches a philosophy of science approach to the study of dreams and dream interpretation, using the concept of “ Wayusa Space” to contribute to a metamethodology for psychoanalytic dream theory. A clinical example of dream interpretation in the rainforest is used to illustrate group processes in the Wayusa ritual. Careful consideration of these processes reveals how “ Wayusa Space” contributes new levels of analysis for the psychoanalytic understanding of dreams.

items.title: Physics-informed 3D source localization from multichannel seismocardiography
items.abstract: Seismocardiography (SCG) provides a non-invasive means of monitoring cardiac mechanical activity using wearable accelerometers. However, conventional SCG is typically recorded at a single chest location, limiting the spatial interpretation of the measured vibrations. In this study, we investigate whether multichannel SCG can be used to reconstruct the three-dimensional distribution of cardiac mechanical sources. We developed a physics-informed framework combining an electromechanical finite-element heart model, an attenuating transverse-shear radiation model, and a three-dimensional inverse reconstruction pipeline. Synthetic multichannel SCG signals without valve transients (hence not clinical SCG) were reconstructed using delay-and-sum (DAS), minimum variance distortionless response (MVDR), CLEAN, and sparse Bayesian learning (SBL). Three of the four recovered both position and shape on at least one array geometry. Our sparse Bayesian implementation localized the source but recovered no volume, collapsing onto a few voxels; thus, we report it as an approach we could not successfully adapt. Localization and robustness were evaluated against null controls and under varying noise levels, propagation uncertainties, and array geometries. With the source displaced 2 cm from the array center, a fully enclosing array, as a theoretical upper bound rather than a wearable configuration, recovered the centroid to 0.7–0.9 cm. On a more realizable one-sided array, the estimators separated: sparse deconvolution reached 1.0 cm and the adaptive beamformer 1.7 cm, both inside a 2.0 cm no-information baseline, while conventional delay-and-sum fell well outside it. Shape recovery cleared that baseline on both array geometries and collapsed when inter-channel phase was randomized. Reconstruction remained robust to measurement noise and moderate wave-speed mismatch but was more sensitive to geometric and registration errors. These findings indicate that multichannel seismocardiography, in principle, carries spatial information sufficient to localize cardiac mechanical activity in three dimensions. However, on a one-sided array, that recovery depends on the estimator, and centroid accuracy there requires an unmodeled local shear-speed contrast to stay within roughly 20– 30 % for the most tolerant estimator, and about 10 % for the adaptive one. Shape recovery is the more robust of the two. Forward and inverse models share the same physics, a limit that a structural mismatch test bounds but does not remove.

items.title: The solar-cycle and 27-day patterns of solar-wind plasma types at earth and the magnetospheric reactions
items.abstract: There are 27-day patterns and solar-cycle patterns to the passage of different solar-wind plasma types at Earth given off by the different regions of the rotating, changing Sun. The four types of solar-wind plasma are coronal-hole-origin plasma, streamer-belt-origin plasma, sector-reversal-region plasma, and ejecta. The different plasma types have systematically different properties (e.g., solar-wind speed, magnetic-field strength, Mach number, and Alfvénicity) The different plasmas produce different environments for the Earth and each plasma type drives the Earth differently, producing 27-day and solar-cycle temporal patterns of geomagnetic activity. Geomagnetic storms occur mainly during coronal-hole-origin plasma (modulated by the Russell-McPherron effect) and during ejecta and geomagnetic calms occur during sector-reversal-region plasma and streamer-belt-origin plasma. For coronal-hole-origin plasma at Earth, an interplay between the hemispheric-number asymmetry of sunspots and the 22-year Hale magnetic cycle has been seen that will affect the occurrence of high-speed-stream-driven storms at Earth and the intensity of the electron radiation belt by biasing the Russell-McPherron effect. For the different solar-wind plasmas, the difference in driving and the different ambient environments both effect the particle populations of the Earth’s magnetosphere such as the cold plasmasphere, the magnetotail plasma sheet, and the electron radiation belt. The interactions of solar-wind plasmas, geomagnetic activity, and magnetospheric particle populations are explored in the present study, with particular attention paid to 27-day and solar-cycle variations.

items.title: The Diagnostic Dilemma of Acute Vestibular Syndrome: Why HINTS Outperforms Diffusion-weighted magnetic resonance imaging?
items.abstract: Objectives To evaluate the diagnostic approaches, specifically the comparative accuracy of bedside clinical examinations versus early neuroimaging, in differentiating central from peripheral causes of Acute Vestibular Syndrome (AVS). Methods A comprehensive narrative literature review was conducted utilizing established scientific databases, including PubMed/Medline, Scopus, Web of Science, and Embase, covering articles published up to 2024. A structured search strategy was applied using keywords such as "Acute Vestibular Syndrome", "Central vestibular dysfunction", "Peripheral vestibular dysfunction", and "HINTS protocol". Peer-reviewed clinical trials, mechanistic studies, and authoritative guidelines were included to synthesize the current evidence regarding the diagnosis and management of acute vertigo. Results The synthesis of the literature reveals that targeted bedside neuro-otological examinations demonstrate superior sensitivity (96.8%) and specificity (98.5%) compared to early "Diffusion-weighted magnetic resonance imaging" in detecting posterior circulation strokes within the initial 48 hours. Early neuroimaging frequently yields false-negative results in up to 14.3% of ischemic events. Conclusion Accurate differentiation of etiologies in continuous vertigo relies heavily on structured bedside clinical assessments rather than immediate neuroimaging. Implementing these clinical protocols prevents severe neurological sequelae from missed posterior fossa strokes while simultaneously avoiding unnecessary healthcare expenditures for benign peripheral conditions.

items.title: Cryo-EM structures of an anti-MLC1 Fab in apo and peptide-bound states reveal the basis of antigen recognition.
items.abstract: Monoclonal antibodies are widely used to detect and characterize membrane proteins, yet for most such reagents, the molecular basis of target recognition remains structurally undefined. Here, we report the structural and biochemical characterization of 37E5, a monoclonal antibody that recognizes MLC1, an astrocytic membrane protein implicated in gliovascular homeostasis and megalencephalic leukoencephalopathy with subcortical cysts. 37E5 specifically detects endogenous MLC1 across multiple experimental systems, including brain lysates and mouse and human brain tissues, and binds purified human MLC1 with nanomolar affinity as determined by biolayer interferometry. To define the molecular basis of recognition, we determined 3.2 and 3.0 Å cryo-EM structures of the 37E5 Fab in apo and antigen-bound states, respectively. The antigen-bound structure revealed continuous density for an MLC1-derived peptide within the paratope, stabilized by coordinated hydrogen-bonding, ionic, and hydrophobic interactions. Structural comparison between apo and bound states showed localized conformational changes confined to the complementarity-determining regions, consistent with a restrained, local induced-fit adjustment of the paratope; because these backbone deviations are small, they are interpreted only in the context of the coordinate uncertainty expected at this resolution. Comparative analyses further explained species-dependent recognition through sequence variation at key epitope residues, corroborated by binding assays across four MLC1 orthologs. These findings define the structural basis of selective MLC1 recognition by 37E5 and illustrate, for this antibody-peptide pair, how experimental cryo-EM structures complement AI-based prediction methods by resolving peptide orientation and interaction geometry at the antibody-antigen interface.

items.title: Mapping myelin oligodendrocyte glycoprotein antibody-associated disease (MOGAD) and neuromyelitis optica spectrum disorders (NMOSD): A global review of publicly listed patient disease registries and databases.
items.abstract: Background Real-world data are crucial to improving care for patients with rare diseases. Objectives To develop the first global map of myelin oligodendrocyte glycoprotein antibody-associated disease (MOGAD) and neuromyelitis optica spectrum disorders (NMOSD) patient registries/databases. Registries/databases were identified through rare disease portals, registry websites, and other sources, and surveyed. Results Of the respondents ( N = 26), the majority were established within the past 15 years and reported being self-funded. Most collect diagnostic, clinical, and laboratory data. Major objectives included supporting scientific research and advancing disease understanding. Conclusions Despite cost, time, resource, and data quality challenges, registries/databases provide important insights into addressing unmet needs in MOGAD and NMOSD.

items.title: Ecological assessment of executive functions and reasoning in Colombian children: cross-validation and measurement invariance of the Spanish CORE-6/10.
items.abstract: Ecological assessment of executive function (EF) in children relies heavily on informant-report instruments that rarely include logical-abstract reasoning, while culturally grounded measures developed originally in Spanish for Latin American populations remain scarce. This study examined the psychometric structure, internal cross-validation, and measurement invariance of the CORE-6/10, a Spanish-language informant-report instrument for children aged 6-10 years assessing five executive domains and two naturalistic reasoning dimensions: verbal-logical and perceptual-analytical reasoning. Validation used non-overlapping calibration and confirmation subsamples ( N = 391; EFA: n = 195; CFA: n = 196), polychoric matrices, parallel analysis, ULS oblimin EFA, and WLSMV CFA; invariance was tested across sex, age, and informant type. The seven correlated-factor model was retained as the best-fitting admissible solution (CFI = .940, TLI = .935, RMSEA = .049, SRMR = .081). An exploratory bifactor analysis suggested substantial general-factor saturation (ωh = .71; ECV = .50), although estimation anomalies precluded treating it as a primary confirmatory model. Internal consistency was adequate (ordinal α = .76-.87), with change-based evidence consistent with approximate scalar invariance across comparisons (|ΔCFI| ≤.005). Reasoning dimensions showed general-factor loadings (.476-.735) comparable to core EF domains, suggesting shared variance with general executive functioning while retaining domain-specific variance. Findings support the empirical relevance of reasoning within this ecological measurement framework and the CORE-6/10 as a promising culturally grounded instrument for research in Colombian children, with potential future applications in school-based screening pending independent replication, multimethod validation, normative development, and evidence of classification accuracy.

items.title: EXPRESS: Brain Age Gap from Non-Contrast CT Is Independently Associated with Functional Outcome after Acute Ischemic Stroke.
items.abstract: BackgroundOutcomes after acute ischemic stroke (AIS) vary beyond lesion burden and clinical severity, suggesting a role for baseline structural brain vulnerability. We evaluated whether brain age gap (BrainAGE) derived from routine non-contrast computed tomography (NCCT) is associated with functional outcome after AIS.MethodsWe analyzed 1,173 AIS patients from a prospective multicenter cohort. A deep learning model estimated brain age from contralesional baseline NCCT to minimize lesion-related confounding. BrainAGE was defined as predicted minus chronological age. The primary outcome was 90-day functional status, assessed using proportional odds regression adjusted for age, sex, baseline stroke severity, early ischemic changes, and reperfusion therapy.ResultsBrainAGE was higher in AIS patients than in controls (+3.1 ± 9.1 years; p<0.001). Higher BrainAGE was associated with worse functional outcome after adjustment for age, sex, and other clinical predictors (POR 1.091 per 5 years; 95% CI 1.023-1.162; p=0.008). BrainAGE improved model fit but modestly improved discrimination.ConclusionsBrainAGE from routine NCCT provided modest incremental prognostic information beyond age and conventional clinical predictors. These findings support CT-based BrainAGE as a marker of brain health complementary to established prognostic factors. Whether BrainAGE improves patient-level risk stratification or clinical decision-making requires independent external validation and prospective evaluation.

items.title: Transcriptional and Epigenetic Regulation of Atoh1 and Its Therapeutic Applications for Hair Cell Regeneration in the Inner Ear.
items.abstract: This review centers on the transcription factor Atoh1 (Atonal homolog 1, also known as Math1) and its pivotal regulatory role in the development and regeneration of inner ear hair cells (HCs). It systematically elucidates the activation mechanisms of Atoh1, its integrated upstream and downstream regulatory networks, and the involvement of key signaling pathways. Additionally, the review comparatively analyzes the differences in regenerative capacity between cochlear and vestibular HCs and provides a comprehensive evaluation of the research progress and existing challenges associated with various Atoh1-targeted intervention strategies. By constructing a systematic theoretical framework, this review aims to offer a solid foundation for deciphering the molecular mechanisms underlying HC regeneration, optimizing clinical therapeutic strategies, and advancing the translational application of research in this field.

items.title: The expansion of kinase drug discovery: new targets, platforms and indications.
items.abstract: In the past 25 years, kinase drug discovery has grown into one of the most thriving areas in pharmaceutical research and development. What began as a field dominated by ATP-competitive small molecules has diversified into a broad therapeutic landscape that includes allosteric and covalent inhibitors, activators, proximity-induced modulators, targeted protein degraders and antibody-based therapies, with more than 150 regulatory approvals so far worldwide. In this Review, we provide a comprehensive analysis of the current kinase therapeutic landscape, including more than 2,100 kinase-targeting agents that have entered clinical development in more than 23,000 clinical trials. We cover drug platforms, new targeting approaches, the expanding target spectrum, approvals and clinical trends. Nearly half of the canonical human protein kinases have at least one clinical-stage agent, placing kinases among the most intensively explored drug target classes. Nevertheless, development remains highly concentrated around a small set of blockbuster kinase targets, such as EGFR. We also examine the features associated with successful kinase-targeting agents and causes of agent discontinuations and regulatory withdrawal.

items.title: UNC13A splice correction rescues synaptic dysfunction induced by TDP-43 loss.
items.abstract: TDP-43 nuclear depletion is a defining pathological feature of amyotrophic lateral sclerosis and frontotemporal dementia that induces widespread cryptic splicing defects in hundreds of transcripts 1-8 . Despite this, whether TDP-43 loss affects synaptic function has remained unclear. Here we show that TDP-43 loss induces a predegenerative state in which neurons remain structurally intact but suffer a substantial breakdown in synaptic communication. Genetic correction of a single cryptic splicing event in UNC13A was sufficient to rescue these deficits. We developed splice-switching antisense oligonucleotides that correct UNC13A cryptic splicing in human cortical and spinal motor neurons and in a humanized mouse model. In human neurons this intervention restored spontaneous and evoked synaptic vesicle release, release probability at individual synapses and wider network synchrony. Together, this establishes UNC13A splice correction as a mechanistically defined and genetically validated therapeutic strategy relevant to roughly 97% of patients with amyotrophic lateral sclerosis and roughly 50% of patients with frontotemporal dementia with TDP-43 pathology.

items.title: Are cueing effects really "negligible" when accuracy is emphasized and single masks eliminate uncertainty about target location?
items.abstract: Does spatial attention operate primarily by minimizing decision-related noise or by enhancing information from the attended location? While emphasizing and only reporting accuracy, Shiu and Pashler (Journal of Experimental Psychology. Human Perception and Performance, 20 (5), 1037-1054, 1994) found "negligible" effects of spatial pre-cues when uncertainty about the target's location was eliminated by a single mask, a finding often cited in favor of the idea that spatial pre-cues improve performance by reducing uncertainty (and not by signal enhancement). In a similar, single-mask condition, and while emphasizing reaction time (RT), Prasad and Hommel (Experimental Psychology, 71 (3):135-143, 2024), found significant cueing effects in reaction time and accuracy, which is consistent with signal enhancement. Stimulated by this empirical discrepancy, we implemented the fundamental methods of these studies to explore how invalid versus valid cues affected participant RT and accuracy. In each of two experiments we included a speed-stress manipulation: emphasizing response speed in one group and accuracy in the other. In Experiment 1, clear cueing effects were found in RT and accuracy across all conditions. In Experiment 2, with randomized single- and multiple-mask trials rather than blocked, the consistent cueing effects found in E1 were generally supported. Importantly, regardless of speed versus accuracy emphasis, we found robust cueing effects in the single-mask condition in both RT and accuracy. Whereas our results support signal enhancement as one mechanism of cueing effects, we acknowledge that multiple mechanisms may be operating to affect performance in a Posner-style cueing paradigm. OPEN PRACTICES STATEMENT: The studies presented here were preregistered on the Open Science Framework (OSF). The preregistrations, raw (trial-level) data from both experiments, experimental code, and analysis script can all be found can be found at: https://osf.io/2dcvj/.

items.title: FlAsH-ID enables live-cell photoproximity labeling with a short peptide tag.
items.abstract: Proximity labeling has emerged as a valuable tool for the interrogation of protein-protein and protein-RNA interactions. Almost all proximity labeling methods are deployed using large fusion proteins, which, while powerful in many contexts, can disrupt native biology or obscure important epitopes on the protein under study. Here we develop a photoproximity labeling method that is localized to a short 6-aa peptide sequence. Termed FlAsH-ID, this method uses the combination of the Tsien tetracysteine tag with the FlAsH dye for localized singlet oxygen generation. We demonstrate that this green-light-based method is nontoxic and can be used to label proteins within several cellular compartments. Lastly, we establish that FlAsH-ID can be deployed in primary CD8 + T cells to assess the interactome of the transcription factor RUNX3. Our results suggest this technique will expand the field of proximity labeling to small, functionally sensitive proteins in primary cells without perturbing their function.

items.title: Pharmacological chaperone treatment with Cystadane in aspartylglucosaminuria: an open-label, phase Ib/II trial.
items.abstract: This phase Ib/II investigator-initiated, open label trial aims to show the safety and efficacy of Cystadane (betaine) in aspartylglucosaminuria, a lysosomal storage disorder characterized by progressive cognitive decline, in Finnish patients homozygous for the Finnish major mutation, aged between 3 and 17 years at study begin (recruited: 25, analyzed: 21). Oral Cystadane efficacy and safety were studied over 48 months. The primary endpoint of the study, reduction of glycoasparagines in the urine, was quantitatively determined using liquid chromatography/mass spectrometry and normalized to urine creatinine. Urine glycoasparagines are significantly reduced upon Cystadane treatment (by 68.6% ±10.8%; p = 0.000), and the study thus meets its primary endpoint. Our data show that Cystadane/betaine efficiently improves the main disease biomarker, and it is safe to use in aspartylglucosaminuria. Further studies should be carried out in a larger patient population over a longer time to demonstrate the effects on disease progression. EudraCT registration number 2017-000645-48.

items.title: Experience modifies the synaptome architecture in the developing and adult mouse brain.
items.abstract: Synaptome architecture describes the spatiotemporal distribution of highly diverse excitatory synapses throughout the brain. Whether and how this architecture is impacted by experience and sensory input is unknown. We found that environmental enrichment and monocular visual deprivation drive large-scale reconfiguration of excitatory synapse populations in more than one hundred regions of the mouse brain. Different experiences modify distinct subsets of synapse types and subtypes, with patterns aligned with protein turnover rates and connectome architecture. Similarity in experience-dependent reconfiguration during development and adulthood indicates shared mechanisms of synaptome adaptation across the lifespan. Our findings support a population-selection model in which experiences drive adaptation by selectively modifying synapse types and subtypes distributed across the brain. Experience-driven reconfiguration of synaptome architecture shares features with the response to aging, sleep deprivation, brain injury and genetic mutations, supporting a unifying principle of brain adaptation.

items.title: Effects of Cerebellar and Primary Motor Cortex tDCS Montages on Vocal Performance in Singers: A Randomized Trial.
items.abstract: Transcranial direct current stimulation (tDCS) is a non-invasive method to transiently adjust cortical excitability. Initial studies have reported changes in vocal parameters; however, it remains unclear whether tDCS can enhance the effects of structured vocal training. Therefore, this study aimed to compare the effects of sham stimulation with active tDCS using primary motor cortex (M1) or cerebellar electrode montages, when combined with vocal exercises in singers. Forty-five adult singers, without vocal symptoms or brain dysfunction, participated in this triple-blind randomized clinical trial. The participants underwent a 2-week intervention consisting of daily 20-minute tDCS sessions combined with a vocal exercise protocol, assigned to one of three groups: active anodal tDCS (2 mA) over either cerebellum or M1, or sham stimulation. All groups performed straw phonation in water (SPW). Voice recordings were taken before the intervention, after five and 10 sessions of intervention and at the follow-up (1 month after the intervention program) to assess the following vocal parameters: vocal range profile (VRP); vocal quality (jitter, shimmer, irregularity, glottal-to-noise excitation ratio - GNE, harmonic-to-noise ratio - HNR, smoothed cepstral peak prominence - CPPS and dysphonia acoustic index - DAI); Laryngeal neuromuscular control and coordination (Laryngeal diadochokinesis - LDDK), and self-reported vocal effort. Cerebellar anodal tDCS was associated with gains in VRP that were sustained over time, along with improvements in vocal quality during low-intensity phonation and an early reduction in perceived vocal effort compared with sham stimulation. In contrast, exploratory within-group changes were observed in the M1 group in high-intensity vocal quality (DAI), laryngeal coordination, and perceived vocal effort, without establishing an additional benefit over sham. Overall, superiority of active tDCS over sham during vocal training was not established, and the exploratory findings require confirmation.

items.title: From Rapid Synaptic Events to Lasting Antidepressant States: Convergent and Divergent Mechanisms of Ketamine and Psychedelics.
items.abstract: Rapid-acting antidepressants have challenged the long-standing view that therapeutic improvement in major depressive disorder requires chronic treatment with monoaminergic agents. Ketamine and classical psychedelics act through distinct proximal targets, yet both can produce rapid and persistent behavioral effects that implicate synaptic and circuit plasticity as the core mechanisms of antidepressant action. This review, based on a minisymposium presented at the 2026 Society for Neuroscience meeting, examines how brief pharmacological perturbations translate into lasting changes in mood-related networks. We first discuss hippocampal mechanisms underlying ketamine action, which include brain-derived neurotrophic factor (BDNF)/tropomyosin receptor kinase B (TrkB)-dependent homeostatic potentiation, TrkB cross talk with metabotropic glutamate receptor 5 (mGluR5) at CA3→CA1 synapses, extracellular signal-regulated kinase (ERK)-dual-specificity phosphatase 6 (DUSP6)-mediated extension of synaptic metaplasticity, and BDNF release at mossy fiber synapses and dentate gyrus neuronal maturation. We then consider how these local plasticity mechanisms interface with distributed circuits that regulate motivation, stress coping, and reward. Across brain regions, emerging work highlights the importance of cell type- and region-specific mechanisms that mediate ketamine's therapeutic actions. We expand on local prefrontal cortical inhibitory cellular signaling dynamics, including the interplay of various G-protein-coupled receptors (GPCRs) in cortical somatostatin interneurons and input-specific adaptations in accumbal circuits. Finally, we compare ketamine with psilocybin, an emerging therapeutic classic psychedelic for treatment-resistant depression that targets the 5-hydroxytryptamine 2A (5-HT2A) receptor primarily. A recurring theme is that an interplay of GPCRs can help shape the timing, localization, and persistence of ketamine-induced neuroplasticity. Together, these studies suggest that antidepressant efficacy arises not from a single pathway or brain region but from coordinated, temporally staged plasticity across molecules, synapses, cells, and circuits.

items.title: Transforming Neuroscience Research through AI-Driven Data Integration and Analysis.
items.abstract: Integrating multimodal data is essential to advance neuroscience as a discipline. Large-scale collaborative efforts, exemplified by the BRAIN Initiative, together with advances in single-cell and spatial omics, multimodal imaging, human genetics, behavioral phenotyping, protein structure prediction, and related technologies, are transforming neuroscience into a data-rich, highly interconnected science. As experimental resources, scientific literature, and collaborative networks continue to expand, integrating discoveries across modalities, species, and levels of biological organization has become the field's central bottleneck. This Perspective argues that artificial intelligence (AI) is becoming essential for overcoming these constraints. Using six evolving approaches we outline strategies to accelerate AI adoption through community building and pilot projects that drive AI transformation at both the organizational and technological levels. Organizational transformation cultivates broad AI awareness and a pro-AI culture while technological transformation improves the efficiency, scalability, and quality of data analysis, allowing researchers to generate insights more rapidly and effectively. Together, these advances position AI as a key driver for advancing neuroscience at scale.

items.title: Integrating Cytoskeletal Systems in Neurons and Glia: Dynamic Orchestration of Structure and Function.
items.abstract: Neurons and glia form the circuitry of our nervous system, allowing nerve cells to communicate with each other and other cell types throughout the body in a highly specific manner to integrate sensory, motor, and cognitive functions. The ability of these cells to do this is profoundly dependent on an elaborate and dynamic cytoskeleton which allows these cells to adopt complex shapes and specialized structures such as myelin sheaths, the blood-brain barrier, axonal growth cones, dendritic spines, nodes of Ranvier, synapses, and elaborate sensory organs. The cytoskeleton is also critical for morphogenetic movements, the migration of neuronal precursors, and axon growth, which together establish the organization and wiring pattern of the central and peripheral nervous system during development. This review provides a primer on our current understanding of the cytoskeleton of neurons and glia, with an emphasis on how the protein polymers of the cytoskeleton-microtubules, actin filaments, intermediate filaments, and septins-work together to orchestrate the remarkable shapes and functions of these cells. We also highlight key questions and challenges for the field and technological advances that may help address them.

items.title: Focused Ultrasound Neuromodulation: Biophysical Mechanisms, Neural Effects, and Clinical Translation.
items.abstract: Low-intensity transcranial ultrasound stimulation (TUS) has emerged as a promising noninvasive neuromodulation technology capable of targeting both cortical and deep brain structures with millimeter-scale spatial precision. Recent advances in ultrasound hardware, acoustic modeling, neuronavigation, and multimodal imaging have accelerated the field from proof-of-concept demonstrations toward mechanistic investigation and early clinical translation. In parallel, growing evidence from animal and human studies has begun to clarify how ultrasound influences neural activity across cellular, circuit, and systems levels. In this review, we synthesize recent progress in understanding the biophysical mechanisms, neurophysiological effects, and network-level consequences of TUS. We discuss insights from optical imaging, electrophysiology, EEG source imaging, and functional MRI, highlighting how these complementary approaches reveal cell-type-specific responses, bidirectional modulation of neural circuits, and distributed changes in functional connectivity beyond the sonicated target. We further examine evidence that functional imaging is evolving from a simple measure of regional activation to a multidimensional biomarker of target engagement, circuit modulation, and treatment response. Despite these advances, important challenges remain. We conclude that TUS is approaching a translational inflection point in which rigorous mechanistic studies, standardized methodologies, and imaging-based biomarkers can establish ultrasound as both a powerful causal neuroscience tool and a clinically viable neuromodulation therapy for disorders involving dysfunctional brain circuits.

items.title: Placental-Neural Cross Talk: Biological Mechanisms Shaping Brain Architecture.
items.abstract: Impact of placental function on normal and pathological brain processes and supported behavior is an integrative research area dubbed "neuroplacentology." Placental functional genetics, structure, and vascular function have been discovered to have links to multiple clinical outcomes: autism, schizophrenia, and developmental cognitive impairment in offspring and postpartum depression and cognition in mothers. There are significant data showing that long-term impacts of preterm birth, diseases of pregnancy (preeclampsia), and maternal stress and depression may all be mediated by placental mechanisms, providing clinical and translational insights. Here, we will provide an up-to-date introduction to this emerging field. Mechanistic links between variations in placental structure and function and features of human and animal brain development and function will be discussed, clarifying basic biological connections and highlighting new targets to prevent clinical impairments.

items.title: Learning to Navigate a Changing World: From Brain Systems to Novel Algorithms.
items.abstract: Natural organisms navigate a world in constant flux and are frequently confronted with sensory ambiguity and shifting goals. While biological systems can adapt rapidly to navigate in novel and nonstationary environments, this challenge remains a significant hurdle for artificial intelligence. In this review, we examine recent progress in understanding neurobiological systems that allow for adaptive, efficient spatial and abstract navigation in dynamic environments and how these observations have informed new developments for the same behavior in machines. We highlight how predictive learning serves as a unifying framework to describe the organization of neural activity across distributed systems for navigation, including the hippocampal formation, parietal cortex, and higher-order associative structures. Specifically, we explore how such neurobiological systems encode expected future states, dynamic target trajectories, action plans, and internal behavioral strategies. Finally, we contrast the diffuse, inefficient exploration of canonical artificial agents with the structured, efficient control policies for goal-directed navigation observed in natural organisms. By grounding learning in the interplay between action, prediction, and natural behavioral statistics, navigation provides a roadmap for building resilient, neurobiologically inspired continual learning in artificial agents.

items.title: Hidden Vision and Beyond: Multiscale Foundations of Thalamic Organization.
items.abstract: The subcortical visual system is traditionally described through a small number of canonical pathways, with the dorsal lateral geniculate nucleus (LGN) viewed primarily as a first-order relay to primary visual cortex and additional routes through the superior colliculus, pulvinar and koniocellular LGN considered secondary or residual. Here, we review recent evidence across species, methods, and scales that challenge this framework and suggest that the visual thalamus is an active, dynamically regulated component of visual processing. We first consider primary and nonprimary visual pathways, showing how thalamic inputs shape cortical responses through the timing, spatial arrangement, synaptic organization, laminar targeting, and circuit-level integration of feedforward signals. We then reconsider the "first-order" status of LGN itself, reviewing evidence that nonretinal subcortical inputs, local inhibition, and corticothalamic feedback can alter LGN responses and the signals routed onward to cortex. This shifts the view of LGN from a passive relay supplying a dynamic cortex to a dynamically regulated node in its own right. Next, we review advances in higher-order thalamic organization, highlighting structured thalamocortical connectivity, network-level coordination, and state-dependent dynamics. Finally, we consider how thalamic functions change in the injured brain, where emerging models disentangle acute effects of damage from chronic compensation to reveal how surviving thalamic and downstream pathways may be remodeled, reweighted, or recruited to support residual visual function and recovery. Together, these findings support a multiscale view of the thalamus as a collection of specialized, adaptive nuclei embedded within distributed cortico-subcortical networks, with implications for perception, cognition, sensory disorders, and rehabilitation.

items.title: Postnatal Development of Sensory Circuits Supporting Lifelong Social Behaviors.
items.abstract: Sensory systems are essential for young animals as they interact with their environments in order to survive and grow. These environments frequently involve other animals, especially early in life. Thus, animals' social interactions fundamentally shape and are shaped by their sensory circuit development. This Review and its associated Minisymposium will highlight new discoveries centered around the reciprocal relationship between sensory development and social interactions. Points of intersection range from gene expression in peripheral sensors to functional connectivity and neural coding in cortical circuits and span varied sensory systems and species. Taken together, we identify a common theme of refinement and specialization of sensory processing during limited developmental windows for species-relevant social behaviors. Consequently, early disruptions to sensory processing can have significant and long-lasting consequences for animals' lifelong behavior and may even contribute to the etiology of autism and related developmental disorders. Thus, the work presented herein offers mechanistic insight into the complex interplay between early sensory and social development with potentially significant clinical implications. Many of these insights are made possible by technological advances in measuring and manipulating sensory circuit functions and behaviors in developing animals. This Review aims to highlight recent advances and outstanding questions that lie at the nexus of sensory, social, and developmental neuroscience.

items.title: Capturing Habits in Humans: Neural Circuitry, Computations, and Clinical Mechanisms.
items.abstract: Habits allow repeated behaviors to be executed efficiently, but habitual control can contribute to maladaptive inflexibility when it dominates despite changing goals or consequences. This review examines recent advances in understanding habitual control across neural circuits, computation, clinical phenotypes, and measurement. We first consider dorsomedial striatal mechanisms that support action-outcome learning and flexible goal-directed behavior and how chronic stress can alter striatal inputs to bias learning toward habitual control. Progress on what computational reinforcement-learning accounts for arbitration between goal-directed and habitual systems is described along prefrontal mechanisms guiding model-based control, action perseveration, and compulsivity in obsessive-compulsive disorder (OCD). A wider behavioral spectrum beyond action initiation is provided, reviewing emerging work on habitual inhibition and frontostriatal circuit dynamics of avoidance in OCD. Recent laboratory paradigms aim to reveal habit formation more sensitively than traditional outcome-devaluation paradigms, whereas real-world digital approaches use smartphones, wearables, and intensive longitudinal measurement to track habit formation and expression in everyday life. Integrating these approaches can help link habits to physiology, symptoms and neural circuits across laboratory to real-world and clinical contexts.

items.title: Mu-Opioid Receptor in Habenula Circuits as a Substrate for Psychiatric Disorders and Addiction.
items.abstract: The habenula is a critical regulator of affect, negative reinforcement, avoidance, and coping behavior. It is thus unsurprising that accumulating evidence supports pivotal roles for habenular circuits in the expression of major psychiatric illnesses including depression and addiction. Though high levels of mu-opioid receptors (MORs) were identified in the habenula more than a generation ago, the functional effects of MORs on habenular circuits remained largely unexplored due to challenges of selectively targeting this small and heterogeneous brain structure. In this SfN mini-symposium report, we highlight studies that resolve how MOR is distributed across medial and lateral habenular subnuclei and how MOR expression maps onto molecularly defined habenular cell types. We further describe some of the habenula-intersecting circuits that express MORs and how MOR signaling modulates neural activity and neurotransmission within these unique habenular circuits and cell types. Going beyond cellular-level effects of MOR signaling, we illustrate how neural activity in the habenula can influence affect and behaviors associated with opioid analgesia, opioid seeking, opioid dependence, and opioid withdrawal. Drawing on works outside the opioid field, we suggest commonalities through which drugs of abuse may influence habenula circuits to induce states of negative affect that contribute to continued drug use or relapse. Finally, we discuss how better understanding the molecular and functional properties of habenular cell types and circuits can identify new druggable targets, such as the orphan receptors GPR151 and GPR139, for the treatment of pain, mood disorders, or opioid and other substance use disorders.

items.title: Cross-Species Approaches to Understanding Human Cognition.
items.abstract: Recent methodological advances including high-density intracranial recordings and population-level analytical frameworks enable deeper and more direct integration between animal models and human neuroscience. As a result, there is an increasing need for standardized behavioral paradigms and circuit-level analyses that can be used in both animals and humans. Cross-species approaches provide crucial foundations for treating neurological and psychiatric disorders. Parallel experiments validate therapeutic targets and enable development of mechanistically grounded behavioral biomarkers for early disease detection. Here, we provide a brief review of recent findings that have direct implications for attention deficits, memory impairments, and decision-making dysfunctions. By linking mechanism to behavior, these approaches guide targeted interventions and effective clinical translation. While challenges remain, these integrated approaches are advancing our understanding of the mechanistic foundation of human cognition.

items.title: Beyond Transcriptomes and Dissociated Cells: Spatial Proteomics for Mechanistic Neurobiology.
items.abstract: Single-cell transcriptomic studies have revealed remarkable molecular heterogeneity across neuronal and glial populations during development, aging, and disease. However, dissociation-based approaches disrupt tissue architecture, and RNA measures alone incompletely capture cellular function. These limitations are particularly relevant in neurodegenerative diseases, where pathology develops within cellular microenvironments and diseased cells progressively lose canonical cell-state identity markers. Spatial proteomic approaches are beginning to address this critical gap by enabling high-dimensional molecular profiling within the intact tissue, preserving the spatial relationships between vulnerable cells and their surrounding cellular environments across scales ranging from subcellular single-cell imaging to large-volume three-dimensional mapping. Here, we discuss emerging spatial proteomic technologies and their applications in aging and neurodegeneration, emphasizing how integration with complementary modalities, including transcriptomics, glycomics, three-dimensional genome architecture, and quantitative neuropathology, is providing new insight into disease biology. We further highlight how these approaches are beginning to accelerate therapeutic target validation, biomarker discovery, and treatment response monitoring. Realizing the full potential of spatial proteomics will require continued advances in cross-platform harmonization, analytical standardization, and computational methods capable of integrating increasingly complex, multimodal datasets.

items.title: Janus in Thermosensation: The Dual Interoceptive-Exteroceptive Nature of Thermal Signals in Body Ownership.
items.abstract: Thermosensation has traditionally been studied for its essential role in survival, enabling detection of environmental thermal stimuli and the maintenance of thermal homeostasis. Interestingly, unlike most sensory systems, thermosensation provides information about both the external world and the body's internal physiological state. In this review, we conceptualize these two dimensions as exteroceptive thermosensation, which conveys information about the thermal properties of external objects and the environment, and interoceptive thermosensation, which conveys information about the body's thermal state. Growing evidence suggests that this dual nature serves functions that extend beyond survival and homeostasis. Alterations in both thermal perception and thermoregulation have been associated with changes in body ownership, the experience that one's body belongs to oneself, while manipulations of thermal signals can influence ownership itself. Here, we review the physiological and neural bases of exteroceptive and interoceptive thermosensation, from peripheral encoding to central processing, and examine their relationship with body ownership in healthy and clinical populations. We discuss evidence suggesting partially distinct yet potentially convergent neural substrates for these two dimensions of thermosensation, highlighting the insular cortex and its broader connectivity network as a candidate through which thermal information may sustain body ownership. Finally, we consider how emerging neurotechnologies offer new opportunities to investigate the contribution of thermosensation to body ownership while also opening novel avenues for neurorehabilitation. We propose that thermosensation represents an underexplored contributor to body ownership, opening new avenues for future research on how bodily and environmental thermal signals are integrated to support the sense of self.

items.title: Six Challenges for a Mechanistic Science of Human Interoception.
items.abstract: Human interoception has become a major focus of systems, cognitive, and clinical neuroscience. Work across the past decade has shown that signals originating within the body shape perception, emotion, cognition, behavior, and health. Despite rapid methodological and conceptual progress, which substantially expanded our understanding of how bodily signals are processed and represented, much of the field remains constrained by descriptive methods. As these approaches passively assess bodily signals or subjective awareness, they have limited ability to establish causal mechanisms or translate interoceptive findings into clinically informative frameworks. Here, we identify six challenges and corresponding methodological directions for advancing human interoception research: strengthening integration of animal and human models, developing causal perturbation paradigms, capturing interoception in ecologically valid contexts, standardizing multidimensional measurement across bodily systems, adjudicating between computational accounts, and translating mechanistic insights into clinically informative models of health and disease. These challenges are best understood as linked requirements for moving interoception research from relevance to mechanism. Together, they highlight the need to move beyond predominantly static, passive, and single-modality approaches toward studies that can test how internal bodily signals relate to neural activity, behavior, and health.

items.title: Maternal Immune Activation and Neurodevelopmental Disorders: A Cross-Species Perspective.
items.abstract: Prenatal exposure to infection increases the likelihood of neurodevelopmental disorders (NDDs). This association is attributed largely to the maternal inflammatory response, maternal immune activation (MIA), rather than to single pathogen. In this review, we discuss the molecular, cellular, and behavioral consequences of MIA and their contribution to NDDs in clinical cohorts and preclinical models across different species. We first trace the pathophysiology linking maternal infection to altered fetal neurodevelopment, describing how diverse immune challenges converge on shared nodes including cytokine signaling, oxidative and nutritional stress, placental dysfunction, and epigenetic modification. We then describe how these perturbations affect neural circuits and behavior, focusing on the disrupted social development. Next, we consider sources of individual variation, including gestational timing, fetal sex, and later-life "second hits," that may contribute to the greater vulnerability. Finally, we discuss the translational implications of this work in terms of maternal cytokine and epigenetic signatures as candidate biomarkers for risk stratification and potential therapeutic approaches.

items.title: Parallel Claustral Networks for Behavioral Control in Health and Disease.
items.abstract: The claustrum is among the most highly interconnected structures in the mammalian brain, with reciprocal projections spanning the cortical mantle and a growing roster of functions that range from sleep regulation to attentional control. Here we review current understanding of claustral circuit organization and function, synthesizing findings from anatomical, physiological, computational, and behavioral studies. We argue that a unifying logic underlies the apparent diversity of claustral functions: the claustrum operates through projection-defined subnetworks whose input selectivity, output targets, and local circuit interactions collectively determine their functional contribution and whose impact on cortical targets varies with arousal and ongoing brain state. Corticoclaustral connectivity is organized into matched input-output modules, local inhibitory circuits confer spatial filtering properties that amplify strong cortical signals while suppressing weaker ones and claustral output populations differ in their laminar targets, postsynaptic cell-type preferences, and molecular properties, producing diverse and context-dependent effects on cortical dynamics. These circuit properties translate into claustral regulation of cortical population dynamics across multiple timescales, from the moment-to-moment coordination of brain states to the consolidation of frontal control strategies. In pain and addiction, specific claustral projection populations are selectively dysregulated, and distinct subnetworks exert opposing influences on nociceptive sensitivity and drug-related behavior according to their cortical targets. Together, these findings position the claustrum as a modular subcortical hub for the selective regulation of distributed cortical networks and identify it as a candidate therapeutic target for disorders characterized by dysregulated cortical network activity, including chronic pain, addiction, and impulsivity.

items.title: NeuroAI's Next Steps: Balancing Computation and Embodiment.
items.abstract: Deep neural networks trained at scale now predict neural activity across sensory cortices, raising a question that divides neuroscience: does the convergence between artificial and biological representations constitute understanding, or does understanding require models of biological processes grounded in the embodied, evolved character of natural intelligence? In this Dual Perspectives article, Bing Brunton and Patrick Mineault articulate two research programs-Process and Convergence-to engage this question about the future of NeuroAI research. The conversation is organized around four questions that probe what scaled model-brain alignment reveals, what the brain is coupled to and evolved to do, what success beyond the lab looks like, and where the field should invest over the coming decade. Their exchanges reveal the distance between the two programs to be primarily about the level of analysis and priorities for what to build next. The conversation converges on shared ground: measure broadly, then distill to causal principles.

items.title: Hormonal Effects during the Reproductive Years on Brain and Behavior: Molecular Discovery to Promising Therapeutics for Women's Mental Health.
items.abstract: Beginning at puberty and throughout the lifespan, women experience greater rates of depression, anxiety disorders, eating disorders, post-traumatic stress disorder, and hormone-linked mood disorders relative to men. How these disorders relate to hormonal fluctuations and associated changes in physiology and brain circuitry in women during the reproductive years is only partially understood. In this review, the molecular, structural, and functional brain changes during the reproductive years are discussed, with a specific focus on transitional changes during the perinatal period. Preclinical and clinical models of neuroplastic change are also discussed, along with neuromodulatory approaches that account for the contextual, spatial, and temporal parameters of interventions delivered during the postpartum period. Future directions may consider how hormonal fluctuations during reproductive years may improve preclinical and clinical models for women's mental health while acknowledging that greater work is needed to understand the role of a broader range of hormonal and environmental factors linked to mental health including lactation, trauma, contraceptive use, menstruation, and perimenopause.

items.title: The Noncanonical Hippocampus: Shared and Distinct Features of the CA2-FC-IG Hippocampal System.
items.abstract: The hippocampal CA2 region has received considerable interest in recent decades, earning a functional understanding beyond the previously held view as a small transitional zone. However, related hippocampal structures called the fasciola cinereum (FC) and indusium griseum (IG) have been largely neglected to date. While CA2, FC, and IG are typically presented as discontinuous structures on conventional atlases, recent work unveils a surprisingly high degree of overlapping gene expression and anatomical continuity, raising questions of their shared versus distinct functions. Here we review the molecular, anatomical, physiological, and behavioral features of each area, to begin to address whether these regions are subcomponents of a greater hippocampal structure or independent entities with distinct contributions to physiology and disease. Early evidence supports that the CA2-FC-IG axis is indeed a cohesive network unified by shared molecular and anatomical profiles, although regional differences in structure and function need to be taken into account. Notably, transcriptomics has revealed multiple subclusters within this complex of structures with no region-specific cell types, raising the need to understand whether cell types or anatomical subfields are the main functional units of this system. This conceptualization of these noncanonical hippocampal areas as a unified, multifaceted system raises many questions discussed here, along with the need for coordinated investigation across regions in future work.

items.title: Illuminating the Diversity of Electrical Synapse Form and Function.
items.abstract: While the nervous system is organized by two main types of connections between neurons, electrical and chemical synapses, most studies focus upon the contribution of the molecularly complex and functionally diverse chemical synapse. Electrical synapses, in contrast, are perceived as simple, neuronal gap junction channels between contacts, often thought to be replaced in early development by more sophisticated chemical synapses. However, recent work and new tools push for the redefining of electrical synapse molecular architecture and function to allow for an updated interpretation of their ongoing contributions to neural circuit formation and function. Here, we describe fresh insight into neuronal gap junction structure, function, and molecular composition within invertebrate (nematodes, drosophila) and vertebrate (zebrafish, rabbit, rodent) model organisms across a variety of time periods and brain regions. Through molecular, genetic, connectomic, and functional explorations, our results argue for a new appreciation of electrical synapse heterogeneity. Based on these and other points of emerging new evidence, we argue for increased consideration of electrical synapses as complex and diverse structures which interact with chemical synapses to drive circuit formation and function.

items.title: Embodied Computation: How Does Embodiment Impact Sensorimotor and Cognitive Processing?
items.abstract: Animals act on the world through a physical body and continually adjust behavior in response to the sensory feedback their actions produce. This closed loop between brain, body, and environment is central to motor control, but its role in other neural computations remains less clear. This review focuses on embodied computation: how the physical body shapes neural activity and behavior across functions ranging from motor control to cognitive processes. We examine the impact of embodiment in several domains, including compositional reuse, intrinsic motivation, metabolic costs, and connectome-constrained computation, with the broader aim of asking when the body can be abstracted away and when it is essential for explaining what the brain computes.

items.title: Glial Regulation of Motor Circuit Formation, Function, and Regeneration.
items.abstract: From simple planaria to humans, proper assembly and maintenance of motor circuits is key to organismal survival. Each year, ∼250,000-500,000 individuals suffer a spinal cord injury with little hope of successful recovery. Moreover, motor circuits are a primary target of prevalent neurodegenerative conditions like ALS and Parkinson's disease. Thus, understanding the mechanisms that build, maintain, and rebuild motor circuits is of substantial clinical interest. Recent data indicate that glia, a heterogeneous group of non-neuronal cells within the nervous system, directly communicate with neurons to tune motor circuit dynamics. We now know glia are often active drivers of neural development and pathology, rather than passive bystanders. This mini-review will highlight recent advances in our understanding of how diverse glial cell types promote proper construction, function, and deconstruction of the key circuits that drive motor behavior.

items.title: The Neural Correlates of Sickness.
items.abstract: The brain protects animals during infection by detecting immune activity, coordinating behavioral and physiological defenses, anticipating potential infectious threats, and limiting excessive inflammation. Collectively termed sickness, these centrally organized responses include changes in body temperature, activity, energy balance, appetite, fluid intake, social behavior, neuroendocrine function, and autonomic output. Rather than constituting a single uniform state, sickness is generated by distributed and partially dissociable neural pathways that translate immune signals into responses appropriate to the nature and stage of an infection. Work presented at a symposium at the 2026 Society for Neuroscience meeting highlights how humoral and cranial sensory pathways detect ongoing immune responses; how social cues, expectations, and prior experience prepare the organism for anticipated threats; and how endocrine and autonomic circuits constrain inflammation and promote recovery. Together, these findings establish the brain as an active regulator of immunity across the full course of illness.
