items.title: Thalamic Reticular Nucleus Excitability and Cholinergic Signaling are Disrupted in a Mouse Model of Alzheimer's Disease Neuropathology.
items.abstract: The thalamic reticular nucleus (TRN) forms powerful GABAergic connections with thalamic nuclei that regulate sleep, attention, and sensory processing. TRN neurons receive dense cholinergic innervation from the basal forebrain and brainstem, dynamically shaping TRN function across brain states. We previously showed reduced TRN activity and sleep deficits in amyloid precursor protein transgenic mice (APP mice), implicating TRN dysfunction as an early contributor to Alzheimer's disease (AD) pathophysiology. Here, using slice electrophysiology in mice of both sexes, we determined whether changes in intrinsic membrane properties or cholinergic synaptic transmission contribute to TRN hypoactivity in APP mice. We found that TRN neurons located in the inner core and outer shell regions undergo substantial increases in excitability after the first postnatal month. In mature animals, core neurons exhibited higher firing rates and diverse firing patterns, including persistent firing, whereas shell neurons fired at lower rates and displayed more homogeneous firing patterns without persistent activity. Firing diversity in core neurons was mediated in part by low-threshold T-type Ca²⁺ channels. Cholinergic synaptic activation, mediated predominantly by basal forebrain afferents, produced biphasic excitatory-inhibitory postsynaptic responses in both core and shell neurons, with the ratio of postsynaptic excitation and inhibition varying across postsynaptic targets. Overall, cholinergic activation suppressed TRN firing. In APP mice, core neurons showed reduced intrinsic excitability and cholinergic afferents evoked postsynaptic responses with a larger muscarinic receptor-mediated inhibitory component, leading to delayed TRN firing. Together, these findings identify both intrinsic and cholinergic synaptic mechanisms that may contribute to TRN dysfunction during early AD. Significance Statement Alzheimer's disease (AD) is typically diagnosed after cognitive symptoms emerge when treatments are less effective, highlighting the need to understand preclinical disease mechanisms. Cholinergic signaling and slow-wave sleep are disrupted before symptom onset, but the mechanisms underlying these changes remain poorly understood. Because the thalamic reticular nucleus (TRN) receives strong cholinergic input and mediates sleep-related rhythms, it is well positioned to contribute to early AD pathophysiology. We previously found reduced TRN activity and disrupted sleep in an AD mouse model. Here, we show that intrinsic excitability and cholinergic synaptic signaling are altered in TRN neurons during preclinical AD. These changes may contribute to thalamic dysfunction and sleep disturbances, providing a potential circuit mechanism linking early AD pathology to disease progression.

items.title: Levodopa boosts hippocampal activity and strengthens generalizable rule representations in prefrontal cortex during the inference of meaning.
items.abstract: Dopamine has long been implicated in a variety of higher-order cognitive functions, including language processing. However, the neural processes and representations by which dopamine influences language processing remain unclear. Here we show that administration of levodopa to young healthy volunteers (n = 70, 47 females) boosts hippocampal processing and neural representations of generalizable abstract rules for successful inference of novel word meaning. We used a novel experimental paradigm that required participants to build new artificial word meanings by inferring and applying abstract affixation rules. A repetition suppression procedure was combined with multivariate representational similarity analyses to isolate the neural locus of both the abstract rules required for the compositional inference process, as well as the novel word meaning representations that were composed based on these abstract rules. Levodopa modulated not only inference-related signals in the hippocampal formation, but also abstract rule representations in the medial frontal cortex. These results support the hypothesis that dopamine boosts hippocampal activity and strengthens prefrontal representations of abstract rules when building novel meaning. Significance statement Dopamine has long been implicated in a variety of higher-order cognitive functions, including language processing. However, the neural processes by which dopamine boosts language processing have remained unclear. Here we show that administration of levodopa to young healthy volunteers enhances hippocampal activity and strengthens prefrontal representations of generalizable abstract rules when building novel word meanings.

items.title: Characterization of the 3D Structure of Chromatin in D1 and D2 Medium Spiny Neurons of the Nucleus Accumbens.
items.abstract: The 3D structure of chromatin is tightly regulated in concert with cell differentiation during development and with epigenetic regulation of gene expression throughout life. Despite extensive characterization at the transcriptional and epigenetic levels of D1-type and D2-type medium spiny neurons (MSNs) in the nucleus accumbens (NAc) - the ventral portion of the striatum important for reward - a 3D map of chromatin structure in these two neuronal cell types is lacking. Here, we provide a high-density map of chromatin structure from male mice in D1 and D2 MSNs including chromatin loops, topological associating domains (TADs), sub-TADs, and compartments. The data suggest broad convergence in overall 3D chromatin structure between these two closely aligned cell types, but also clear differences consistent with transcriptional divergence previously demonstrated for the two MSN types. We also demonstrate that various exposures to cocaine (acute, chronic, or chronic + acute) - which dramatically alter transcriptional patterns in NAc MSNs - produce far more subtle changes in 3D chromatin structure. Thus, while the 3D structure of chromatin in NAc MSNs appears to be an important concomitant of cell type, it is not broadly leveraged by cocaine to mediate changes in gene expression that contribute to a state of addiction. Significance Statement D1-type and D2-type subtypes of medium spiny neurons are present in the nucleus accumbens and perform different roles in drug addiction. This study maps the genome-wide 3D structure of chromatin in the neuronal subtypes and examines how chronic cocaine exposure alters the chromatin landscape of D1 and D2 MSNs.

items.title: Neural Responses to Unexpected Stimulus Repetitions and Omissions in Auditory Cortex Provide Mixed Evidence for Predictive Coding.
items.abstract: Humans and other animals process sensory uncertainty by integrating stimulus information with prior knowledge and expectations. Predictive coding conceptualizes perception as a form of Bayesian inference wherein hierarchical brain circuits update internal models to reconcile bottom-up sensory input with top-down predictions. Whereas predictive coding is a leading theory, the extent to which it is implemented in primary sensory cortices remains a matter of debate. To further investigate this issue, we examined single-neuron spiking activity in male macaque primary auditory cortex (A1) to expected versus unexpected stimulus repetitions and to expected versus unexpected stimulus omissions. On average, we found that A1 neurons did not show enhanced responses to unexpected stimulus repetitions, contrary to predictive-coding theory. However, they did show enhanced responses to unexpected stimulus omissions. Taken together, these mixed results place empirical constraints on how predictive coding is implemented in A1. Significance Statement Perception depends on the brain's ability to infer the causes of sensory inputs by integrating new information with prior knowledge under uncertainty. Our results reveal nuanced evidence for predictive coding within the primary auditory cortex (A1). Specifically, spiking activity during unexpected stimuli and unexpected stimulus omissions provide conflicting and supporting data, respectively, for this Bayesian framework. These findings refine our understanding of neural mechanisms underlying perception and provide empirical constraints on the neurobiological implementation of predictive processing.

items.title: Pharmacological Modulation of the Striatal mGluR5-NR2B Association Attenuates L-DOPA-Induced Dyskinesia in 6-OHDA Lesioned Parkinsonian Rats.
items.abstract: The clinical utility of L-DOPA is severely limited by the development of L-DOPA-induced dyskinesia (LID). Although metabotropic glutamate receptor 5 (mGluR5) antagonists alleviate LID, the underlying molecular mechanisms, particularly those involving striatal glutamate receptor crosstalk, remain incompletely understood. This study investigated the role of the striatal association between mGluR5 and the NMDA receptor subunit NR2B in LID pathogenesis. We observed aberrant elevation of the mGluR5-NR2B interactions in the striatum of 6-hydroxydopamine (6-OHDA)-lesioned parkinsonian rats exhibiting LID. Administration of the mGluR5 antagonist MTEP or the NMDA receptor antagonist MK-801 reduced the co-immunoprecipitated association, reduced the synaptic association of mGluR5 with NR2B, and markedly attenuated LID severity. Mechanistically, the decoupling of these receptors was accompanied by decreased ERK1/2 phosphorylation, reduced PKC protein expression, and decreased L-DOPA-induced c-fos and prodynorphin mRNA levels. Furthermore, abnormal involuntary movement (AIM) scores significantly correlated with the extent of NR2B-mGluR5 interaction and downstream signaling activation. These findings suggest that increased mGluR5-NR2B association is associated with LID and may contribute to its expression. Consequently, the therapeutic efficacy of MTEP or MK-801 is likely mediated by reducing this receptor interaction and downstream signaling, highlighting a potential molecular target for LID treatment.

items.title: Disease-modifying therapies in development for post-traumatic epilepsy.
items.abstract: Post-traumatic epilepsy (PTE) is a chronic neurological disorder that develops following traumatic brain injury (TBI), a condition affecting nearly 69 million people worldwide. PTE accounts for 20% of acquired epilepsies and is characterized by spontaneous recurrent seizures and long-term neurological deficits. Current antiseizure medications primarily suppress early seizures but do not prevent epileptogenesis or improve neurological dysfunction. This review critically evaluates the current landscape of disease-modifying therapies for PTE with an emphasis on pathophysiological basis, therapeutic pipeline and challenges in developing antiepileptogenic drugs for preventing PTE and improving long-term neurological outcomes after TBI. Epileptogenesis following TBI is driven by dynamic interactions among neuronal, glial, vascular, immune, metabolic, and epigenetic pathways that evolve from the acute injury phase through the latent period to chronic epilepsy. Consequently, therapeutic interventions differ in optimal timing and target objectives of acute neuroprotection, prevention of epileptogenesis, or modification of established epilepsy and its comorbidities. Promising disease-modifying approaches include epigenetic modulators, anti-inflammatory & immunomodulatory agents, JAK-STAT inhibitors, mTOR inhibitors, antioxidant & mitochondrial-targeted therapies, tau-directed interventions, adenosine augmentation, neurosteroids, and regenerative cell-based therapies. Among these, epigenetic therapy targeting histone deacetylases has emerged as a particularly attractive strategy. Pharmacological inhibition of histone deacetylase has demonstrated robust disease-modifying effects in experimental PTE by normalizing aberrant histone deacetylase activity, suppressing neuroinflammation, reducing seizure burden, and attenuating biomarkers of epileptogenic progression. Despite multiple approaches in development, no therapy has yet demonstrated clinical efficacy for preventing human PTE. Major translation barriers include the heterogeneity of PTE, limitations of experimental models, inconsistent biomarker validation, and challenges in clinical studies. Future progress will require standardized paradigms, rigorous preclinical evaluation, biomarker-guided clinical trials, and optimization of disease-modifying therapies capable of preventing epilepsy and improving long-term neurological outcomes after brain injury.

items.title: The Burden of Occult Cerebrovascular Disease in CKD: A Scoping Review.
items.abstract: Rationale & objective Occult cerebrovascular diseases (OCCD) including extracranial and intracranial atherosclerotic disease (ECAD and ICAD) and cerebral small vessel disease (CSVD) are asymptomatic cerebrovascular abnormalities associated with future risk of stroke and dementia. Although chronic kidney disease (CKD) is strongly associated with adverse brain health outcomes, the breadth of evidence regarding OCCD in people with CKD has not been comprehensively characterized. This scoping review summarizes the available literature on OCCD among adults with CKD without clinically overt cerebrovascular disease. Sources of evidence PubMed, EMBASE, Web of Science, and Scopus were searched for studies published between January 2000 and July 2025. Eligibility criteria Peer-reviewed studies reporting the frequency or characteristics of OCCD manifestations in adults with CKD without a known history of stroke or transient ischemic attack. Charting methods Two reviewers independently screened studies and extracted data on study characteristics, CKD definitions, neuroimaging modalities, and reported OCCD findings. Methodological quality was assessed using a modified Newcastle-Ottawa Scale. Results Forty-six studies comprising 5,153 participants with CKD were included. Study populations varied substantially with respect to CKD stage, dialysis status, study design, and imaging methodology. Two studies evaluating ICAD reported moderate-to-severe intracranial stenosis in approximately one-quarter of participants with CKD. Across studies evaluating ECAD, the frequency of significant extracranial carotid stenosis ranged from approximately 3% in patients with non-dialysis-dependent CKD to 28% among patients receiving dialysis. Thirty-eight studies evaluated manifestations of CSVD, including cerebral microbleeds, silent cerebral infarctions, white matter hyperintensities, and enlarged perivascular spaces. Several studies suggested a greater burden of CSVD manifestations among patients with advanced CKD or dialysis dependence. Reported frequencies varied considerably across studies. Limitations Considerable heterogeneity in study populations, CKD definitions, imaging protocols, and outcome ascertainment methods limited direct comparison across studies. Conclusions Occult cerebrovascular abnormalities are frequently reported across diverse CKD populations, particularly among patients with advanced kidney disease. Variation in the prevalence of abnormalities may reflect differences in CKD severity, participant characteristics, neuroimaging protocols, and outcome definitions. These findings highlight the need for standardized neuroimaging approaches and prospective studies to better characterize the clinical implications of OCCD in CKD.

items.title: TAT-Cx43<sub>266-283</sub> limits recurrence-associated features and improves survival after tumor resection in preclinical glioblastoma models.
items.abstract: Glioblastoma (GBM) remains an incurable disease with an extremely poor prognosis. Tumor resection represents a first-line treatment when possible, but most patients suffer tumor recurrence, the primary cause of mortality. One of the functions of connexin43 (Cx43), a gap junction-forming subunit that also has a role in channel-independent signaling, is the inhibition of Src, an oncoprotein involved in tumor progression and recurrence. We previously developed a Cx43 mimetic peptide TAT-Cx43 266-283 that recapitulates the inhibition of Src and exerts antitumor effects in patient-derived and mouse in vitro and in vivo models, and here we aimed to explore its effect in GBM recurrence. Analysis of clinical datasets shows a marked increase of Src activity after the standard of care treatments, suggesting that targeting Src activity could prevent GBM recurrence. Importantly, we found that the combination of tumor resection and TAT-Cx43 266-283 extended survival in two syngeneic, immunocompetent GBM resection models, which recapitulated key complementary histological features of GBM. TAT-Cx43 266-283 in combination with tumor resection increased tumor cell apoptosis and decreased important hallmarks of GBM recurrence by targeting the specific dominant features in each model, such as aberrant vascularization or tumor infiltration. These effects occurred alongside the recruitment of tumor-associated macrophages and microglia (TAMs) to tumor border and their shift towards an antitumor phenotype. Our findings suggest the possible involvement of the immune system in the antitumor effects of TAT-Cx43 266-283 and reveal the efficacy and safety of the intracavitary application of TAT-Cx43 266-283 after tumor resection, supporting its potential in a clinical setting.

items.title: Cannabis addiction and cerebellum: A focus on endocannabinoid signaling and reward.
items.abstract: Cannabis is the most widely used psychoactive drug, with an estimated 219 million users, according to the United Nations Office on Drugs and Crime (UNODC, 2023). Since 2019, there has been a 32% increase in cannabis use. Although increasing evidence suggests that the cerebellum is involved in addiction-related neural networks, limited research has explored how cannabis exposure impacts cerebellar endocannabinoid (eCB) signaling and how these changes affect reward processing and the development of cannabis use disorder. Signals related to reward can be observed within cerebellar circuitry, particularly in tasks that focus on goal-directed learning. This involves a complex interaction among the cerebellar cortex, basal ganglia, and cerebral cortex, supporting the growing consensus that the cerebellum plays a crucial role in cognitive processing. Moreover, evidence suggests that the cerebellum may integrate both supervised learning and reinforcement learning to improve goal-directed actions. In drug addiction, learned reinforcing properties create powerful motivational triggers for seeking the drug when individuals encounter cues associated with it. Neuroimaging studies in humans indicate that the cerebellum is involved in maintaining memories related to drug use. A detailed understanding of the interplay between cerebellar function, eCB signaling, and reward processing provides a comprehensive framework for understanding the development and persistence of cannabis addiction.

items.title: RNA decay in neurodegenerative diseases.
items.abstract: RNA homeostasis is increasingly recognized to play critical roles in neuronal health and defects in RNA decay have emerged as important contributors to neurodegeneration. We discuss evidence linking defects in RNA decay to neurodegenerative diseases, and highlight emerging questions and potential therapeutic opportunities.

items.title: The active inference framework and social cognitive theory: informing therapeutic approaches for medically unexplained symptoms.
items.abstract: Persistent physical symptoms for which no medical explanation can be found affects hundreds of millions of people globally. The active inference framework from cognitive neuroscience, which describes the brain's capacity for adaptive learning, is now providing the explanatory power and evidence to understand the phenomenon of medically unexplained symptoms. The active inference framework calls for a reconsideration of the evidence approach for people with persistent physical symptoms. In this paper, I provide an overview of the active inference framework. I show how combining the active inference framework with learning theories from behavioural psychology, in particular, social cognitive theory, can inform an approach to recovery. I develop a "therapeutic domains approach" embedded within the social cognitive theoretical model of learning and the active inference framework to guide the selection of evidence-based strategies to support recovery. The approach allows for all the sensory inputs that can contribute to the formation of medically unexplained symptoms to be targeted, and would enable patient centred, tailored, multi-strategic therapeutic plans to be developed and adopted. I demonstrate how the therapeutic domains approach is consistent with, but builds on the biopsychosocial model, by articulating and integrating the behavioural underpinnings and explanatory power for how and why a multi-strategic, therapeutic domains based approach would provide a roadmap for recovery for people with medically unexplained symptoms.

items.title: Convergent and Divergent Neural Signatures of Cue-Induced Response in Substance and Behavioral Addictions: A Coordinate-Based Neuroimaging Meta-Analysis.
items.abstract: Addiction-related cues trigger craving and precipitate relapse, yet whether substance use disorders (SUDs) and behavioral addictions (BAs) share a universal neurobiological cue-reactivity core remains unresolved. We conducted a coordinate-based meta-analysis using Seed-based d Mapping with Permutation of Subject Images (SDM-PSI) to synthesize whole-brain fMRI studies comparing visually evoked cue-reactivity in strictly diagnosed SUDs and BAs versus healthy controls. An updated systematic search through September 12, 2026, yielded 50 eligible articles comprising 53 independent contrasts and 2,578 participants. Pooled analyses across all addictions revealed convergent cue-elicited activations in the mid-cingulate cortex, precentral gyrus, and a midline midbrain region. However, a formal SUD ∩ BA conjunction analysis yielded no family-wise error (FWE)-corrected shared clusters. Direct comparisons demonstrated greater activation in the left hippocampus, pregenual anterior cingulate cortex, and precuneus for SUDs relative to BAs. Importantly, the left hippocampal and precuneus differences survived age adjustment; furthermore, the hippocampal finding remained robust when restricting analyses to highly controlled cue-versus-neutral paradigms, while the precuneus finding was retained within picture-cue modalities. Furthermore, exploratory analyses of clinical characteristics indicated that cue-elicited neural responses were associated with specific clinical states and treatment variables (e.g., methadone maintenance in heroin use disorder), highlighting the modulatory effect of clinical symptom profiles on these regional functional signatures. Overall, the results motivate further investigation of memory- and self-related processes, as well as control- or action-related processes. These findings offer a critical foundation for developing targeted clinical interventions, distinguishing between generalized transdiagnostic neuromodulation targets and disorder-specific therapies tailored to distinct clinical and demographic profile.

items.title: Perioral motor stabilization without classical proprioception: a trigeminofacial force-balance model.
items.abstract: Voluntary perioral movements, including speech articulation, deliberate lip posturing, and postural stabilization during oral closure, require motor precision despite the absence of muscle spindles and proprioceptive receptors in perioral musculature. The facial nerve is purely efferent, providing no direct sensory return. How the motor system achieves stable control under these constraints has remained unresolved. We propose the Orofacial Region as Integrated System (ORIS) model as a mechanistic candidate tailored to voluntary and automatic segmental perioral behaviors. The model identifies cutaneous mechanoreception via the trigeminal nerve as the primary afferent channel for perioral motor stabilization and proposes that the controlled variable is the spatial equilibrium of dermal surface tension across the perioral sheet, monitored by slowly and fast-adapting mechanoreceptors concentrated in the perioral region. The orbicularis oris sphincter provides circumferential tensile stability against which directional muscles act, with the modiolus anguli oris serving as the primary force-transmission junction. Three testable predictions follow from this architecture. Clinical implications for facial motor rehabilitation are discussed.

items.title: Feedback Processing in Individual and Dyadic Group Risk Decisions Under Gain-Loss Framing: Evidence from FRN and P3b.
items.abstract: Decision-making in social contexts is influenced by gain-loss framing and interpersonal responsibility, yet how these factors jointly shape the neural dynamics of outcome evaluation remains unclear. Using event-related potentials (ERPs) and a dyadic turn-taking Balloon Analogue Risk Task (BART), this study examined how decision context (individual vs. dyadic group), gain-loss framing, and feedback valence influence risky choice and feedback processing. Participants completed the task in both individual and dyadic contexts while EEG was recorded. Behaviorally, participants exhibited greater risk-taking in the dyadic group than in the individual context and showed reduced risk-taking following negative relative to positive feedback. ERP analyses revealed significant interactions between decision context and feedback valence for both feedback-related negativity (FRN) and P3b, suggesting that decision context modulated neural responses associated with both early and later stages of outcome evaluation. Specifically, FRN responses to negative feedback were enhanced in the dyadic context, whereas P3b responses were larger in the individual context. The dyadic context also enhanced neural differentiation between positive and negative feedback. In addition, P3b showed a descriptive pattern consistent with a possible interaction between decision context and gain-loss framing, although this interaction did not reach statistical significance after correction for multiple comparisons. These findings demonstrate that social decision context shapes both behavioral risk-taking and the neural dynamics of feedback processing during interactive sequential decision-making. The study extends previous research by providing neurophysiological evidence from a real dyadic interactive paradigm, highlighting how social context influences outcome evaluation under risk.

items.title: Selective elimination of Foxp1-positive motor neurons by programmed cell death in the upper cervical spinal cord of the developing mouse.
items.abstract: Programmed cell death (PCD) helps establish neuronal populations during development. In avian embryos, early cervical PCD selectively eliminates Foxp1+ motor neurons (MNs), implying that PCD regulates MN numbers and refines MN subtype composition. However, whether a similar subtype-specific mechanism operates in mammals remains unknown. We examined the timing, spatial distribution, and subtype specificity of PCD in the upper cervical spinal cord of mouse embryos. Using terminal deoxynucleotidyl transferase dUTP nick-end labeling (TUNEL), we found that PCD peaked at embryonic day 11 (E11) in the upper cervical spinal cord but was delayed until E13 in the cervical enlargement. At E11, TUNEL+ cells localized to the lateral-to-middle MN domain, expressing Mnx1 with low Lhx3 expression. Many of these MNs expressed Foxp1, and their overall proportion significantly decreased following this wave of PCD. This reduction was prevented in Bax knockout mice, and surviving Foxp1+ MNs expressed Aldh1a2. These findings demonstrate that subtype-specific PCD occurs in the upper cervical spinal cord of mouse embryos and preferentially affects Foxp1+ MNs, indicating that PCD contributes to the developmental refinement of MN subtype composition in mammals.

items.title: Bimodal versus unimodal high-definition Transcranial random noise stimulation of auditory cortex for tinnitus: A double-blind, sham-controlled crossover trial.
items.abstract: Transcranial random noise stimulation (tRNS) targeting auditory cortex has shown preliminary promise for chronic tinnitus, but evidence is dominated by small studies and powered trials are scarce. A single-session pilot suggested that pairing HD-tRNS with acoustic input may augment its effects, whether this holds over repeated sessions is unknown. We investigated whether repeated sessions of HD-tRNS over bilateral auditory cortex, delivered alone or combined with acoustic stimulation, modulate tinnitus loudness, auditory deviant processing, and resting-state connectivity. Thirty-five participants with chronic tinnitus completed a double-blind, sham-controlled crossover trial. Participants were assigned to bimodal (HD-tRNS plus acoustic stimulation) or unimodal (HD-tRNS alone) arms, each with active and sham blocks of 10 sessions over bilateral Heschl's gyrus. Outcomes included minimum masking level (MML), visual analogue scales for loudness and distress, mismatch negativity to intensity deviants, and resting-state connectivity. No consistent treatment effect emerged. Bayesian evidence favoured the null for the primary loudness outcome (BF01=4.79), and neither primary mismatch negativity outcome survived correction. For MML, the main treatment effect was null, but an unexpected group × treatment interaction emerged at post (p=0.039), mirrored in connectivity. Repeated HD-tRNS produced no group-level benefit, alone or combined with acoustic stimulation, adding a well-controlled null to a mixed literature.

items.title: From insulin resistance to neurovascular breakdown: mTOR signaling as a convergence point in Alzheimer's disease.
items.abstract: Alzheimer's disease (AD), the leading cause of dementia, is increasingly recognized as a metabolic disorder characterized by disrupted insulin and insulin-like growth factor-1 signaling in the brain, a concept now referred to as type 3 diabetes. Central to this perspective is the insulin receptor substrate-1/phosphoinositide 3-kinase/protein kinase B/mechanistic target of rapamycin (IRS-1/PI3K/Akt/mTOR) cascade, which acts as the primary convergence point linking systemic insulin resistance to neurodegeneration. Impaired insulin signaling in astrocytes, neurons, microglia, and cerebral endothelial cells disrupts glucose metabolism, energy production, and amyloid-β (Aβ) clearance, while promoting tau hyperphosphorylation through glycogen synthase kinase-3β activation. Chronic mTOR hyperactivation exacerbates these dysfunctions by suppressing autophagy, impairing insulin sensitivity, and compromising blood-brain barrier (BBB) integrity through tight junction disassembly, pericyte loss, and endothelial senescence. These processes collectively establish a self-perpetuating cycle of metabolic dysfunction, protein aggregation, neuroinflammation, and vascular breakdown. Neuron-derived extracellular vesicles have emerged as a promising non-invasive biomarker platform for monitoring central insulin resistance and therapeutic response in real time. Metabolically targeted interventions, including intranasal insulin, glucagon-like peptide-1 receptor agonists, and mTOR inhibitors such as rapamycin, demonstrate encouraging preclinical and early clinical efficacy in restoring insulin sensitivity, reducing tau and Aβ pathology, and preserving BBB function. However, challenges related to delivery and dosing remain significant barriers to clinical translation. Continued investigation into neurovascular unit and multi-target combination therapies may facilitate the development of effective, biomarker-guided treatments for AD.

items.title: Comparing the conformational diversity of α1A-adrenoceptor in micelles and phospholipid bilayer models.
items.abstract: α1A-adrenoceptor (α1A-AR) is a class A G-protein coupled receptor (GPCR) that stimulates smooth muscle contraction in response to adrenaline and noradrenaline. GPCRs exist in a dynamic equilibrium between multiple conformational states. Ligand binding induces structural rearrangements via conserved microswitches, which are thought to shift the equilibrium and trigger signalling. For structural and biochemical studies, GPCRs must be extracted from the membrane, typically using detergent micelles. However, detergents can disrupt native dynamics of membrane proteins, potentially confounding experimental results. To address this, phospholipid bilayer mimetics such as nanodiscs and saposin nanoparticles (SapNPs) have been developed to provide a more native-like environment. Thermostabilised α1A-AR serves as a GPCR prototype and can be expressed and isotopically labelled for NMR purposes. To investigate how membrane mimetics influence the conformational diversity of α1A-AR, we compared 1H,13C-HMQC spectra of 13CH3-Met α1A-AR incorporated into DDM, LMNG, or SapNPs, in the presence of ligands with varying efficacies. Several methionine residues are positioned near key microswitches, including M2035.57, located close to the G-protein-binding site. Its resonance has been proposed as a readout of receptor conformational state, shifting with ligand efficacy. Spectra of 13CH3-Met α1A-AR in LMNG closely resembled those in DDM with some temperature-dependent dynamic variation. In contrast, incorporation into SapNPs led to a complete loss of M2035.57 signal, consistent with an intermediate exchange rate. These findings demonstrate that the membrane environment can profoundly influence GPCR conformational dynamics, highlighting the need to consider membrane environment when interpreting NMR data and underscore the value of benchmarking against biologically relevant controls.

items.title: Acute effects of oxyhemoglobin and subarachnoid hemorrhage on postsynaptic transmission.
items.abstract: Delayed cerebral ischemia (DCI) is a major complication of subarachnoid hemorrhage (SAH), but its mechanisms remain unclear. Hemoglobin, particularly oxyhemoglobin (OxyHb), is a potent vasoconstrictor in vitro and is thought to contribute to DCI. This study aimed to clarify how OxyHb affects frequency-dependent synaptic transmission and plasticity in the hippocampus and whether these effects relate to impaired neural function after SAH. Unlike most previous studies, we applied maximally diluted OxyHb containing only minimal reductant, thereby minimizing the confounding effects of the reducing agent. We examined hippocampal CA1 slices from Wistar rats, analyzing field excitatory postsynaptic potentials (fEPSPs), population spikes, and inhibitory postsynaptic currents (IPSCs), and compared the findings with those of an SAH model. At baseline test stimulation frequencies of 0.1 and 0.05Hz, OxyHb did not alter the fEPSP slope. However, OxyHb exerted a bidirectional modulation on IPSC amplitude, significantly increasing it at 0.05Hz (p = 0.004) and decreasing it at 0.1Hz (p = 0.011). Furthermore, theta-burst stimulation (TBS)-induced LTP was preserved at 0.1Hz, but was inhibited at 0.05Hz in the presence of OxyHb. In the SAH model, LTP was impaired, and population spike amplitude was reduced, whereas the fEPSP slope was unaffected. These results suggest that frequency-dependent changes in synaptic transmission and neural plasticity observed in the presence of OxyHb may contribute to the pathophysiology of neural dysfunction associated with SAH and DCI.

items.title: Distinct impulsivity profiles in a transdiagnostic framework: Associations with diagnosis, psychopathology, cognition, and brain metrics.
items.abstract: Impulsivity is a heterogeneous trait linked to psychiatric vulnerability, but its clinical stratification, neurocognitive mechanisms, and developmental trajectories remain poorly understood. Using baseline and 2-year follow-up data from the Adolescent Brain Cognitive Development (ABCD) Study (N = 9078), we identified three distinct impulsivity profiles through latent profile analysis and latent transition analysis: low impulsivity (baseline: 56.1%; follow-up: 48.9%), motivational impulsivity (high urgency and sensation seeking; baseline: 33.5%; follow-up: 43.6%), and executive impulsivity (low perseverance and premeditation; baseline: 10.4%; follow-up: 7.4%). Cross-sectionally, the executive profile was associated with elevated risks for most psychiatric diagnoses and psychopathology symptoms, poorer performance on all cognitive tests, and distinct structural and functional alterations in certain brain regions at baseline. Longitudinally, this profile showed greater worsening in most psychopathology measures and some cognitive tests over two years, though not in brain metrics. In contrast, the motivational profile exhibited significant but milder effects both cross-sectionally and longitudinally. Additionally, transitions between profiles were associated with changes in some psychopathology and cognitive measures, but not in brain metrics. These findings underscore the clinical and neurobiological specificity of impulsivity profiles, advancing precision psychiatry by mapping impulsivity heterogeneity onto differential risk pathways and neurocognitive mechanisms.

items.title: Comparative efficacy and tolerability of pharmacological interventions for the acute treatment of obsessive-compulsive disorder across the lifespan: a systematic review and network meta-analysis.
items.abstract: Pharmacological treatment is recommended for obsessive-compulsive disorder. Several options are available, yet little is known on comparative effects of individual medications. We aimed to elucidate the efficacy and tolerability of pharmacotherapy for people with obsessive-compulsive disorder, across the lifespan. We did a systematic review and network meta-analysis comparing short-term pharmacological interventions for obsessive-compulsive disorder. We searched multiple databases, including MEDLINE, Embase, PsycInfo, and the Cochrane Central Register of Controlled Trials, for literature on licensed or recommended pharmacological treatments for obsessive-compulsive disorder, without age restrictions, from database inception up to March 11, 2026. We included double-blind, randomised controlled trials with outcomes between 8 and 16 weeks. Two reviewers independently and in duplicate extracted outcomes, with a quality check done by a third reviewer. Primary outcomes were efficacy, defined as change from baseline score, and tolerability, defined as the proportion of participants discontinuing treatment due to adverse events. Separately for children and adolescents (aged 0-17 years) and adults (aged ≥18 years), we calculated standardised mean differences (SMDs) and odds ratios (ORs) with random-effects pairwise and network meta-analysis. The certainty of evidence was assessed using the Confidence in Network Meta-Analysis (CINeMA) framework. People with lived experience of obsessive-compulsive disorder were involved in the entire review process, including protocol development, writing, and interpretation of the findings. The study was preregistered in Open Science Framework (identifier 4V3GS). We included 52 randomised controlled trials with 7316 participants. Nine trials were included for children and adolescents (N=822; median age 12·5 years [IQR 11·6-13·2]; 352 [55%] male and 285 [45%] female among 637 participants with reported sex distribution). 43 trials were included for adults (N=6494; median age 36·4 years [35·0-37·9]; 3105 [49%] male and 3200 [51%] female among 6305 participants with reported sex distribution). Data on ethnicity were reported in 15 (29%) of 52 randomised controlled trials, using inconsistent definitions. In children and adolescents, clomipramine was more efficacious than placebo (SMD -1·19, 95% CI -1·73 to -0·64, CINeMA low), as were sertraline (-0·52, -0·80 to -0·02, low), fluoxetine (-0·43, -0·76 to -0·10, low), and fluvoxamine (-0·39, -0·71 to -0·07, low). Clomipramine was more efficacious than fluoxetine (SMD -0·75, 95% CI -1·39 to -0·11; very low), fluvoxamine (-0·79, -1·43 to -0·16; very low), paroxetine (-0·87, -1·51 to -0·22; very low), and sertraline (-0·87, -1·51 to -0·22; very low). Only sertraline was less tolerable than placebo (OR 4·51, 95% CI 1·36 to 14·96; low). In adults, clomipramine (SMD -0·71, 95% CI -0·88 to -0·54; high), fluvoxamine (-0·63, -0·83 to -0·43; high), paroxetine (-0·51, -0·73 to -0·29; moderate), sertraline (-0·49, -0·70 to -0·28; moderate), escitalopram (-0·43, -0·85 to -0·02; moderate), and fluoxetine (-0·37, -0·6 to -0·08; moderate) were more efficacious than placebo, and clomipramine was more efficacious than fluoxetine (-0·34, -0·65 to -0·04; low). Clomipramine (OR 4·65, 95% CI 3·27 to 6·60; moderate), fluvoxamine (2·73, 1·77 to 4·20; moderate), fluoxetine (2·52, 1·27 to 4·98; moderate), sertraline (2·23, 1·49 to 3·34; moderate), and paroxetine (1·99, 1·36 to 2·93; moderate) were less tolerable than placebo. Clomipramine was less tolerable than all active comparators (OR range 1·70 to 3·50; moderate) except fluoxetine (moderate) and venlafaxine (low). Clomipramine showed the largest estimated efficacy for obsessive-compulsive disorder but had a lower tolerability than SSRIs. The evidence of its superiority over individual SSRIs was more pronounced in children and adolescents. Our findings suggest that the trade-off between efficacy and tolerability should be discussed within an individualised, shared, decision-making framework. None.

items.title: Glial progenitor-like state is preferentially co-opted in glioblastoma and sustained by POU3F3.
items.abstract: Oncofetal reprogramming in glioblastoma (GBM) relies on the co-option of still poorly defined pathways that are transiently active during brain development, thereby exposing therapeutically actionable vulnerabilities. To better characterize GBM biology in the context of neurodevelopment, we create an expanded human spatiotemporal multi-omic dataset that resolves both gliogenic and neurogenic lineage fate and assess oncofetal reprogramming at the tumor core and infiltrative margin in both primary and recurrent disease. Analyses reveal the preferential enrichment of a glial intermediate progenitor cell (gIPC)-like state, which is most reminiscent of third-trimester germinal matrix gIPCs, across tumor regions and in recurrence. We uncover EGFR and the long non-coding RNA (lncRNA) NRXN1-DT as co-opted gIPC-specific markers, demonstrate NRXN1-DT's clinical utility in GBM diagnostics, and prioritize POU3F3 as a gIPC-like oncofetal driver, confirming its regulatory role in NRXN1-DT enhancer activity, EGFR expression, and maintenance of GBM stem/progenitor-like properties. This study lays the groundwork for future investigations into targeting POU3F3 and other co-opted gliogenic drivers as GBM therapeutics.

items.title: Ancestral state reconstruction of acoustic traits in tinamous (Aves: Tinamidae): a first approximation to the evolutionary history of complex phenotypes.
items.abstract: Reconstructing ancestral acoustic signals can reveal which aspects of animal communication are conserved, transformed, or reorganized during evolutionary diversification. However, these signals have a complex structure that is difficult to represent using conventional descriptors. Here, we used deep-learning models to characterize acoustic structure in Tinamidae, a lineage of Neotropical birds well suited for exploring the evolutionary history of vocal signals under a phylogenetic comparative framework. We processed 2,630 recordings from 46 species, extracted high-level acoustic traits, and reconstructed ancestral states using a dated phylogeny and a sample of posterior trees. We then sonified these reconstructions to interpret hypothetical acoustic structures at ancestral nodes and their evolutionary trajectories. We assessed methodological uncertainty and compared the reconstructions with ancestral states estimated from conventional acoustic traits. High-level acoustic traits showed strong phylogenetic signal and were best described by an Ornstein-Uhlenbeck model. Ancestral sonifications retained interpretable temporal and spectral organization, and spectral centroid showed strong consistency between conventional and high-level reconstructions. Overall, our results suggest that acoustic evolution in Tinamidae has unfolded within functional limits that allow variation among lineages without indefinite phenotypic drift. We emphasize that these reconstructions should be interpreted as hypotheses about ancestral acoustic structures, not as replicas of particular signals.

items.title: Beyond the value of reproductive value.
items.abstract: Research Highlights: Lebreton, J.-D., & Oli, M. K. (2026). Reproductive value as a key concept in ecology and evolutionary biology. Journal of Animal Ecology. https://doi.org/10.1111/1365-2656.70343. Ecologists are good at counting things. Yet individuals are not interchangeable in what they contribute to a population's future. Lebreton and Oli's synthesis of reproductive value (RV) shows that this deceptively simple idea connects demographic theory, life-history evolution, spatial ecology, epidemiology and conservation. Indeed, RV provides a common currency for asking not simply how many individuals occupy a population, but where its demographic future resides. Here, I highlight this unifying perspective and argue that new technologies could take RV from a predominantly class-based quantity towards a dynamic, individualised and spatially explicit description of populations. Combining demographic models with biologging, automated monitoring, genomic information and ecological digital twins could reveal reproductive value at resolutions Fisher himself could scarcely have imagined. I further suggest that RV could enrich community-stability theory by weighting species' fluctuations by their contribution to future population persistence, thereby connecting population resilience, biodiversity insurance and ecosystem stability.

items.title: Matrix-dependent enantioselective degradation and persistence of prothioconazole and prothioconazole-desthio in cereal agroecosystems.
items.abstract: Background To elucidate the enantioselective degradation behavior of prothioconazole and its metabolite prothioconazole-desthio in wheat-soil and rice-paddy water-sediment ecosystems, this study conducted degradation experiments under field conditions employing high-performance liquid chromatography-tandem mass spectrometry (HPLC-MS/MS) combined with established residue analysis methods. Field trials investigated the degradation kinetics and enantioselectivity differences of the two compounds in different matrices, and final residues in wheat flour, rice grain, and rice husk were determined. Results Prothioconazole degraded faster than its metabolite in all matrices. The parent compound followed first-order degradation kinetics throughout the entire experimental period, whereas prothioconazole-desthio exhibited a two-phase temporal pattern (formation followed by degradation); first-order kinetics was applied only to the post-peak degradation phase. In wheat plants, wheat field soil, rice plants, paddy water, and sediment, R-(-)-prothioconazole was preferentially degraded, leading to relative accumulation of S-(+)-prothioconazole with enantiomer fraction (EF) values reaching up to 0.64 in wheat plants and soil, and 0.56-0.63 in the rice ecosystem. Prothioconazole-desthio formation and degradation were also enantioselective: R-(+)-prothioconazole-desthio was preferentially formed and S-(-)-prothioconazole-desthio preferentially degraded in wheat plants, rice plants, paddy water, and sediment, with EF values increasing to 0.67 and 0.72 in wheat and rice plants, respectively, whereas no significant enantioselective degradation was observed in soil. Final residues of both prothioconazole and prothioconazole-desthio enantiomers in wheat flour, rice grain, and rice husk were all below the limit of quantification (LOQ = 0.005 mg/kg for these matrices). Conclusion These findings provide data support for environmental risk assessment and scientifically sound application of prothioconazole. © 2026 Society of Chemical Industry.

items.title: An Investigation on the Association Between HIV-1 Integrase and Gene Knock-out.
items.abstract: Lentivirus-mediated gene therapy has shown promise to provide therapeutic genes for permanent treatment of several diseases. This process relies on integration of the virus genome into that of the host using the virus integrase, which cuts open host DNA for insertion before repair by the cell's non-homologous end joining (NHEJ) pathway. NHEJ can result in insertions or deletions (indel mutations), which may result in genotoxicity. Vector integration is known to activate oncogenes, primarily due to the interaction of the lentivirus vector (LV) genome with genes found near to the site of vector integration. Inactivation of tumor suppressor genes, or gene knockout is also known to occur. In the production of virus particles, genome empty particles are also generated alongside full vector genome containing LV, each still carry the integrase enzyme. Hence, the frequency of genotoxicity associated with NHEJ activity following vector integration or integrase activity alone is difficult to quantify, particularly for gene knock-out. In this study, we used the HPRT locus as a genetic target to investigate gene disruption by genome-containing and empty LV particles to identify the integrase contribution to HPRT mutagenesis. The HPRT gene is large at 35 kb in size and has been used for several mutagenesis studies by carcinogens. It offers forward and reverse selection, where cells with functional HPRT selected for and then cells with inactivated HPRT caused by mutagenesis can be selected to quantify the mutagenic effects of the carcinogen. We firstly used V79 and MRC5 cell lines and primary human T cells derived from healthy donors (male and female) with functional NHEJ DNA repair pathways and AT5BIVA cells with impaired DNA damage repair to follow the cleavage and repair process associated with integrase activity using a fluorescent marker against γH2AX that binds to broken DNA, which is then released after repair. By this analysis, the activity of the virus integrase was also compared for LV with and without virus genome and cells not exposed to virus infection. We next used forward and reverse selection to measure the presence and loss of HPRT activity in infected cells that was observed for genome full and empty LV particles. To further support our findings that integrase activity can cause gene knockout, we expressed HIV-1 integrase in yeast to measure knockout of the CAN-1 gene and found this also occurs. These data show genotoxicity by LV particles is possible even for particles not carrying a therapeutic vector genome and suggest to reduce this potential, empty particles should be removed during LV during manufacture.

items.title: Indicators for tracking progress of effective, representative ecosystem protection.
items.abstract: To halt and reverse rapid biodiversity loss, countries are pursuing the ambitious goals and targets in the Kunming-Montreal Global Biodiversity Framework (GBF) to restore and protect biodiversity in representative networks of protected areas. However, the associated monitoring framework lacks indicators of ecosystem representativeness for Target 3. Using South Africa as an example, we tested different indicators that could fill this gap and made recommendations for globally relevant options for national and international reporting. Specifically, we calculated seven indicators that use different combinations of data on protected areas, ecosystem types, and ecological condition. We used these indicators to measure progress in effective, representative ecosystem protection at different scales in South Africa: country, ecosystem group (e.g., realm), and ecosystem type. The indicators revealed more informative insights, such as which ecosystem types are best progressing toward meeting their protection targets and where protection levels could improve if degraded habitat within protected areas was restored, than protected area coverage (PAC; total % protection). We tabulated the data requirements, advantages, and disadvantages for the indicators and provided recommendations for their use. We recommend condition-adjusted representativeness (CAR) and the ecosystem protection level index be added as component indicators in the GBF monitoring framework for Target 3. These two indicators could also be assessed using the Global Ecosystem Typology (GET) for standardized aggregation or disaggregation of ecosystem types at different levels. For single time points, plotting PAC, representativeness, CAR, and ecosystem protection level by ecosystem functional groups (GET level 3) can be informative. Applying these indicators can strengthen biodiversity reporting under the GBF.

items.title: Accounting for hidden wild inputs in conservation substitutes.
items.abstract: Artificial propagation, wildlife farming, ranching, cultivation, and aquaculture support commercial markets and livelihoods, and their products may be promoted as substitutes for wild harvest. However, production labels for these products cannot be used to determine conservation benefit because output may depend on wild inputs. Thus, we developed hidden wild-input (HWI) accounting as a bounded assessment framework. HWIs are wild-derived biological inputs that are important for producing substitutes but also potentially for conservation, and they are underrepresented in labels, statistics, and assessments. Through conceptual analysis and comparison, we identified establishment, maintenance, and scaling production inputs and conducted a counterfactual evaluation to determine the avoided harvest of wild targets, source-population burdens, and other ecological effects, such as wild-input intensity, wild-origin proportion, supplementation frequency, and elasticity. We examined four examples of wild-input use to illustrate the framework: Convention on International Trade in Endangered Species of Wild Fauna and Flora (CITES) source code Y exposed the gap between production-origin categories and upstream accounting; crocodile ranching showed recurring wild inputs can coexist with conservation gains under regulated management; capture-based European eel (Anguilla anguilla) aquaculture demonstrated production-extraction coupling; and the artificial production of Chinese caterpillar fungus (Ophiocordyceps sinensis) revealed potential commercial dependence when recurring inputs are not reported. Together, the examples showed that source categories cannot be used to quantify upstream burdens, recurring inputs do not indicate conservation failure, and input-output coefficients demonstrate coupling but not net effects. Conservation benefit should be assessed against a credible no-expansion counterfactual by asking whether additional output reduces target harvest, added wild-input burdens remain sustainable, and other ecological effects reverse the gain. Complete biological independence is neither necessary nor sufficient. When input, demographic, and market-substitution data are unavailable, uncertainty should be reported rather than replaced by assumptions based on production labels.

items.title: Severe drought and warming increase the extinction risk of cacti.
items.abstract: Extreme climatic events are increasing in frequency and intensity with climate change 1 . Their effects on species' distributions and extinction risk remain poorly understood 2-9 . Most species distribution models rely on long-term mean climate, overlooking potentially important nonlinear effects of extremes. Here we integrate new spatial data on severe drought 10 , including compounding effects of warmer temperatures, with a comprehensive curated dataset of cactus occurrences (648,316 records) and species distribution models to assess how severe drought alters projected suitable climatic area for 993 species of Cactaceae, a highly threatened family 11 that is commonly considered drought tolerant. In 91% of cases, models including severe drought were better supported than mean-climate models. Across emissions scenarios (Shared Socioeconomic Pathways (SSPs) SSP1-2.6 to SSP5-8.5) with 100-km dispersal, including severe drought increased the share of species losing suitable climatic area from 58-61% to 69-72%. The proportion of species projected to lose over a quarter of suitable area increased from 26-43% to 55-58%, and the proportion projected to lose over four-fifths increased from 1-15% to 25-35%. With severe drought, restricting dispersal from 100 to 0 km increased the share losing suitable area from 69-72% to 84-85% across SSPs. These declines reduced regional richness, with five bioregions potentially losing over 25% of species. These findings demonstrate that accounting for climatic extremes can alter assessments of biodiversity vulnerability under climate change. Integrating climatic extremes into ecological forecasting will be critical for assessing biodiversity loss and designing effective conservation strategies across taxa and ecosystems.

items.title: A plant RNA-binding protein senses 2',3'-cNMP produced by insect effectors.
items.abstract: RNA-derived 2',3'-cyclophosphate-terminated nucleotides act as immune signalling molecules in prokaryotes and eukaryotes 1-3 , but how plants perceive them remains unknown. Sucking insects inject digestive enzymes including RNases into the host plant to acquire nutrients. Here we demonstrate that NIB1, a glycine-rich RNA-binding protein in rice, senses 2',3'-cyclic nucleotide monophosphates (2',3'-cNMPs; 2',3'-cAMP and 2',3'-cGMP) and adenylyl-(3'→5')-guanosine 2',3'-cyclic phosphate (ApG>p) produced by a salivary T2 ribonuclease of green stink bug during feeding. Binding of the RNase products promotes formation of nuclear condensates containing NIB1, which recruit the core immune regulator Enhanced Disease Susceptibility 1 (EDS1) and activate defence, potentially contributing to the immune signalling of Toll/interleukin-1 receptor (TIR) proteins that also produce the nuclease products. Exogenous application of 2',3'-cAMP, 2',3'-cGMP or ApG>p elicits NIB1 and EDS1-mediated immune responses. Our findings unveil a conserved pathway in plants, in which glycine-rich RNA-binding proteins perceive the nuclease-generated second messengers to launch defence and point to a potential link between plant TIR nuclease activity and EDS1 signalling.

items.title: A haplotype-resolved genome assembly of Cardamine amara.
items.abstract: The genus Cardamine (Brassicaceae) includes several well-established model species widely used in evolutionary biology, ecology, and developmental studies. While a chromosome-scale reference is available for Cardamine hirsuta, its close relative Cardamine amara, with unique ecological and reproductive traits, as well as a tendency toward polyploidy, has lacked genomic resources. This gap has limited genomic investigation of an otherwise extensively studied system. Here, we present two chromosome-scale, haplotype-resolved genome assemblies for a C. amara individual from Velký Rečkov, Czech Republic, generated using 444-fold PacBio HiFi long-read data and 320-fold Hi-C data. The two haplomes span 211.96 Mb and 212.03 Mb, with scaffold N50s of 27.01 Mb and 26.41 Mb, respectively. Gene space completeness is high in both assemblies (complete BUSCOs ≥ 99.6%). Comparative analyses confirmed a major pericentromeric inversion between C. amara and C. hirsuta and revealed large structural variants even between haplomes within this single heterozygous individual. These high-quality assemblies provide essential genomic references that will enable deeper insights into genome structure, evolution, and adaptation across the diverse Cardamine genus.

items.title: Cone chemistry, thermogenesis and specialised erotylid beetle pollination of the West African cycad Encephalartos barteri (Zamiaceae) in Benin.
items.abstract: Increasing evidence shows that most cycad species rely on cone thermogenesis and volatile emissions to facilitate pollination by specialised insects that utilise male cones as brood sites. However, African cycads remain poorly studied outside South Africa, leaving major biogeographic gaps in our understanding of pollination systems across the continent. Encephalartos barteri is the only cycad native to West Africa and is currently listed as Vulnerable. We investigated cone thermogenesis, volatile emissions and insect visitors of E. barteri across seven sites in Benin in West Africa. Cone volatiles were collected using dynamic headspace sampling and analysed by gas chromatography-mass spectrometry (GC-MS). Pollination potential was assessed using enclosure and fluorescent dye experiments. Volatile profiles of both male and female cones were dominated by the benzenoid p-methyl-anisole, while the alkene (3E)-1,3-octadiene also occurred in high relative amounts but was largely restricted to male cones. Male cones were thermogenic, reaching temperatures averaging 4.4 °C above ambient. Pollinator surveys revealed a single undescribed erotylid beetle (Coleoptera: Erotylidae) across all sites. In behavioural experiments, dye-marked erotylid beetles deposited fluorescent dye on the micropyles of receptive ovules, and the enclosure of pollen-laden beetles on female cones resulted in seed set, confirming their potential role as pollinators. Our results demonstrate that E. barteri possesses a specialised beetle-mediated pollination system associated with cone thermogenesis and distinctive volatile emissions. This study provides the first evidence of insect pollination in a West African Encephalartos and highlights the importance of conserving specialised pollinator mutualisms in threatened cycads.

items.title: The development of individuality: beyond nature and nurture.
items.abstract: How does behavioral individuality arise? Theoretical models have highlighted the potential roles of genes and the environment. However, Gallagher et al. show that behavioral individuality occurs in the absence of genetic variation and is unaffected by experimentally manipulating the developmental environment. This suggests that behavioral individuality may originate even before birth.

items.title: Multi-model insights into racial and ethnic heterogeneities in early COVID-19 transmission and severity in the U.S.
items.abstract: The COVID-19 pandemic was marked by unequal disease burden across racial and ethnic groups in the US. Using a multi-model ensemble framework, we retrospectively assessed the impact of racial and ethnic heterogeneities in COVID-19 transmission and disease severity on mortality during the winter 2020-2021 surge in California and North Carolina. Models incorporating race and ethnicity projected mortality more accurately than null models, while the ensemble outperformed all individual models on average by weighted interval scores. Eliminating transmission heterogeneities produced larger mortality reductions than eliminating severity differences alone, particularly for Latino populations in California (55% reduction) and Black populations in North Carolina (28% reduction). Reducing severity heterogeneity also lowered mortality, with the greatest benefit among Black populations in both states (21% and 16% reductions in California and North Carolina, respectively). Eliminating both transmission and severity heterogeneity yielded the largest reductions overall, predicting 49-70% lower mortality across racial and ethnic groups in California and 23-40% in North Carolina. Mitigating transmission inequities also produced indirect benefits for non-targeted populations, highlighting the broad impact of reducing disparities in exposure risk and access to protective resources.

items.title: Identification, Antimicrobial Susceptibility Profiling, and Genomic Characterization of Aeromonas Species Isolated from Cultured Freshwater Fish in Pakistan.
items.abstract: Globally, Aeromonas infections pose a significant threat to the aquaculture sector and food security because of associated disease and production losses. In this study, different Aeromonas isolates were identified from the diseased fish. Matrix-assisted laser desorption ionization time-of-flight mass spectrometry (MALDI-TOF MS) based analysis was used for phenotypic identification. Antimicrobial susceptibility testing (AST) was performed to determine the minimum inhibitory concentrations (MICs) of the tested antimicrobial agents using the broth microdilution method. Genome sequencing was performed to characterize the Aeromonas isolates and identify virulence and antimicrobial resistance genes. Whole-genome sequencing (WGS) identified six Aeromonas species among 18 isolates, while one isolate remained unresolved at the species level. A. veronii (27.8%, 5/18) and A. dhakensis (22.2%, 4/18) were the most frequently detected species. MALDI-TOF MS correctly identified the isolates at the genus level but showed limited accuracy at the species level, particularly for A. dhakensis. Most isolates had allelic profiles that were not assigned to existing sequence types in the PubMLST database. Chromosomally encoded β-lactamase genes were commonly detected, whereas acquired antimicrobial resistance genes were infrequently detected. Genes allied with Type III and Type VI secretion systems were identified in several isolates, indicating the presence of putative virulence-associated features that require phenotypic validation. These findings provide baseline information on the identification, antimicrobial susceptibility, genomic diversity, resistance determinants, and virulence-associated genes of Aeromonas isolates recovered from diseased freshwater fish. Further studies involving larger and more geographically representative collections are needed to determine the broader epidemiological significance of these findings.

items.title: DNA hypomethylation licenses cell-cycle re-entry and accelerates coelomocyte replenishment after evisceration in Apostichopus japonicus.
items.abstract: Evisceration in the sea cucumber Apostichopus japonicus causes a substantial loss of coelomocytes, potentially affecting its innate immune defense. Studies have shown that epigenetic regulation, particularly DNA methylation, may play a critical role in coelomocyte replenishment. In this study, we investigated the role of DNA methylation dynamics in coelomocyte replenishment following evisceration. Intracellular SAM concentrations declined from 53.5 ± 1.4 ng/mL before evisceration to 22.7 ± 5.6 ng/mL at 6 h, representing a 57.6% reduction. DNMT1 expression decreased to 0.20-fold of the pre-evisceration level at 12 h, whereas TET2 expression increased to 2.32-fold the pre-evisceration level. Following pharmacological inhibition of DNMT activity with 5-azacytidine, the expression levels of E2F, Cyclin A, and Cyclin B in the DNMTiEVI group were 7.43-fold, 5.69-fold, and 18.0-fold higher than those in the EVI group at 0, 24, and 24 h, respectively. Flow cytometric analysis revealed that, following DNMT inhibition, the proportion of S-phase cells in the DNMTiEVI group increased from 10.04% at 0 h to 17.85% at 72 h, whereas that in the EVI group rose from 8.58% at 0 h to 12.53% at 72 h. The proportion of EdU-positive cells in the DNMTiEVI group increased from 5.3% at 0 h to 13.5% at 72 h, whereas that in the EVI group rose from 3.3% at 0 h to 10.2% at 72 h. At 72 h, coelomocyte density reached 3.6 × 10 5 cells/mL in the DNMTiEVI group compared with 2.0 × 10 5 cells/mL in the EVI group, and cell viability was 1.91-fold higher following DNMT inhibition. These findings suggest that DNMT inhibition is associated with increased expression of cell-cycle-related genes, enhanced cell-cycle progression, and accelerated coelomocyte replenishment following evisceration in A. japonicus.

items.title: Carbon-Cloth-Templated Oxygen Vacancies Enable Direct Benzene Ring-Opening for Cleaner Photocatalytic VOC Abatement.
items.abstract: Gaseous benzene, a Group-1 carcinogenic volatile organic compound (VOC) widely released from petrochemical and solvent-based industries, poses a persistent obstacle to cleaner industrial production owing to the leakage of toxic aromatic intermediates, such as phenol and p-benzoquinone, during incomplete photocatalytic oxidation. Conventional MnO 2 -based photocatalysts further suffer from weak substrate adsorption and sluggish charge separation, resulting in high energy penalties and secondary pollution. Herein, a carbon-cloth (CC)-induced defect-engineering strategy was developed to fabricate an oxygen-vacancy-enriched MnO 2 monolithic photocatalyst (Vo-MnO 2 @CC) for low-energy, by-product-suppressed photocatalytic benzene oxidation (PBO). Density functional theory (DFT) calculations combined with EPR, XPS, COHP, and in-situ DRIFT evidence demonstrate that electron donation from CC weakens surface Mn-O bonds and spontaneously generates abundant, thermally stable surface oxygen vacancies (Vo) without chemical reductants. The Vo-modulated surface up-shifts the Mn d-band center from 2.62 to 3.77 eV, strengthens the chemisorption of benzene (E ads = -2.31 eV), H 2 O, and O 2 , and accelerates the generation of ·OH and ·O 2 - radicals. Concurrently, covalent C-O-Mn linkages establish a directional electron-transport channel that prolongs carrier lifetime from 2.85 to 10.39 ns and suppresses electron-hole recombination. Critically, GC-MS and DFT analyses reveal that Vo-MnO 2 @CC reverses the conventional ring-opening energy landscape, lowering the activation barrier of direct benzene ring-opening (1.38 eV) below those of phenol (1.60 eV) and p-benzoquinone (1.47 eV), thereby unlocking a "direct ring-opening pathway" that bypasses toxic aromatic intermediates. Consequently, Vo-MnO 2 @CC achieves 99.13% benzene conversion with 96.93% CO 2 mineralization within 30 min, retains 95.09% activity over 15 h of fixed-bed operation and 90.32% benzene conversion over 60 h of continuous-flow operation, and shows broad-spectrum efficacy toward formaldehyde, acetaldehyde, and toluene. This work offers mechanistic insight into vacancy-mediated thermodynamic regulation and a scalable, binder-free, low-energy photocatalyst platform aligned with cleaner-production goals for the sustainable abatement of recalcitrant aromatic VOCs.

items.title: Long-term risk prediction of 1,2-dichloroethane transport in an industrial park based on coupling of HYDRUS-2D and Bayesian network.
items.abstract: The decommissioning of chemical industrial parks under China's industrial restructuring has left numerous sites contaminated by volatile organic compounds (VOCs). Among these contaminants, 1,2-dichloroethane (1,2-DCA) is of particular concern due to its high mobility, toxicity, and frequent regulatory exceedance. However, risk characterization relying solely on monitoring data is constrained by sparse spatial coverage and high costs, while standalone numerical models such as HYDRUS-2D struggle to incorporate stratigraphic heterogeneity and parameter uncertainty, resulting in limited long-term predictive reliability. To address these challenges, this study develops a coupled HYDRUS-2D and Bayesian network framework for a typical decommissioned site, integrating process-based transport simulation with probabilistic inference to optimize key parameters and quantify prediction uncertainty over a 10-year horizon. The standalone HYDRUS-2D model captures vertical 1,2-DCA migration well (R 2 = 0.90), with longitudinal dispersivity and adsorption partition coefficient identified as the dominant controls. Through Bayesian inference, the coupled model achieves improvement in at least one performance metric at 57 of the 77 monitoring points (74.03%) and achieves a lower overall WRMSE, while the improvement in R 2 is limited. Under a source-elimination scenario, the 10-year simulation reveals a stratified migration pattern: rapid surface leaching, transitional middle-layer transport, and persistent deep-layer retention. In the representative profile, 98.06% of the simulated deep low-permeability layer remained categorized as high-risk after 10 years, suggesting its potential as a long-term secondary source. This coupled framework offers a probabilistic, uncertainty-aware approach for VOC risk assessment at decommissioned industrial sites, providing a transferable methodological reference for remediation planning and safe land reuse.

items.title: PFAS pollution in Portuguese estuaries: linking multi-matrix distribution and bioaccumulation to risk assessment.
items.abstract: Per- and polyfluoroalkyl substances (PFAS) contamination was investigated in two major Portuguese estuaries, the Douro and Tagus, across multiple compartments (surface water, suspended particulate matter (SPM), and biota), to assess spatial and seasonal variability, bioaccumulation, and ecological risk. PFAS were detected in all compartments, showing distinct patterns linked to local anthropogenic pressures and compound-specific behaviour. The Douro estuary exhibited higher concentrations and greater variability, with peak levels in winter and autumn, consistent with industrial and urban inputs. The Tagus estuary showed lower background concentrations but distinct contamination hotspots, particularly in summer. Long-chain perfluorocarboxylic acids, especially PFOA, dominated the dissolved phase, whereas perfluorosulfonates, including PFOS, were more prevalent in SPM and biota, indicating greater bioaccumulation potential in both estuaries. SPM generally exhibited low PFAS concentrations, confirming dominance of the dissolved phase, although compound-dependent partitioning was observed. Biota analyses revealed species-specific accumulation, with higher uptake in the macrobenthic bivalve Scrobicularia plana. Bioaccumulation factors and partitioning metrics showed weak correlations with environmental variables, suggesting that physicochemical conditions alone exert limited control. Environmental risk assessment identified high risk for PFDA and PFDoDA in the Douro, while human health risk was low at the assessed sites. Complementary ToxPi analysis prioritised PFTeDA and PFTrDA in both estuaries, highlighting the importance of considering multiple-criteria PFAS screening. PFOS concentrations exceeded Environmental Quality Standards in both estuaries, indicating potential long-term environmental concern despite generally low RQ-based risk. Overall, the results emphasise the importance of integrated multi-compartment monitoring for PFAS management under the Water Framework Directive.

items.title: Quantifying the distribution of perfluorooctane sulfonate and perfluorooctanoic acid in the global marine environment by marine birds via guano transport.
items.abstract: Marine birds are important biovectors of marine-derived nutrients and pollutants to island breeding colonies via mainly guano deposition. However, their impact on global pollutant transport has not been estimated. Here, we reported the fluxes of perfluorooctane sulfonate (PFOS) and perfluorooctanoic acid (PFOA) excreted by marine birds, based on a model considering the global marine bird distribution (including 332 species and 2678 colonies) and a bioenergetics model. The highest biotransport fluxes of PFOS and PFOA were 13.0 and 1.70 g/km 2 /year on islands, respectively. The polar regions were contamination hotspots for biotransport. Biotransport flux of PFOS exceeded regional midpoint atmospheric deposition in 77.4% of Antarctic colonies. The marine bird biotransport of PFOS and PFOA outweighs long-range air transportation in remote marine areas, which is different from the fate of semi-volatile persistent organic pollutants. The results suggest that biotransport should not be overlooked in future global PFOS and PFOA cycling models.

items.title: NLRP12 negatively regulates RIP2, TRAF6, TRAF3, and TBK1 mediated type I IFN signaling and inflammatory response in large yellow croaker Larimichthys crocea.
items.abstract: Nucleotide-binding leucine-rich repeat-containing receptor 12 (NLRP12) functions to restrain inflammatory and type I interferon signaling, thereby contributing to maintenance of host immune homeostasis. In large yellow croaker (Larimichthys crocea), an NLRP12 ortholog, designated Lc-NLRP12, was isolated and identified. Genomic analysis showed that Lc-NLRP12 comprised eight exons separated by seven introns. Its 3,312 bp open reading frame encoded a protein of 1,104 amino acids. The predicted protein contained a PYRIN domain at the N terminus, a FISNA and an NACHT domain, five LRR motifs, and a C-terminal SPRY domain. Confocal imaging indicated predominant cytoplasmic localization of Lc-NLRP12. Basal Lc-NLRP12 transcripts were detected by qRT-PCR throughout the tissue panel, with maximal abundance in the head kidney and minimal in the brain. Transcript levels of Lc-NLRP12 increased significantly in the gill, intestine, spleen, and head kidney after poly(I:C), LPS, PGN or Pseudomonas plecoglossicida challenge. Overexpression Lc-NLRP12 alone activated NF-κB, IRF3, IRF7, IFNd, and IL-1β promoters, whereas co-expression with Lc-RIP2, Lc-TRAF6, Lc-TRAF3, or Lc-TBK1 predominantly attenuated inflammatory and type I IFN signaling associated with these partners. Under these co-expression conditions, the transcript levels of immune-related genes, including IL-1β, TNF-α, and g-type lysozyme were also reduced. Co-immunoprecipitation assays showed that Lc-NLRP12 was associated with the four signaling proteins described above. These results support a model in which Lc-NLRP12 can attenuate inflammatory and type I interferon signaling through functional associations with Lc-RIP2, Lc-TRAF6, Lc-TRAF3, and Lc-TBK1, thereby broadening current functional knowledge of NLRP12 in teleosts.

items.title: Dietary inclusion of spent coffee grounds (SCG) shifts black soldier fly larvae towards catabolism: insights from metabolomics and nutrient mass balance.
items.abstract: Black soldier fly (Hermetia illucens, BSF) larvae efficiently convert organic residues into nutrient-rich biomass for use as animal feed, but the metabolic responses to nutritionally challenging substrates remain poorly understood. In this study, the effects of incorporating spent coffee grounds (SCG) into the BSF larval diet were evaluated by combining growth performance metrics, fatty acid and amino acid mass balance analysis and untargeted nuclear magnetic resonance (NMR) metabolomics. SCG inclusion reduced larval performance and overall nutrient retention. Metabolomic profiling confirmed diet-driven multivariate shifts in central metabolism after partial least squares discriminant analysis (PLS-DA, p < 0.001), with SCG-fed larvae exhibiting markers of intensified lipid and protein catabolism (acetylcarnitine and β-alanine, respectively), which may represent changes arising from altered glycolysis. Together, these results indicate that although SCG provides usable nutrients, its incorporation imposes metabolic constraints that ultimately limit larval growth. Our findings inform biowaste valorisation in BSF bioconversion and reveal metabolic plasticity of insect larvae to nutritional stress.
