items.title: Perceptive Humanoid Motion from Simulation
items.abstract: Humanoid robots have the potential to automate a wide range of physical tasks. Progress toward generalist humanoid autonomy, however, remains constrained by a data bottleneck: mapping pixels and free-form language to low-level joint commands requires paired supervision, and no corpus of such data exists at sufficiently large scale. Some approaches rely on human teleoperation and wearable capture devices, which require at least an hour of human time to produce an hour of data. We present HALO, a humanoid autonomy system powered by a pipeline that synthesizes vision-language-motion data across a thousand procedurally generated homes. The corpus scales with compute rather than human labor. HALO acquires a repertoire of physical skills, including sitting on chairs, navigating to named objects, stepping sideways through half-open doors, crouching and crawling beneath tables, and pushing boxes. It orchestrates these skills to solve composite, long-horizon tasks. Without ever seeing a real home during training, HALO transfers zero-shot to the physical world, achieving a 91% success rate across 360 trials in six unmapped real-world environments. See https://apple-aiml-research.github.io/ml-halo/ for code and videos.

items.title: Enabling AWS Cloud FPGA Development Using High-Level Vitis HLS
items.abstract: We present a toolchain for development of ML models on AWS EC2 F2 cloud FPGA infrastructure from high-level language, implementing a complete Vitis HLS to HDK bridge to AFI workflow that has been absent from the academic literature despite eight years of AWS FPGA availability. We introduce a four-level methodology (FP32 PyTorch, bit-accurate quantized Python, HLS C-simulation, physical FPGA) to aid in localizing errors, including FPGA-specific circuit errors. Together these tools allow coding agents to effectively implement FPGA designs from user directions, testing and debugging as needed. We document the deployment workflow, timing closure strategies, and practical HLS engineering decisions that proved crucial. We validate using TinyBERT fine-tuned for address Named Entity Recognition, implementing the embedding layer and the first of four encoder layers on the FPGA hardware. Our implementation streams weights from host DRAM, yielding poor performance compared to CPU/GPU implementations; we discuss forward paths.

items.title: A Frame-Level View and Image-Quality Annotation Tool for Fetal Echocardiography: Comparison with Spreadsheet Annotation
items.abstract: Objective: To develop the Cardiologist Annotation Tool (CAT) for frame-level cardiac view and image-quality annotation in fetal echocardiography and compare it with spreadsheet-based annotation. Methods: CAT provides cine playback, frame navigation, and keyboard-based labeling without manual frame-range entry. Experts annotated 25 studies using both methods, and spreadsheet annotations were audited for predefined data-entry errors. In a randomized crossover study, six medical students annotated two normal studies, one with each method, against an expert reference. Results: Among 1,746 spreadsheet-annotated files, 6.2% contained major or critical data-entry errors, more frequently in congenital heart disease than normal studies (10.9% vs 3.4%). CAT yielded more annotated view segments per clip (3.6 vs 1.5). Rates of labeled and correctly labeled frames per minute were 1.77 and 1.68 times those with spreadsheets, respectively (both P = 0.031), with gains in all six students. No detectable difference in view-label accuracy was observed. Conclusion: CAT eliminates manual frame-range entry and enables finer-grained, structured annotation of fetal echocardiography, providing a practical approach to preparing datasets for AI research.

items.title: Go-Go-Go: the game of Go without turns
items.abstract: The study of variants of classic games has a long history, with chess alone inspiring countless variants that have been proposed, analyzed, and studied. The game of Go, despite rivaling chess in age, cultural relevance, popularity, and strategic depth, has seen drastically fewer variants. We introduce Go-Go-Go, a variant of the classic game of Go where there are no turns, and players play stones simultaneously and asynchronously on the board. The variant (which is to be played through a computer) includes a basic mechanism to avoid excessive spamming of moves, by imposing a minimal delay between moves that depends on their relative spatial distance. Apart from the lack of time discretization, most of the ruleset of the original game is either directly maintained or adapted in a natural way that preserves the original spirit. The first playtesting indicates that this results in the preservation of much of the emerging strategies and "flavor" of Go, while replacing the long strategic reasoning with fast paced, instinctive action fueled by quick reflexes. Play testers also report the need to balance immediate but suboptimal reactions with more reasoned but slower plays. We offer a publicly available, playable, OpenSource, and online reference implementation of Go-Go-Go at http://gogogo.di.unimi.it

items.title: Smartphone-Aided VR Exergames for HIIT: Gamifying Fitness with Real-Time Pose Estimation
items.abstract: This paper introduces an innovative virtual reality (VR) exergame system designed to gamify High-Intensity Interval Training (HIIT) workouts through 11 predefined combo moves, including squat-punch combinations, bilateral arm strikes, and diagonal stretch combos. Unlike conventional tracking methods that often rely on wearable motion capture suits or limited headset-based sensors, our system uses a standard smartphone camera placed on a tripod to capture full-body movement. This approach offers a cost-effective and scalable alternative, particularly well-suited to the fast, dynamic motions typical of HIIT routines. The smartphone footage is processed in real time using a pose estimation algorithm, with extracted biomechanical data analyzed by a backend server built on the Model Context Protocol (MCP), Anthropic's open standard for connecting AI models to structured data sources and tools, and a GPT-4o large language model. The system generates personalized assessments of form accuracy, movement efficiency, exercise intensity, and potential injury risks, tailored specifically to high-impact, time-sensitive exercises. A within-subject study involving 20 participants (ages 18-25) compared experiences in VR and Non-VR HIIT sessions. Results indicated significantly higher enjoyment (Mean = 3.5 vs 2.8, p = 0.02), improved immersion/focus (Mean = 3.2 vs 2.8, p = 0.03), and increased likelihood to recommend (Mean = 3.2 vs 2.7, p = 0.04) under the VR condition. Confidence to continue did not differ significantly between conditions (p = 0.15), while perceived intensity remained comparable. The MCP system showed strong agreement with expert evaluation (87.5%, N = 10 sessions, one certified trainer), supporting its reliability as a feedback tool.

items.title: Dexterous Robotic Hands in the Foundation-Model Era: A Full-Stack Survey of Hardware, Data, Cross-Embodiment Transfer, Learning, and Evaluation
items.abstract: Dexterous robotic hands are increasingly coupled to large-scale human data and foundation models, yet progress in hardware, representation learning and evaluation is often assessed separately. This survey reviews work from January 2024 to early November 2026, with earlier studies included to establish technical lineages. We organize the literature into five interdependent layers: hardware; data collection and curation; cross-embodiment transfer; learning and foundation models; and evaluation and applications. Human hand-object understanding and tactile sensing provide two cross-cutting perspectives. A system-level architecture, comparative tables and five case analyses connect design choices across these layers. We distinguish within-study experimental comparisons from heterogeneous corpus statistics, vendor specifications and company-reported results. Three conclusions emerge. First, the value of human data depends on kinematic, visual and contact alignment, not recording volume alone. Second, shared action representations and foundation policies do not remove embodiment-specific constraints on force, latency and contact. Third, task completion is insufficient to establish physical correctness or deployment readiness. Evidence remains limited for zero-shot transfer of contact-rich skills between morphologically different hands, long-duration reliability, and cross-sensor tactile generalization. We identify eleven open problems and propose reporting interfaces and controlled comparisons that can make full-stack progress more measurable. The review is a structured narrative synthesis rather than a pooled performance ranking or an exhaustive systematic review.

items.title: Beyond the principle-practice gap: Responsible AI as situated epistemic and ethical practice
items.abstract: Responsible AI scholarship has found that ethical principles are frequently not reflected in AI design and development. Conceptualised as a `gap' between principle and practice, this is framed as a problem of implementation, awareness or compliance, and by implication, a deficit of systems or individual behaviour. This paper sets out an alternative explanation. Drawing on fourteen semi-structured interviews with actors designing and governing AI-enabled anti-trafficking systems across law enforcement, commercial, research, and survivor-support contexts, it argues that such apparent gaps emerge from the varied and complex institutional and professional conditions through which actors come to recognise some issues, but not others, as ethical problems requiring action. We show that epistemic choices are intertwined with ethical judgements, and trace four interconnected moments---perception, judgement, situated action and socio-technical materialisation---through which concerns become intelligible, are weighed and acted upon, and are embedded in technical artefacts and governance arrangements. Actors often hold genuine ethical commitments, but these commitments are shaped by institutional logics and professional moral economies: some concerns are materialised, while others are narrowed, deferred or left unrealised. We show that ethical agency is exercised within and between competing constraints of profession, role, prior experience, and institutional settings. The paper argues that responsible AI governance requires purposeful and well-developed epistemic infrastructures that can cut across these constraints to establish institutional conditions through which the knowledge of affected communities and potential harms becomes receivable and actionable in design.

items.title: You Know What You Will Like: People Predict Their Own Ratings Better Than Recommender Systems
items.abstract: Recommender systems usually learn what people want from what they have done. Platforms could also ask people directly, but asking is costly: 98.8% of the prompts in our data went unanswered. Theories of statistical prediction imply that a person's own forecast adds little to a recommender algorithm built from many people's behavior. Theories of dispersed knowledge imply that people hold information about their own taste that the data lack. We test the two with the MovieLens Beliefs dataset. In 2023-2024, a homepage prompt asked members how they expected to rate movies they said they had not seen. Of 26,020 such expectations, 551 from 277 members were followed by a rating at least a day later. We compare each expectation with four benchmarks: the platform's own predicted rating, two collaborative-filtering models (matrix factorization and an item neighborhood), and a stack trained on other members' outcomes. The trained models use each member's latest ratings. People predict their own ratings more accurately than all four benchmarks (correlation 0.69, against 0.34 for MovieLens and 0.54 to 0.59 for the trained recommenders). Added to all the machine forecasts and features, the expectation lowers out-of-sample mean squared error by 26%. The gain holds when models are trained on earlier expectations and tested on later ones. A member's earlier expectations about other movies do not replace the current one. In ordering a member's own movies, the trained recommenders are statistically indistinguishable from the person. On old, heavily rated movies, the machines do as well or better. The results reconcile the two theories: the crowd's data suffice where they are rich, and the person adds information about the specific item. We derive four design principles for preference elicitation and recommender evaluation.

items.title: Cognitive and Behavioural Effects of Haptic Feedback for ROV Teleoperation in Hazardous Environments
items.abstract: Teleoperating a Remotely Operated Vehicle (ROV) in complex underwater environments presents unique challenges. Dynamic, three dimensional obstacles and unseen water currents pose real risks to expensive robotic hardware in environments in which recovery can be next to impossible. This paper explores the cognitive effects of haptic feedback to improve vehicle safety in such environments. An in-water study is analysed with a ROV exposed to controlled cross-currents, with environmental information presented via a soft and vibrating haptic touchpad. Results demonstrate that while encountering an unseen cross-current significantly increases an operator's physical and temporal demand, the introduction of haptic feedback mitigates these factors and improves self-assessed performance. Interestingly, the haptic condition also produced the highest levels of mental demand and operator frustration. Despite this increased mental workload, operators drove the ROV significantly faster when receiving haptic cues compared to the current-only condition, indicating a higher level of user confidence. Ultimately, these findings suggest that while haptic feedback may initially require more cognitive processing to interpret unseen hazards, it successfully enhances operator awareness and promotes more confident navigation in hazardous environments.

items.title: Perceived Trust and Transparency in AI-Altered vs. Human-Written LinkedIn Posts
items.abstract: People increasingly draft a social media post themselves and then let an AI model refine it (AI-altered), a common but understudied middle case between fully human-written and fully AI-generated content. We ask whether this changes how trustworthy and transparent readers perceive the post to be, and whether they can even tell. We first analyze real ChatGPT conversations (WildChat) to find how people actually alter social media posts, which we use to design realistic alteration prompts. We then run a pre-registered, within-subjects online experiment (n=214) in which participants rate unlabeled human-written and AI-altered LinkedIn-style posts for perceived trustworthiness and transparency, and separately judge whether each post was AI-altered. We find that AI-alteration itself has no detectable effect on either perceived trustworthiness or transparency (both estimates near zero, not significant). At the same time, readers did not reliably detect AI-alteration (49\% accuracy, near chance) and defaulted to assuming human authorship when unsure. However, our analysis shows significant differences in transparency and trustworthiness ratings across the specific post, the AI model, as well as the prompt used to alter it. For instance, more detailed prompts raise both perceived trustworthiness and transparency but also make the alteration more detectable. Surprisingly, the prompt that shifted ratings most also asked the model to add one new idea absent from the original post: readers nonetheless rated this AI-invented, unverifiable content as more trustworthy and transparent.

items.title: Does Frontier AI Strengthen Cyber Defense? Evidence from Project Glasswing
items.abstract: Defenders and attackers race to find the same software flaws. I use the launch of Project Glasswing, which gave a small group of large US tech firms early access to Claude Mythos Preview, a model for finding software vulnerabilities, to study how access to frontier AI affects defenders, external researchers, and attackers. Using the universe of publicly disclosed vulnerabilities, I find that firms with access more than doubled their disclosures relative to Chinese and Russian tech firms without access, disclosed about 150 percent more high-impact vulnerabilities, and fixed reported flaws as quickly as before. As treated firms found more flaws themselves, external researchers, who sell their findings through bug bounties, reported about half as many vulnerabilities in treated firms' code and more in other firms' code, without leaving the market. There is no evidence that attackers exploited the additional vulnerabilities: the share exploited within a month of disclosure fell by about two thirds, mainly because a smaller share was already exploited when disclosed, while the number exploited did not change. Frontier AI helped defenders find and fix more flaws before attackers exploited them, but its restricted release creates an asymmetry in software security between firms in different countries.

items.title: Learning Time-Varying Connectomes for Stable Behavior Across Development
items.abstract: Neural circuits must maintain functionality to drive effective behavior while their size, topology, geometry, and intrinsic dynamics change across development. To model developing visuomotor circuits and behavior, we investigated whether a single compact generative encoding could produce functional recurrent controllers across such changes. Building on the HyperNEAT algorithm, we represented this program as a compositional pattern-producing network that received developmental time as an input to generate age-specific connectivity. The developmental substrate prescribed neuronal birth, position, sensory organization, and intrinsic time constants. We tested this approach using two geometrically distinct developmental substrates and two visuomotor tasks: optomotor responses and phototaxis. Controllers optimized at only the initial or mature substrate generally failed when evaluated at other ages. In contrast, controllers optimized across multiple developmental snapshots maintained substantially higher and more consistent performance across trained and unseen ages. Optimization at only three developmental snapshots was often sufficient to produce effective behavior across the tested developmental interval. The resulting connectomes changed substantially with age and did not converge on a single trajectory of sparsity or connection-weight statistics. Controllers also differed in whether they relied on neurons born later in development. These results demonstrate that a shared spatiotemporal time-varying connectivity program can produce recurrent neural networks that preserve behavior across substantial developmental changes. Together, these results provide a framework for studying how functional stability can emerge without requiring structural or dynamical stability.

items.title: Cell-type-specific modularity in E/I networks shapes dynamical regimes and computational capabilities
items.abstract: Structural modularity is a ubiquitous feature of brain networks that shapes neural dynamics and information processing. Yet excitatory and inhibitory populations can differ in their modular organization, and it remains unclear how this asymmetry affects network dynamics and computation. Here, using dynamical mean-field theory and simulations of networks performing complex temporal tasks, we show that independently tuning excitatory and inhibitory modularity controls the dynamical regimes of balanced E/I networks. In particular, such tuning can generate a dominant spectral outlier despite overall E/I balance, producing a topology-controlled transition between bulk- and low-rank-dominated regimes, with different dynamical bifurcations leading to chaos and bistability, respectively. In chaotic time-series prediction tasks, computational performance is enhanced near these dynamical boundaries, including both the onset of chaos and the transition to bistability. Favorable configurations exhibit strongly modular excitation and comparatively homogeneous inhibition, similar to what is observed in cortical connectivity.

items.title: Synchronized Hearts, Desynchronized Brains: A Nonlinear Dynamics Perspective for Function and Failure
items.abstract: Both the heart and the brain are built from electrically excitable cells, yet the emergent dynamics of these organs could not differ more. In the myocardium, a coherent traveling wave of action potentials ensures coordinated contraction; in the cerebral cortex, distributed, irregular spiking underlies efficient information processing and the generation of behavior. Here, we illuminate the principles that underlie the emergence of such distinct nonlinear dynamics using concepts from complex systems. We trace these principles across scales from ion channels and cellular action potential generation, through cellular coupling mechanisms and network architecture, to organ level dynamics and clinical phenotypes. Designed to support either synchronized waves or desynchronized information processing, the heart and the brain can thus be understood as operating on opposite sides of a synchronization phase transition. Crossing this transition implies pathological dynamics in both organs: Loss of synchrony in the heart produces arrhythmia; excess synchrony in the brain leads to epileptic seizures. We discuss how adaptation mechanisms, including plasticity, modulation, remodeling, and learning, maintain the appropriate level of (de)synchronization. Overall, we provide a unified excitable-system perspective, together with an educational notebook, to foster cross-disciplinary insights into cardiac and neural function and pathology.

items.title: Modeling Gene Expression Noise: From Transcriptional Dynamics to Cell Growth and Division
items.abstract: Gene expression is inherently noisy, leading to substantial cell-to-cell variation in mRNA and protein levels. The telegraph model and the simpler bursty model provide good fits to single-cell count distributions and have been used extensively to understand transcriptional kinetics and estimate the kinetic parameters. However, these models all describe a static cell. Here, we review models of stochastic gene expression in growing and dividing cells which aim to understand how a cell's own life history, from its birth, through copying its genome, to its division, leaves a distinct fluctuation signature on molecule numbers. We discuss the biochemical and biophysical processes captured by these models, their analytical tractability, the concept of cyclo-stationary behavior, when this is well approximated by the steady-state of static models and how the distributions of molecular numbers measured under these conditions sensitively depend on the experimental setup. This is followed by a discussion of how these models are fitted to single-cell measurements, how biological variability can be separated from measurement noise, and which computational advances make this feasible for thousands of genes. We finish by highlighting the open problems in the field.

items.title: Mind Control of LLMs via Closed-Loop Stimulation: Out-of-Distribution Robustness
items.abstract: Brains and large language models need not be considered equivalent systems to reveal an interpretable commonality: both exhibit high-dimensional, nonlinear dynamics whose behavior can only be modeled imperfectly. This creates a shared challenge whenever we seek to intervene in their dynamics. A controller may either rely on a model identified around a particular operating regime and risk failure as the system moves away from that regime, or explicitly account for uncertainty and a changing internal state. Neurostimulation has confronted an analogous problem for decades. The limitations of fixed, open-loop stimulation have motivated closed-loop and state-dependent approaches that condition intervention on the ongoing state of the neural system. Inspired by this principle, we formulate LLM steering as a feedback-control problem in which the network's internal state, rather than a fixed intervention alone, determines how the system is perturbed. We further account for the mismatch between tractable dynamical models and the nonlinear transformer they approximate through robust control. As one principled realization of this framework, we develop an $H_\infty$-based steering controller that limits sensitivity to disturbances and linearization mismatches. Across multiple steering benchmarks, the controller improves performance over existing baselines, with particularly pronounced gains under out-of-distribution conditions and varying length complexities. Beyond controller performance, we introduce robust steerability, $S_{\mathrm{rob}}$, a pre-deployment measure of tolerance to dynamics mismatch; across model-task pairs, it exhibits task-specific structure and varies systematically with model scale. Beyond robust LLM steering, our measure asks not merely whether control is possible, but how much uncertainty it can survive; a principle that may span artificial and biological neural systems.

items.title: A minimal E/I circuit model explains differential recovery from amblyopia under TTX and reverse occlusion
items.abstract: Recovery from amblyopia beyond the critical period remains a major challenge in visual neuroscience. Experimental studies show that transient inactivation of the fellow eye with tetrodotoxin (TTX) produces stronger and more persistent recovery than reverse occlusion (RO), despite both interventions reducing competition from the fellow eye. The circuit mechanisms underlying this difference remain unclear. We develop a minimal cortical circuit model combining excitatory-inhibitory population dynamics, BCM-like metaplasticity, homeostatic regulation, and eye-specific synaptic plasticity. Monocular deprivation drives the network into an amblyopic operating regime with reduced excitatory activity and fellow-eye dominance. Phase-plane and operating-regime analyses show that TTX and RO subsequently place the circuit in distinct dynamical states. TTX lowers inhibitory activity while maintaining excitatory activity above the BCM modification threshold, creating a larger plasticity-permissive regime than RO. These differences produce stronger recovery of amblyopic-eye responsiveness and greater correction of ocular dominance under TTX. A local robustness analysis across 300 perturbed parameter sets shows that the TTX advantage is not dependent on a narrowly tuned parameter choice. These results provide a mechanistic account of the differential efficacy of fellow-eye inactivation and suggest that recovery from sensory deprivation depends not only on changes in sensory input, but also on the dynamical operating regime of the cortical circuit.

items.title: Can a self-sustaining chemical network emerge due to just a few catalysts?
items.abstract: Understanding how self-sustaining chemical reaction networks can emerge from simple molecules is an important question in chemical approaches to the origin of life. Reflexively autocatalytic and food-generated (RAF) sets provide a mathematical framework for investigating this question. This line of research goes back to the early work of Kauffman on autocatalytic reaction networks and was subsequently developed through the probabilistic framework of Mossel and Steel. Further contributions by Hordijk, Steel, and collaborators extended the theory to more heterogeneous forms of catalysis, including reaction-dependent probabilities or power-law distributions of catalytic activity. We introduce a stochastic model that combines heterogeneous molecular catalytic activity with reaction-dependent molecule-reaction compatibility. By assigning random catalytic weights to molecules and incorporating compatibility through an explicit formulation of catalysis probabilities, our model provides a concrete and flexible setting that captures both sources of heterogeneity while remaining mathematically tractable. We establish novel and general criteria for RAF formation and nonformation. We further demonstrate that classical phase-transition criteria need not remain valid in the presence of reaction-dependent catalysis. For heavy-tailed catalytic weights, we identify and rigorously quantify an additional phase transition. In models with finite-mean catalytic weights, RAF formation and nonformation are governed by a catalytic intensity parameter. For infinite-mean weights, however, we show that RAFs may emerge with probability tending to one even when the catalytic intensity parameter tends to zero.

items.title: Population synthesis of substellar companions surviving common-envelope evolution
items.abstract: Predicting the population of substellar companions around white dwarfs (WDs) requires accounting for both companions that avoid engulfment during stellar evolution and those that survive common-envelope (CE) evolution. While the former population was investigated in our previous population-synthesis study, a comprehensive population synthesis of the latter remains lacking. We investigated the fate of engulfed substellar companions within the same population-synthesis framework. We aim to predict the occurrence rates and properties of companions surviving CE evolution, identify the conditions permitting survival, and assess their detectability. We determined the stellar structure at the onset of CE evolution and calculated CE outcomes for different ejection efficiencies considering gravitational and thermal energy or the full internal energy of the envelope. Survival is rare and strongly depends on the evolutionary stage at engulfment. No companions entering CE evolution during the red-giant branch or early asymptotic-giant branch survive. Survivors originate exclusively from the thermally pulsing asymptotic-giant branch, when stellar envelopes can become weakly bound, allowing even relatively low-mass companions to survive. The resulting systems typically have orbital periods of a few hours. We predict occurrence rates of up to 0.16% among WDs, corresponding to an upper limit of 2.53 companions to WDs within 50 pc. Transit detection is primarily limited by orbital geometry, whereas all predicted survivors would produce detectable infrared excess with JWST out to 50pc. We predict that CE evolution produces a small but observable population of close substellar companions to WDs. Survival is governed not only by companion mass but critically by the envelope structure at engulfment, particularly during thermal pulses, and by the contribution of recombination energy to envelope ejection.

items.title: Phase Locking in Oscillator Networks with Uncertain and State-Dependent Couplings
items.abstract: Phase locking in oscillator networks depends critically on the interaction strengths between coupled units. In many applications, however, these couplings are uncertain, state dependent, or time varying. We derive rigorous conditions for phase locking in Kuramoto-type networks when each coupling strength is known only within prescribed bounds. Building on a convex formulation of the nonlinear fixed-point equations, we obtain edge-wise error bounds for arbitrary feasible approximations that hold uniformly over all admissible couplings. These bounds yield sufficient conditions for the existence of phase-locked states with prescribed phase-difference limits. We illustrate the framework for AC power grids with uncertain voltage magnitudes and adaptive oscillator networks with state-dependent couplings. For the latter, the bounds can be further tightened by exploiting the state dependence of the couplings.

items.title: Understanding mathematics anxiety and its impact on cognitive effort in second-grade children: a pupillometry investigation
items.abstract: Introduction Many individuals struggle with mathematics, and mathematics anxiety (MA) is associated with poor mathematics performance. The reasons for this association are unclear, but one explanation is that MA reduces the working memory capacity available for problem solving. Because changes in pupil diameter index cognitive effort, this study used pupillometry to examine whether MA is related to cognitive effort in second-grade children. Methods Ninety-eight second-grade pupils in Norway solved easy and hard addition problems while their pupil diameter was recorded with an eye tracker. Arithmetic competence, working memory, and general intelligence were measured as control variables, and the data were analysed with linear mixed models. Results Hard problems elicited more cognitive effort than easy problems. MA moderated this effect: children with higher MA showed a smaller increase in cognitive effort with increasing problem difficulty, even after controlling for arithmetic competence, working memory, and general intelligence. When only correctly solved trials were analysed, the interaction was no longer significant, but higher MA was associated with lower overall cognitive effort. Discussion Children with higher MA did not show the heightened effort predicted by working memory interference accounts; the pattern may instead reflect reduced task engagement or avoidance. Because pupil diameter change indexes overall psychophysiological effort, the precise cognitive and affective mechanisms remain unclear.

items.title: Incentives and strategic behaviour: an experiment
items.abstract: Abstract How do incentive levels affect strategic behaviour? We address this with an experiment that separately identifies own- and opponent-incentive effects in two dominance-solvable games that differ in strategic complexity. Higher own incentives favour more strategically sophisticated actions and increase best responding to stated beliefs. Beliefs shift in a parallel direction and participants expect more sophisticated opponent actions. Furthermore, although higher own incentives increase belief accuracy, opponents with higher incentives are harder to predict. Higher incentives also increase response times, and longer response times are associated with better performance and more sophisticated actions and beliefs. Taken together, the evidence suggests that incentives affect strategic behaviour through two main channels: by reducing payoff-dependent mistakes and by increasing the effort devoted to reasoning, with the returns to that effort shaped by strategic complexity of the environment.

items.title: Evidence on the Robustness of the Links Between Social Relationships and Mortality
items.abstract: Despite a substantial literature on the links between social relationships and mortality, the size of the relative risks from loneliness, social isolation, and living alone, remain controversial. Further research is therefore important given demographic changes meaning that more people are living alone, for longer, and with chronic health conditions. Using 19 waves of high-quality Australian longitudinal data we provide new evidence using multiple measures of social relationships, model specifications, and adjustments for confounding. We focus on chronic measures of (poor) social relationships and provide separate estimates by gender. We find that both functional and structural aspects of social relationships are independently strongly associated with all-cause mortality. We estimate a hazard ratio for loneliness of 1.41, which is greater for males (1.55) than females (1.24). These hazard ratios are larger than found for social isolation (1.19). We also find a strong relationship between being an active member of a club and reduced mortality risk, but no evidence that living alone is an independent risk factor. We provide useful comparisons with the mortality risks associated with smoking and household income. Overall, our findings suggest that interventions should focus on reducing both loneliness and social isolation, as well as encouraging active social participation.

items.title: Factorial variation of saccade vigor with dual decision processes
items.abstract: Canonical stochastic models of decision-making treats decision and action as independent and sequential processes. However, studies involving limb movements consistently show that movement duration and kinematics are influenced by the quality of evidence. We tested whether saccade velocity varies with the quality of evidence in monkeys performing a visual search GO/NOGO task in which singleton elongation cued the GO/NOGO stimulus-response rule and the location of a color singleton specified saccade endpoint. We factorially manipulated the efficiency of stimulus-response cue discrimination by varying the elongation of the singleton and the efficiency of singleton localization by varying the color similarity between the singleton and distractors. The effectiveness of the manipulations was revealed by the response times on correct trials that were separately modified by the singleton localizability and stimulus-response cue discriminability, by the incidence of localization and response selection errors with separately modified error response times. Saccade velocity was higher on correct relative to error trials and was inversely proportional to response time. Saccade velocity was separately modified by singleton localizability and stimulus-response cue discriminability. Distinct patterns of error rates and saccade velocity across monkeys indicated individual differences in decision-making strategies. These findings demonstrate that the process selecting endpoints can influence both the timing and dynamics of saccadic eye movements. Incorporating saccade vigor can provide valuable constraints on biologically plausible decision models and help address the persistent challenge of model mimicry.

items.title: Sudden Gains and Losses in Personality Change Interventions: Predictors, Outcomes, and Implications for Individualized Personality Change
items.abstract: Recent research suggests that volitional personality change is possible through structured interventions, yet little is known about the temporal dynamics of such change. In psychotherapy, sudden gains—abrupt, substantial improvements between sessions—are robust predictors of treatment success. Based on 448 participants who completed a 12-week personality intervention, we examined whether similar sudden shifts occur in the context of volitional personality change and whether they explain differences in trait, life satisfaction, and self-esteem changes from the pre-test to the follow-up 3 months later. We compared four different measures for detecting shifts: daily and weekly personality states, generic change factors (e.g., gaining insight), and subjective progress. Sudden gains were relatively common and—with the exception of daily states—consistently associated with improvements in the targeted traits, life satisfaction, and self-esteem. Sudden gains in weekly states co-occurred with increased intervention engagement and key change processes such as gaining insight and practicing new behaviors—paralleling mechanisms found in psychotherapy. In contrast, sudden losses were less frequent and showed no meaningful negative effects for trait changes or life satisfaction. However, high dropout rates may have masked more consequential losses. These findings challenge the assumption that personality change is exclusively gradual and underscore the value of capturing dynamic, within-person fluctuations. Monitoring and leveraging such shifts may help to personalize interventions and optimize their impact. Future research should explore how sudden gains can be intentionally triggered and how interventions can be designed to support lasting change through both gradual and sudden pathways.

items.title: Ecological and social cues orchestrate concerted courtship in Drosophila
items.abstract: Abstract Mating decisions are often attributed to the sensory signalling between prospective sexual partners. Yet these interactions are also shaped by the broader environmental context in which they unfold, to appropriately align sexual arousal with reproductive opportunities 1–6 . Here we show that in Drosophila erecta mating is strictly contingent on the ecological and social environment generated as flies densely aggregate in groups on a food patch. We find that food volatiles directly promote male sexual arousal, triggering individuals to sample and pursue potential mates, giving rise to dynamic interactions across the group. The ensuing visual motion transforms each male’s visual field, which in turn further amplifies his arousal, generating a multisensory feedback loop that coordinately promotes courtship across individuals. D. erecta ’s strict dependence on environmental cues appears latent in related species, such as Drosophila melanogaster , where food odour can promote arousal 7 but is dispensable for vigorous courtship. Comparative circuit analyses show that species-specific thresholds for sexual arousal reflect variation in how olfactory input modulates conserved nodes controlling courtship drive, rendering food volatiles a strict sensory gate only in D. erecta . Together, our findings highlight how environmental cues not directly tied to sexual signalling can profoundly influence reproductive behaviour and reorganize the social landscape to ensure mating occurs in contexts where reproductive opportunities are abundant.

items.title: Promoting responsible tourism using generative AI nudges
items.abstract: Purpose With rapid modernization and globalization, responsible tourism practices at cultural heritage sites are in decline, as many visitors disengage from activities like volunteering, donating or mindful visits. This shift presents a significant challenge for governments, organizations and societies working to promote meaningful interactions with cultural heritage. Encouraging responsible tourism – where visitors respect local cultures while minimizing negative impacts – is crucial. generative artificial intelligence (GAI) offers an emerging avenue for innovative management practices, providing personalized and emotionally resonant digital nudges that can influence visitor engagement. However, limited empirical evidence exists regarding which types of nudges are most effective across cultural contexts. This study aims to investigate the impact of artificial intelligence (AI)-driven nudges delivered on emotional response and engagement, aiming to foster responsible tourism behaviour. Design/methodology/approach Using a mixed-methods approach, this study adopted a three-stage investigation. Firstly, this study conducted a content analysis gathered from 262 articles via web scrapping which identified five key themes surrounding responsible tourism. Stage two consisted of 25 in-depth interviews, which provided deeper insights on the factors influencing emotional response towards cultural heritage tourism. In stage 3, this study conducted 300 experiments and surveys, focusing on responses to six cultural nudge images representing Indian and UK cultures. Each image was categorized into neutral, positive and negative nudges, capturing participants’ engagement. Findings The findings suggest that AI-driven nudges significantly enhance tourists’ emotional responses (β = 0.108, p < 0.05) and engagement towards cultural heritage tourism (β = 0.224, p < 0.001), leading to greater appreciation and respect for local cultures and in turn leads to responsible tourism behaviours. Most importantly, engagement was found to be a powerful predictor of responsible tourism behaviour, demonstrating a strong positive relationship (β = 0.792, p < 0.001). Negative nudges (afraid, bitter) were most effective in encouraging responsible behaviours. However, the effectiveness of nudges varied based on an individual’s cultural identity, perceived cultural accuracy and AI hallucination potential highlighting the importance of tailored approaches for diverse audiences. Research limitations/implications The study is limited by a small sample, focus on Indian and UK contexts to capture participants’ perceptions and immediate responses to AI-driven nudges. It examines short-term behavioural intentions within a controlled experimental setting and applies continuous moderation to explore cultural effects. Building on these insights, future research can expand to broader cultural contexts, adopt longitudinal designs to assess behavioural change over time, incorporate objective behavioural data and explore the role of AI transparency and immersive technologies such as VR and AR in enhancing responsible tourism engagement. Originality/value This study provides novel empirical evidence on the role of Generative AI–driven emotional nudges in shaping responsible tourism behaviour, integrating cultural identity, perceived cultural accuracy and AI hallucination as key boundary conditions in a cross-cultural context.

items.title: Motor Expertise Combines Lower Task Engagement with Enhanced Error Sensitivity
items.abstract: Abstract Skilled motor behaviour relies on complex predictive control and error processing. Despite its indispensable position in our everyday lives, neurobiological mechanisms of motor skill acquisition remain poorly understood. The presented study evaluates the functional dynamics and microstructural substrate of expertise-related reorganisation in predictive timing circuits using multimodal functional and quantitative magnetic resonance imaging (MRI) data. Forty-one baseball/softball players, representing a natural model of optimised motor timing programs, were compared against forty-six non-athletic controls using a structural connectome-informed hierarchical Bayesian framework jointly modelling task-based functional MRI dynamics of feedforward predictive control and error-driven modulation. Expertise-related microstructural differences were then characterised using neurite orientation dispersion and density imaging and adiabatic T₁ρ mapping. In non-athletic controls, predictive control was found to engage a distributed cortico-subcortical sensorimotor, visuospatial, attentional and frontoparietal loops, while higher-order associative systems were relatively down-regulated. However, quantitative deviation from the task optimum was associated with lower response across this predictive network. Expertise was characterised by higher behavioural performance but also by attenuated prediction-related functional engagement alongside enhanced error-related modulation. Furthermore, neurite density and orientation dispersion indices were higher in experts across distributed cortical networks, while the cerebellum exhibited a divergent profile characterised by higher neurite density, lower orientation dispersion and faster T₁ρ relaxation. These findings indicate that expertise involves lower task engagement within an established architecture despite higher behavioural performance, together with enhanced error sensitivity and distributed microstructural differences. This pattern is consistent with more efficient neural dynamics complemented with underlying tissue alterations.

items.title: Reconceptualizing reading practices among pre-service teachers: a structural model of organisation, motivation, and reading intensity
items.abstract: Background Sustained reading is central to academic learning and professional growth in teacher education, yet studies increasingly describe university students’ reading as digitally oriented, fragmented, and requirement-driven. Most research examines behavioural, motivational, or organisational aspects of reading in isolation. Purpose This study examined how organised reading practices and motivational orientations relate to reading intensity among pre-service teachers, drawing on self-regulated learning theory and habit theory. Materials and methods A researcher-developed questionnaire was completed online by 1,594 pre-service teachers in ten teacher education programmes in West Kalimantan, Indonesia. The sample was randomly split: exploratory factor analysis with oblique rotation and parallel analysis was conducted on one half, and confirmatory factor analysis and latent structural equation modelling with a robust estimator for ordinal data on the other. The indirect association was tested with bootstrap confidence intervals. Results Participants relied mainly on online and audiovisual sources, although 66.1% preferred printed to electronic books, and most read one or two books a month. Four dimensions were supported: organised reading and resource management, autonomous motivation, requirement-driven reading, and reading intensity (CFI = 0.961, TLI = 0.956, SRMR = 0.049, RMSEA = 0.091). Autonomous and requirement-driven reasons for reading were unrelated and could not be combined into one factor. Organisation was associated with reading intensity directly (beta = 0.13) and indirectly through autonomous motivation (beta = 0.14, 95% bootstrap CI excluding zero), whereas requirement-driven reading was associated with lower reading intensity (beta = −0.16). Requirement-driven reading increased with year of study; other demographic differences were negligible. Conclusion Self-reported reading practices among pre-service teachers form an interrelated system in which organisation and autonomous motivation are associated with reading more, while reading only for assessment is associated with reading less. Because the design is cross-sectional and habit strength was not measured, habit formation is offered as a theoretical interpretation for longitudinal testing. The findings support autonomy-supportive reading cultures and assessment reform in Indonesian teacher education.

items.title: Remaking “The Unconscious” Paradigm, Act I: ...The Gap” Between Subliminal Processing and the Unconscious “Mind...
items.abstract: Abstract The notion of subliminal processing often refers to perception that takes place below the threshold of conscious visual awareness. This is suggested to lead to behavioural and emotional changes with spontaneous and actionable evolutionary-survival and/or social-adaptation response value. Therefore, it has been suggested that the presentation of imperceptible visual elicitors can lead to responses, such as skin-conductance and heart-rate, and facial-emotional, and participant behavioural and self-report changes without conscious awareness. In a series of experiments, we disproved this theory. We showed that individually-adjusted, truly imperceptible elicitors did not induce any of these changes, when using null-hypothesis-testing, and, furthermore, provided evidence for null responses, when using Bayesian analyses. We proceeded to a series of novel and exploratory experiments on unconscious theory. We tested whether behavioural and emotional responses were reported to precede conscious awareness using overt presentations of visual-emotional elicitors. We showed evidence that the experience of physiological-emotional responses was reported to precede conscious awareness of a perceived visual-emotional content. These early responses were automatic and involuntary; they did not involve or require conscious access, or accessibility, and deliberation, and could not be physiologically restrained by conscious instruction for inhibition. We proposed that responses that can be termed unconscious, but not subliminal, are preceding, spontaneous and conditionally uninhibited experiential components of exposure to perceived, but not imperceptible, emotional elicitors. We extended that they involve genuine evolutionary-survival and social-adaptation value, compared to so-called subliminal processes, because they enable spontaneously-occurring, and progressively-intentional and intended behavioural and emotional adjustments, and readjustments, and adapting refinements.

items.title: Awareness of textual constructedness: Readerly responses to multimodality in post-postmodernist fictions of the digital
items.abstract: This article addresses textual constructedness as a particular kind of foregrounding and focuses on the question of how readers deal with multimodality in post-postmodernist fictions of the digital (PPFDs). PPFDs are contemporary print fictions that imitate, incorporate and/or utilize digital media, and also display thematic concerns for the digitally mediated worlds in which they are set. Multimodal PPFDs combine prose segments with visual representations of emails, text messages, social media posts, memos, online forums, tweets, blogs or non-networked software (such as PowerPoint presentations). By triangulating three datasets (namely responses to open questions, Goodreads reviews and reading group data), we address the following interrelated research questions: (1) How does the awareness of textual constructedness manifest itself in readerly responses to multimodal deviations in PPFDs? (2) How can we account for the impact of researcher-led questions versus reviews written without any knowledge of the research project? (3) How does immediate versus delayed post-processing influence readers’ responses? (4) What are the effects of readers reading text passages versus full texts in their responses? (5) How do readers react to different degrees of multimodality in the texts? We show how multimodality acts as a form of literary self-reflexivity that foregrounds a text’s artificiality, provide evidence that readers notice the shifts between semiotic modes, and present a new typology of eleven distinct reading strategies for processing foregrounding in multimodal PPFDs based on empirical evidence. Overall we thus show what happens when readers become aware of shifts between semiotic modes and determine subdimensions of the awareness of textual constructedness.

items.title: Collaborative Hand Drawing to Conceptualize Usable Privacy and Security Research Problems: Students' Perspectives
items.abstract: In this paper, we explore students' perspectives on incorporating hand drawing to conceptualize usable privacy and security research problems. We surveyed 64 female students who participated in an in-class collaborative hand drawing activity to conceptualize usable privacy and security research problems as part of a group-based student research project on usable privacy and security in an information and computer security course for undergraduate students. Our survey responses suggest that students perceived the drawing exercise positively. That is, they found it helpful in several aspects, enjoyable, and they recommend it to other students taking the course. The students also said that they would like to have such an exercise in other courses, such as Principles of Human-Computer Interaction and Fundamentals of Data Networks. Only three students mentioned downsides of the exercise, namely doubts about their drawing skills. Our results provide useful insights for educators seeking to enhance the student learning experience.

items.title: Fazer o mal em nome do bem
items.abstract: Determinadas ações injustas são praticadas por pessoas que as compreendem como corretas, necessárias ou moralmente obrigatórias. A injustiça permanece encoberta para quem a pratica, embora possa ser reconhecida pelos atingidos ou por terceiros. O argumento aqui desenvolvido explica essa modalidade de prática do mal como um ciclo de três momentos. Influências oferecem um mundo interpretado; uma compreensão formada sob essas influências apresenta a violação de outra pessoa como proteção, reparação ou dever; a ação assim autorizada pode retornar como nova influência, que reforça a compreensão que a tornou possível. Uma compreensão formada pode passar a selecionar as fontes que admite, a prender-se ao pertencimento e à imagem de si do agente e a reinterpretar informações contrárias como confirmação da ameaça percebida. Três episódios documentados põem o modelo à prova: os ataques a hotéis de requerentes de asilo e a uma mesquita na Inglaterra após os assassinatos de Southport, em julho de 2024; a invasão do Capitólio dos Estados Unidos, em 6 de janeiro de 2021; e a invasão das sedes dos três Poderes em Brasília, em 8 de janeiro de 2023. Em cada um deles, os participantes invocaram um bem — a proteção das crianças, a defesa da constituição, a salvação da nação — para autorizar o dano contra pessoas que nada lhes haviam feito. O modelo é defendido contra quatro objeções e completado por um critério normativo que não depende da convicção do agente: a pessoa atingida continua sendo participante de uma condição compartilhada, e a consideração que lhe é devida não é cancelada pela discordância. Sobre essa base, a parte final propõe onde e como o ciclo pode ser interrompido: no momento da influência, no momento da compreensão e no momento da ação, com uma resposta penal que chega depois, permanece limitada e jamais reproduz a exclusão a que responde.

items.title: Quantifying ‘surprise’ in capuchin monkeys ( Sapajus apella )
items.abstract: Abstract Violation-of-expectation (VoE) events offer a fascinating lens into the intersection of cognition and emotion. Research suggests that, like humans, many animals are susceptible to VoE events in many physical domains, susceptibility typically assessed through behaviours such as visual and physical exploration of a stimulus. In humans, such susceptibility has been further documented through emotional surprise, such as delight following positive surprise and frustration following negative surprise. However, evidence in animals remains relatively limited. To address this gap, this study examined behavioural, cognitive and emotional responses of capuchin monkeys (Sapajus apella) to bait-and-switch VoE events of food items. Capuchins were chosen for this study not only for their exploratory and information-seeking behaviours, but also for known emotional responses to VoE events (e.g. frustration following inequity aversion). Contrary to prior research, this study found no evidence for violation susceptibility via behavioural, cognitive or emotional responses. Overall, such findings contribute valuable information to the VoE literature in primates regarding methodology and information salience, as well as underscore the current challenges of investigating emotional surprise in animals. Future research may benefit from establishing stronger expectations (e.g. more salient stimuli), to better investigate and quantify surprise to VoE events in animal species such as capuchin monkeys.

items.title: A Two-layer Annotation Scheme for the Pragmatic Analysis of the Passive
items.abstract: Abstract Current pragmatic research shows that structures such as the periphrastic passive influence the interpretation of utterance meaning, yet none specifies how linguistic structure gives rise to a given pragmatic effect. The existing body of literature remains mainly theoretical and descriptive rather than methodological. This study thus offers a replicable double-layered annotation scheme linking observable linguistic cues such as verb type, lexical polarity, oblique complement, and discursive stakes to interpretive pragmatic categories of agentive attribution and content framing. Inter-annotator agreement reached at least substantial levels across all categories (κ ≥ .60). Applying the framework to a corpus of periphrastic passives from a Corporate Social Responsibility (CSR) report, we show that content framing most frequently foregrounds positive company actions, consistent with the use of the periphrastic passive as a potential resource for managing agent visibility to project a more benevolent image of the company.

items.title: President on Honeymoon: Elections, Media, and the Winner–Loser Gap in Affective Polarization
items.abstract: Abstract Affective polarization has risen to concerning levels in the United States, and elections are among the events that most intensify it. Yet how election outcomes reshape partisan affect and whether they do so differently for winners and losers has only recently drawn scholarly attention. Using the pre- and post-election panels of the American National Election Studies for the seven presidential elections between 2000 and 2024, I measure the within-respondent change in affective polarization toward the presidential candidates and compare winners with losers. Winners become more affectively polarized after the vote, while losers become less so. Rather than reflecting embittered losers, this gap is driven by a presidential ''honeymoon'': both sides come to rate the newly or re-elected president more warmly, even as feelings toward the losing candidate scarcely move. The gap is concentrated among heavy consumers of traditional news but not among social-media users, and a three-election panel shows that the honeymoon is short-lived. Consistent with an emerging winner--loser literature, these findings suggest that elections open brief windows in which partisans grow more tolerant of the opposing side.

items.title: An investigation of novel population models to control aphid outbreaks via a data driven “adaptive” framework
items.abstract: The soybean aphid ( Aphis glycines ) is an invasive pest that causes severe yield loss to soybeans in the North Central United States. Its populations frequently exhibit multiple, unequal-amplitude peaks within a single growing season, a pattern that classical boom-bust models cannot reproduce. We investigate and develop a sequence of population models aimed at capturing this multi-peak behaviour while remaining biologically realistic and useful for pest management. We first show that the variable carrying capacity model (VCM), in which seasonally fluctuating host-plant quality drives a time-dependent carrying capacity, can generate multiple peaks but also admits finite-time blow-up, or population explosion, rendering it unrealistic for high colonisations. We propose an adaptive behavioural model with a density-dependent switch that preserves the multi-peak dynamics while guaranteeing bounded populations. Guided by empirical evidence that abiotic stressors such as flooding alter host-plant fitness, we further devise a novel model with time-dependent, data-fitted periodic plant fitness and aphid growth rate; we prove that it produces transient multi-peak oscillations, with no sustained periodic state. We assess all models against the Economic Threshold (ET) and Economic Injury Level (EIL), and a global Sobol sensitivity analysis identifies the parameters governing outbreak frequency. Across all models, simulated aphid abundances exceed the ET and EIL, indicating that control is required. Lastly, applications of these models to improving current pest management strategies are discussed. Our work provides a stable, data-informed, and biologically grounded framework for predicting aphid outbreaks and guiding management strategies.

items.title: Phenotypic diversity in sorghum [Sorghum bicolor (l.) Moench] landraces in Tigray, northern Ethiopia
items.abstract: Abstract In the present study, frequency distribution, Shannon–Weaver diversity index (H′), and multivariate methods were used to estimate and analyze the phenotypic diversity of 108 sorghum landraces growing in Tigray taking their districts of origin, geographical zones, and altitude classes into considerations. We discover that high and comparable trait distributions among the sorghum landraces. The H′ computed for individual traits varied from 0.33 for grain form to 0.99 for grain plumpness with a mean of 0.83, which reveals huge diversity within the landraces. The estimated H′ of each trait pooled over districts of origin, geographical zones, and altitude classes were high with an overall mean of 0.71, 0.74, and 0.70, respectively. The H′ pooled over traits within the districts of origin, geographical zones, and altitude classes were high with an overall mean of 0.71, 0.74, and 0.69, respectively. On the basis of district origin, the highest (0.84) and the lowest (0.46) H′ values were recorded for the Tahtay adyabo and Raya Azebo districts, respectively. When the geographical zones were considered, the highest (0.83) and the lowest (0.46) H′ values were recorded for the northwestern zone and southern zone, respectively. With respect to altitude classes, the highest (0.80) and the lowest (0.68) H′ value were recorded for 1001 m.a.s.l and > 1600 m.a.s.l, respectively. Disruptive selection is the most likely reason to maintain the huge diversity in the sorghum landraces. The treasure of diversity suggests the potential for exploitation in sorghum improvement and conservation programs.

items.title: Limits to adaptation: Agroforestry buffers but does not offset climate change impacts on maize yields in Dodoma, Tanzania
items.abstract: Abstract Agricultural productivity in the semi-arid region of central Tanzania is low and projected to further decrease due to climate change, exacerbating the already high levels of food insecurity among the rural population. Agroforestry is actively promoted in the region as an adaptation strategy due to its multiple biophysical and socio-economic benefits, but whether it can buffer future climate change impacts on maize yields has not yet been quantified. Previous modelling studies in central Tanzania focused either on maize monocropping or on agroforestry under current climate. Moreover, it remains unclear whether yield gains from agroforestry constitute genuine adaptation. Here, we show for the first time how a comprehensive evaluation framework can be used to disaggregate projected yield changes into four distinct indicators: climate change impact, agroforestry impact, agroforestry adaptation effect, and climate change impact with adaptation. The Agricultural Production Systems Simulator was used to simulate maize yields at six sites in Dodoma under current climate conditions and under a low- and a high-emission scenario (shared socio-economic pathways 1-2.6 and 5-8.5) for two periods centred on 2030 (2016–2045) and 2050 (2036–2065). Above-ground agroforestry effects were represented by 10% and 20% shading, associated temperature reductions, and tree litter input. Without adaptation, climate change is projected to reduce maize yields by 23–33%. Agroforestry increased yields under all climate conditions, and the agroforestry adaptation effect grew towards 2050, with 20% shade being most effective. However, the climate change impact with adaptation shows that agroforestry buffers but does not offset yield losses: under the high-emission scenario, yields remained below the baseline at both shade levels, with losses increasing towards 2050. These results demonstrate both the potential and the limits of agroforestry as an adaptation strategy in semi-arid Tanzania.

items.title: Role of aridity in shaping adaptive genomic divergence and population connectivity in a southern African rodent
items.abstract: Elucidating the drivers of evolution in dry environments is central to understanding how organisms respond to climate change. While research on the genomics of adaptation is growing, aridity-driven intraspecific divergence remains poorly quantified. Here, we address this gap by using genomic data from 230 individuals of the arid-adapted four-striped mouse Rhabdomys bechuanae, sampled across an aridity gradient in southern Africa, a region facing increasing aridification. Combining these data with palaeoclimatic reconstructions and present-day aridity indices, we investigate, from a spatio-temporal perspective, how intraspecific genetic variation relates to aridity. Inference of past effective population size revealed a sharp decline in the late Pleistocene, coinciding with regional aridification and potentially reflecting changes in connectivity during dry periods. Current population structure followed a pattern of isolation by distance and mirrored the aridity gradient. Genotype-environment association analyses identified single nucleotide polymorphisms and genes significantly associated with aridity and genetically differentiated among populations, with functions related to water and energy conservation-as expected under arid conditions-as well as neurotransmission. These findings highlight the underappreciated role of neurological processes in coping with water and resource scarcity. More broadly, our integrative genomics approach suggests that aridity shapes population connectivity and adaptation, with implications for climate resilience.

items.title: Synergy in viral–bacterial co-infection expedites algal bloom demise
items.abstract: Algal blooms are hotspots for diverse microbial interactions affecting bloom dynamics. Viral infections often regulate the demise of these blooms, recycling >25% of oceanic fixed carbon. Although these blooms collapse synchronously, only 10-30% of algal cells show active viral infection, suggesting additional mortality agents. Using microbial communities from natural coccolithophore blooms, we discovered that bacteria significantly enhanced virus-mediated algal mortality. We quantified this interaction using two novel metrics: the Synergy Index (SI) measuring viral-bacterial interaction strength, and the Benefit Index (BI) assessing changes in bacterial fitness. We identified Alteromonas bacteria as drivers of viral-bacterial coinfection, with consistently high SI and BI. In natural communities, Alteromonas exhibited chemoattraction towards infected algal cells, leading to their enrichment in bloom demise particles. This viral-bacterial synergy represents a previously unrecognized mortality agent controlling bloom termination, modulating the balance between the carbon-recycling viral shunt and the carbon-exporting viral shuttle pathways, likely influencing global carbon cycling.

items.title: Sacred waters, broken systems: community experiences of traditional water body renovations in Braj, India
items.abstract: Abstract Traditional Knowledge Systems and community participation have historically sustained water management practices across the Indian subcontinent for centuries. Communities developed sophisticated methods rooted in cultural practices while addressing practical requirements. However, colonial interventions and post-independence policies have systematically marginalised local knowledge and community participation in water management decisions. Replacing them with centralised technocratic approaches that prioritise technical efficiency over cultural continuity. In the Braj region of India, Traditional Water Bodies (Kunds) serve as both cultural anchors and ecological resources, embodying practical knowledge and spiritual meaning within sacred geography. Today, many of these Kunds are facing degradation due to pollution, encroachment, and state-led renovation interventions. That often destroys their essential socio-ecological qualities. This research investigates how communities remember and value traditional water management systems, navigate tensions between religious significance and physical degradation of transformed water bodies, and reveal unintended consequences of development interventions in culturally significant water systems. This study involves field observation, semi-structured interviews, and thematic analysis across the Braj region. This research documents the lived experiences of communities whose traditional water management systems have been altered by state-led development interventions. Findings reveal a fundamental contradiction between official narratives celebrating renovation success and communities' experiences of environmental and cultural degradation. The water that once embodied purity and reverence has become brackish and undrinkable due to deep boring accessing saline aquifers, yet communities continue performing ritual practices requiring direct water contact. Community memories preserve sophisticated ecological knowledge about natural water purification and adaptive management, but contemporary interventions prioritise standardised technical solutions while systematically excluding local knowledge from decision-making processes. This research contributes to understanding how high modernist development projects encounter and transform complex local systems, revealing gaps between development aspirations and everyday experiences of environmental change.

items.title: DNA barcoding of more than one million insect specimens indicates that at least one third of California's insect biodiversity remains undiscovered
items.abstract: Insects are the most diverse terrestrial organisms, yet they are underrepresented in large-scale conservation assessments. To address this gap, the California Insect Barcoding Initiative is developing a publicly accessible, statewide DNA-barcode reference library for California insects to support scalable surveys, establish baseline biodiversity measurements, and generate potential distribution maps that inform conservation planning. Specimens are collected with a hybrid strategy that combines standardized Malaise trapping, to enable replicable sampling, and opportunistic collecting, to maximize taxonomic coverage. To date, we have barcoded over one million specimens; preliminary completeness analyses suggest that current sampling captures roughly 65–69% of the fauna, implying a conservative minimum of circa 61,000 insect species in California. Using all sequenced specimen records, we generated rule-based spatial range interpolations constrained by ecoregion and vegetation type, and used these to infer spatial patterns in insect species richness across the state. We identify areas of both high and low potential species richness, with current peaks in the Southern California Mountains ecoregion and the Mojave Basin and Range ecoregion. Our species richness estimates and spatial patterns are explicitly provisional and are expected to evolve as sampling gaps are addressed. Finally, we make all sequence data, specimen images, and occurrence records publicly available via the Barcode of Life Datasystem. This ongoing effort constitutes the first large-scale DNA barcode-based survey for California insects, providing an expandable foundation for tracking temporal change, testing drivers of insect diversity, and prioritizing regions for conservation and targeted inventory.

items.title: Seagrass sediment organic carbon burial rates are globally significant
items.abstract: Abstract Crucial for coastal carbon sequestration, global seagrass organic carbon (OC) burial rates remain uncertain as early estimates were derived from mixed methodologies across geographically and taxonomically biased datasets. Here, we present a data-driven reassessment from a synthesis of 332 sediment cores spanning the last century. Results show that seagrasses bury OC at 25 ± 3 g OC m −2 yr −1 (geometric mean), with an area-weighted global average of 33 ± 9 g OC m −2 yr −1 . Rates reflect a balance between sediment OC content and sediment accumulation, which share a negative exponential relationship driven by mineral dilution. Based on a revised mapped seagrass extent (247,700–366,400 km 2 ), global burial scales to 6–15 Tg C yr −1 . Although one-fourth of earlier benchmarks, seagrasses account for 3–4% to 3–6% of total oceanic OC burial despite covering <0.1% of the seafloor. Combined with mangroves and tidal marshes, vegetated coastal ecosystems contribute 8–13% of oceanic OC burial.

items.title: Associations of endemic Anas wyvilliana (Koloa Maoli or Hawaiian Duck) are non-random but not influenced by plumage or genetic relatedness
items.abstract: Hawaiian duck, or koloa) is primarily threatened by hybridization with feral mallards and avian botulism outbreaks. We used capture-mark-recapture and genetic data on koloa on the island of Kaua'i, a stronghold of remaining koloa, to construct social networks and examine their associations (inferred from co-occurrence in traps) and spatial genetic structure. Information on associations might shed light on preferences for or against mallards and hybrids, and inform planned translocation efforts. Microgeographic spatial genetic structuring where relatedness among individuals scales with geographic distance is a potential liability for maintaining koloa genetic diversity, and would particularly be detrimental during highly localized outbreaks of botulism that could result in the removal of entire lineages. While we found persistent social associations among adult koloa, they were not apparently influenced by plumage traits or body mass, suggesting a lack of social preference for mallard-like individuals. Importantly, we found no spatial patterns of relatedness within the largest refuge. Therefore, botulism outbreaks remain a demographic threat but are unlikely to remove correlated genetic diversity. There were no sex differences in spatial genetic structure and both sexes moved within a refuge. The lack of spatial genetic structure and the presence of many unrelated conspecifics may enable koloa to limit inbreeding and retain genetic diversity without sex-biased dispersal. In the context of future translocations, our results suggest that translocating koloa captured in the same trap together will reduce disruption of preferred associations while also retaining genetic diversity among translocated individuals. LAY SUMMARY: The koloa maoli (Hawaiian duck, or koloa) is a federally-endangered, island endemic bird. Like other Hawaiian waterbirds, koloa are threatened by introduced predators and habitat loss, but also specifically by hybridization with feral mallards and localized avian botulism outbreaks. Currently, the island of Kaua'i has the largest population of non-admixed koloa. We used capture-mark-recapture and genetic data of koloa at two wetland sites on Kaua'i to examine their sociality and spatial genetic structure.Koloa formed preferential social associations, but they were not based on plumage traits, body mass or genetic relatedness.There was no spatial genetic structure for males and females within a wetland site. Our results suggested that 1) koloa have no preference for mallard-like plumage that might increase hybrid pairing, 2) localized (within-refuge) botulism outbreaks are unlikely to remove close relatives and unique genetic lineages, and 3) translocation of groups could maintain social associations without limiting genetic diversity.
